title: spec
text:
An agent that must call an HTTP API without a client library can fetch pages and run commands. Neither tells the agent what the API accepts. Without a description, the agent guesses paths and field names. A wrong guess can return a plausible 200 or an unhelpful 400.
Most public APIs publish a specification. A specification is a machine-readable document that lists every operation, its HTTP verb and path, and its parameters and their types. This module reads two families of specifications: OpenAPI (including Swagger 2.0 and Azure’s variant) and Google Discovery documents. fastspec parses a document into OpSpec records, one for each operation. Each record holds the verb, path, parameters, types, defaults and documentation. fastcore.apisurface turns each record into a Python signature such as list_repo_issues(owner, repo, state='open').
The result is the api tool group. Ramabana offers the group when it runs with --spec. The group has three tools. api_load reads a specification. api_ops lists its operations with their signatures. api_call calls one operation by name.

title: spec
text:
When to use a specification
A maintained client library is the better choice when one exists. A specification helps with internal services, clients that have fallen behind their API, and one-off endpoints. The web tools find a specification. web_search finds where a service publishes its document, and read_url reads its documentation pages.

title: spec
section: Why the host holds the specifications
text:
Why the host holds the specifications
A loaded specification stays on the host for the rest of the session. The agent can browse its operations again without fetching the document again. The state lives on the host. The terminal and the editor server share one implementation.

title: spec
text:
Reading a document
load_spec takes a URL, a file path, or a dict that is already parsed, and returns the document as a dict. It reads JSON or YAML. A URL is fetched with fossick, which comes with the [search] extra. A link to a file’s page on GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket is first turned by raw_url into the link to the raw file, since the page itself is HTML. parse_spec does the parsing, and when it is handed a web page instead of a document it says so and explains how to get the raw link.
parse_ops builds the fastspec parser for a document, choosing the Discovery or the OpenAPI reader by the document’s shape, and spec_ops returns the operations, at most MAX_OPS of them. norm_paths first merges Azure’s x-ms-paths into paths. op_row turns one operation into the dict that api_ops returns: group, name, verb, path, summary, signature, required parameters and a documentation link. Every failure raises SpecError with a message that says what went wrong.

Azure Blob Storage shows why norm_paths exists. Its Swagger 2.0 document leaves paths empty and declares its operations under x-ms-paths. Swagger 2.0 cannot list operations that differ only in their query string, such as /?comp=list and /?restype=service&comp=properties, under paths. A parser that reads only paths finds no operations.
nbs/fixtures/azure-blob-excerpt.json holds three of the original entries. The example runs without the network and finds six operations. When a path appears in both places, the entry under paths wins. The cell after the example checks raw_url on code-host links and checks that parse_spec refuses a web page.

azure = load_spec(Path('fixtures/azure-blob-excerpt.json'))
assert azure['swagger'] == '2.0' and not azure['paths'], 'the whole point: paths is empty'
assert len(azure['x-ms-paths']) == 3

ops = spec_ops(azure)
rows = [op_row(o) for o in ops]
assert len(rows) == 6, 'three paths, six operations, none of them under `paths`'
assert {r['verb'] for r in rows} == {'GET', 'PUT', 'DELETE'}
assert any(r['path'] == '/?comp=list' for r in rows), 'a query-only path survived'

# `paths` wins a collision
clash = dict(azure, paths={'/?comp=list': {'get': {'operationId': 'mine'}}})
assert norm_paths(clash)['paths']['/?comp=list'] == {'get': {'operationId': 'mine'}}

for r in rows[:3]: print(f"{r['verb']:6} {r['path'][:38]:40} {r['name']}")

PUT    /?restype=service&comp=properties        service__set_properties
GET    /?restype=service&comp=properties        service__get_properties
GET    /?comp=list                              service__list_containers_segment



test_eq(raw_url('https://github.com/stripe/openapi/blob/master/openapi/spec3.json'),
        'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stripe/openapi/master/openapi/spec3.json')
test_eq(raw_url('https://github.com/o/r/blob/main/a/b.yaml?plain=1#L4'),
        'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/o/r/main/a/b.yaml')
test_eq(raw_url('https://gitlab.com/o/r/-/blob/main/api.yaml'), 'https://gitlab.com/o/r/-/raw/main/api.yaml')
for u in ('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/o/r/main/s.json', 'https://api.example.com/openapi.json',
          'https://github.com/o/r', 'specs/local.yaml'):
    test_eq(raw_url(u), u)

test_fail(lambda: parse_spec('<!DOCTYPE html><html><body>hi</body></html>', 'that address'))

title: spec
text:
The host
SpecHost is a LocalHost that also holds specifications by name. It makes the api tool group available. api_load(src, name) reads a document and keeps it under name, or under its title when no name is given. It returns a short summary with the operation count and the groups. When the list is longer than one page, the summary also carries a note. api_names lists the loaded specifications.
api_ops lists the operations. group narrows the list to one group. match narrows it to operations that contain a piece of text in the name or summary. limit and offset page the list. api_count returns the total number of operations that a narrowing matches. api_call(operation, **params) calls one operation by its name, with the parameter names that its signature shows. When more than one specification is loaded, each of these methods needs name to say which specification to use.
headers go with every call to every specification. api_creds sets headers, such as an API key, for one specification only. The last example shows this.


source

SpecHost
def SpecHost(
    roots:tuple=('.',), # the folders the agent is confined to
    specs:NoneType=None, # name -> parsed spec, preloaded
    headers:NoneType=None, # sent with every API call
    creds:NoneType=None, # name -> headers, sent only to that spec
    timeout:float=60.0, # per-call timeout, in seconds
    max_ops:int=400, # rows per `api_ops` page; 0 for all
    *, ns:NoneType=None, # live namespace; fresh dict when None
    approvals:NoneType=None, # write approval handler
    note:NoneType=None, # status callback
    web:bool=True, # use fossick when installed
    index:bool=True, # start a Kosha sync for every open root
    graph:bool=False, # build Kosha's call graph during sync
    rerank:bool=True, # rerank Kosha hits with flashrank
    rerank_model:NoneType=None, # flashrank model; None uses its default
    memory:NoneType=None, # memory, ask and watch backend
    apis:NoneType=None, # API specification backend
    kernel:NoneType=None, # live kernel; None runs in process
    read_outside:bool=False, # let read-only tools name any path on this machine
    deny:tuple=('*/.ssh/*', '*/.aws/*', '*/.gnupg/*', '*/.config/gcloud/*', '*/.netrc', '*/.git-credentials', '*/.codex/auth.json', '*/.claude/.credentials.json', '*/.env', '*/.env.*', '*/id_rsa*', '*/id_ed25519*', '*.pem', '*.key', '*.p12', '*.pfx', '*.kdbx', '*.keychain', '*.keychain-db'), # what `read_outside` still refuses to open
    read_roots:tuple=(), # folders the read tools search and no write may touch
    tmux:NoneType=None, # None detects `$TMUX`; False off; True on; or this host's own pane (target or `Pane`)
    read_guard:NoneType=None, # `(ReadCheck) -> None | str | Refusal`: what the read tools may send
    model_local:NoneType=None, # `() -> (local, model)` for the turn's model
):

title: spec
text:
Examples
The examples build small specifications in the notebook. None of them needs the network. The first example loads a two-operation OpenAPI document and lists its operations with the signature that api_ops gives each one. It also shows the errors that occur when name is missing or names a specification that is not loaded.

SPEC = {'openapi': '3.0.0', 'info': {'title': 'Widgets', 'version': '1.2.0'},
        'paths': {'/widgets': {'get': {'operationId': 'listWidgets', 'tags': ['widgets'],
                                       'summary': 'Every widget',
                                       'parameters': [{'name': 'limit', 'in': 'query',
                                                       'schema': {'type': 'integer'}}]}},
                  '/widgets/{id}': {'get': {'operationId': 'getWidget', 'tags': ['widgets'],
                                            'summary': 'One widget',
                                            'parameters': [{'name': 'id', 'in': 'path',
                                                            'required': True,
                                                            'schema': {'type': 'string'}}]}}}}

h = SpecHost(roots=['.'])
loaded = h.api_load(SPEC, 'widgets')
test_eq(loaded['operations'], 2)
test_eq(loaded['title'], 'Widgets')

rows = {r['name']: r for r in h.api_ops(name='widgets')}
test_eq(sorted(rows), ['get_widget', 'list_widgets'])
assert 'id' in rows['get_widget']['signature'], rows['get_widget']['signature']
assert 'limit' in rows['list_widgets']['signature'], rows['list_widgets']['signature']
test_eq(rows['get_widget']['verb'], 'GET')
test_eq(rows['get_widget']['required'], ['id'])

test_eq([r['name'] for r in h.api_ops(match='one widget', name='widgets')], ['get_widget'])
test_eq(h.api_ops(group='nothing', name='widgets'), [])

h.api_load(SPEC, 'other')
test_fail(lambda: h.api_ops())
test_fail(lambda: h.api_ops(name='nope'))
print(rows['get_widget']['signature'])

get_widget(id: str)



A specification as a document
A real specification can hold hundreds of operations. That is too many to read as a list of rows. spec_markdown(host, name) renders a loaded specification as a reference page in markdown and returns (title, markdown). Each group has a ## heading, and each operation has a ### heading. Under the heading, the page states what the operation does, how to call it and which parameters it requires. The page uses the same rows as api_ops, and it uses all of them instead of one page. op_markdown renders one operation, and op_heading writes its heading.
Operation names are often lowercase, and some markdown readers handle lowercase headings badly. Group headings therefore start with a capital letter. Each operation heading is the verb and the path. This heading stays unique when several operations share a path. The parsed document keeps only its base URL and its operations. api_load saves the title, version and source in spec_info for this page to use.
The first cell below loads a 25-operation document into a host that shows ten operations per page. It checks the paging and the narrowing. The second cell renders a document with two groups.

BIG = {'openapi': '3.0.0', 'info': {'title': 'Big', 'version': '1'},
       'paths': {f'/g{i//10}/thing{i}': {'get': {'operationId': f'getThing{i}',
                                                 'summary': 'the last one' if i == 24 else f'thing {i}'}}
                 for i in range(25)}}
small = SpecHost(roots=['.'], max_ops=10)
info = small.api_load(BIG, 'big')
test_eq(info['operations'], 25)
test_eq(info['shown'], 10)
assert info['truncated'] and 'limit' in info['more'], info
test_eq(len(small.api_ops(name='big')), 10)
test_eq(len(small.api_ops(name='big', limit=0)), 25)
test_eq(len(small.api_ops(name='big', limit=5, offset=22)), 3)
test_eq(small.api_count(name='big'), 25)
test_eq(info['groups'], ['g0', 'g1', 'g2'])

test_eq([r['name'] for r in small.api_ops(name='big', match='the last one')], ['get_thing24'])
test_eq(small.api_count(name='big', group='g2'), 5)

whole = SpecHost(roots=['.'], max_ops=0)
assert 'truncated' not in whole.api_load(BIG, 'big')
test_eq(len(whole.api_ops(name='big')), 25)


ADMIN = {'openapi': '3.0.0', 'info': {'title': 'Widgets', 'version': '1.2.0'},
         'paths': {**SPEC['paths'],
                   '/admin/flush': {'post': {'operationId': 'flush', 'tags': ['widgets'],
                                             'summary': 'Empty the cache'}}}}
d = SpecHost(roots=['.'])
d.api_load(ADMIN, 'widgets')

assert not getattr(d.specs['widgets'], 'title', None)
test_eq(d.spec_info['widgets']['title'], 'Widgets')
test_eq(d.spec_info['widgets']['version'], '1.2.0')
test_eq(d.spec_info['widgets']['url'], '')
test_eq(SpecHost(roots=['.']).spec_info, {})

title, doc = spec_markdown(d, 'widgets')
test_eq(title, 'Widgets')
assert '## Admin' in doc and '## Widgets' in doc
assert '### GET /widgets/{id}' in doc and '### POST /admin/flush' in doc
assert 'Call it as `get_widget(' in doc and 'Required: id' in doc

d.spec_info.clear()
test_eq(spec_markdown(d, 'widgets')[0], 'Widgets')

test_eq(op_heading({'verb': 'delete', 'path': '/widgets/{id}'}), 'DELETE /widgets/{id}')

d.api_load(ADMIN, 'second')
test_fail(lambda: spec_markdown(d, ''))
print(doc)

paged = SpecHost(roots=['.'], max_ops=1)
paged.api_load(ADMIN, 'widgets')
assert spec_markdown(paged, 'widgets')[1].count('###') == 3

A SpecHost offers the three api tools. A plain LocalHost offers none of them:

from ramabana.tools import tools_for
names = {t.__name__ for t in tools_for(SpecHost(roots=['.']))}
assert {'api_load', 'api_ops', 'api_call'} <= names, sorted(names)
assert not {'api_load', 'api_ops', 'api_call'} & {t.__name__ for t in tools_for(LocalHost(roots=['.']))}
print(sorted(n for n in names if n.startswith('api_')))

['api_call', 'api_load', 'api_ops']


A Google Discovery document loads the same way. Its operations are grouped by resource, here buckets. Its base URL comes from baseUrl:

GCP = {
    'kind': 'discovery#restDescription', 'discoveryVersion': 'v1', 'name': 'storage', 'version': 'v1',
    'title': 'Cloud Storage JSON API', 'baseUrl': 'https://storage.googleapis.com/storage/v1/',
    'resources': {'buckets': {'methods': {'get': {
        'id': 'storage.buckets.get', 'path': 'b/{bucket}', 'httpMethod': 'GET',
        'parameters': {'bucket': {'location': 'path', 'required': True, 'type': 'string'},
                       'projection': {'location': 'query', 'type': 'string'}},
        'description': 'Returns metadata for the specified bucket.'
    }}}}
}
gcp = SpecHost(roots=['.'])
loaded_gcp = gcp.api_load(GCP, 'gcp')
test_eq(loaded_gcp['title'], 'Cloud Storage JSON API')
test_eq(loaded_gcp['operations'], 1)
gcp_row = gcp.api_ops(name='gcp')[0]
test_eq((gcp_row['group'], gcp_row['name'], gcp_row['path'], gcp_row['required']),
        ('buckets', 'get', 'b/{bucket}', ['bucket']))
test_eq(gcp.specs['gcp'].base_url, 'https://storage.googleapis.com/storage/v1/')
from fastspec.oapi import OpenAPIClient
assert isinstance(OpenAPIClient(gcp.specs['gcp'], sync=True), OpenAPIClient)



A key for one specification
Headers passed as headers go with every call. Credentials must not go with every call. One host can hold several specifications, and an Authorization header meant for one service would reach all the others. api_creds(name, headers) stores headers for one specification only. Calling api_creds with headers=None removes them. api_keyed shows which specifications carry credentials and the names of their headers. It never shows the values. In the example, only the client for rates sends the API key.

RATES = {'openapi': '3.0.0', 'info': {'title': 'Rates', 'version': '1'},
         'servers': [{'url': 'https://api.example.com'}],
         'paths': {'/v1/latest': {'get': {'operationId': 'latest', 'summary': 'Latest rates'}}}}

k = SpecHost(roots=['.'], headers={'User-Agent': 'ramabana'})
k.api_load(RATES, 'rates'); k.api_load(SPEC, 'widgets')
k.api_creds('rates', {'X-Api-Key': 'secret'})
test_eq(k.api_keyed(), {'rates': ['X-Api-Key']})

test_eq(k._client('rates', k.specs['rates']).transport.base_headers,
        {'User-Agent': 'ramabana', 'X-Api-Key': 'secret'})
test_eq(k._client('widgets', k.specs['widgets']).transport.base_headers, {'User-Agent': 'ramabana'})

assert not callable(getattr(k._client('rates', k.specs['rates']), 'latest'))
test_fail(lambda: k.api_call('nope', name='rates'), contains='no operation')

title: models
text:
CATALOG maps each provider to the model ids a picker offers without any network request, in display order.

claude is what Claude Code’s --model accepts: the tier names fable, opus, sonnet and haiku, which follow the newest model of each family, then the full ids.
anthropic is the same models through the Anthropic API.
openai and gemini are the models offered through those APIs.
codex is what Codex’s own picker lists.

claude_ids returns the full Claude ids without the tier names. claude_aliases maps each tier name to the last id of that family in CATALOG. A newer Opus added at the end of the family’s ids becomes the id that opus means.

title: models
text:
Live discovery
LIVE holds one function for each provider that can be asked for its models. The function returns the ids the provider lists. It returns [] when it cannot ask: no key, no file, no network, or an answer it cannot read. It never raises.

openai_ids asks OpenAI’s /v1/models with $OPENAI_API_KEY.
anthropic_ids asks Anthropic’s /v1/models with $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. It serves both anthropic and claude. Claude Code runs the same models.
codex_ids asks no server. It reads models_cache.json under $CODEX_HOME, which defaults to ~/.codex, where Codex keeps its picker list. It returns the entries marked visibility: 'list'. The test below writes a small cache file and reads it back.



source

codex_ids
def codex_ids():
What Codex’s own picker lists, from its models cache, or [].




source

anthropic_ids
def anthropic_ids():
Every id the current Anthropic key can list, or [] when it cannot be asked.




source

openai_ids
def openai_ids():
Every id the current OpenAI key can list, or [] when it cannot be asked.



import json, os, tempfile
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    cache = {'models': [{'slug': 'gpt-6-astra', 'visibility': 'list'}, {'slug': 'gpt-reserve', 'visibility': 'hide'}, {'slug': 'codex-auto-review', 'visibility': 'hide'}]}
    (Path(d)/'models_cache.json').write_text(json.dumps(cache))
    _old = os.environ.get('CODEX_HOME')
    os.environ['CODEX_HOME'] = d
    try: test_eq(codex_ids(), ['gpt-6-astra'])
    finally:
        if _old is None: del os.environ['CODEX_HOME']
        else: os.environ['CODEX_HOME'] = _old
    os.environ['CODEX_HOME'] = str(Path(d)/'nowhere')
    try: test_eq(codex_ids(), [])
    finally:
        if _old is None: del os.environ['CODEX_HOME']
        else: os.environ['CODEX_HOME'] = _old

title: models
section: What a live listing may add
text:
What a live listing may add
A provider’s listing holds everything it serves: dated snapshots, fine-tunes, realtime and audio models, embeddings, moderation, image and search models. A picker wants none of these. _current decides which listed ids a picker may show. It hides an id by the kind of model, not by generation. A new generation appears the day the provider lists it. _current hides ids that end in an ISO date, such as gpt-6-astra-2026-09-01. It keeps ids that end in an eight-digit date, such as claude-haiku-4-5-20251001. provider_models drops those from a live listing. It keeps one only when CATALOG already names it. Older chat generations (gpt-4*, gpt-3.5*, claude-2-* and claude-3-*) appear only with legacy=True. The cell below lists ids that _current keeps, ids it always hides, and ids it shows only with legacy.

for ok in ('gpt-6-astra', 'gpt-7', 'o5-mini', 'claude-fable-5-1', 'claude-haiku-4-5-20251001', 'gemini-3.5-flash'): assert _current('openai', ok), ok
for hidden in ('gpt-6-astra-2026-09-01', 'gpt-3.5-turbo-0125', 'ft:gpt-3.5-turbo-0125:org::abc', 'ada:ft-org-2023-04-06-20-44-19', 'gpt-realtime', 'gpt-6-audio', 'gpt-image-2', 'gpt-6-transcribe', 'tts-1', 'gpt-live-1', 'gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct', 'text-embedding-4', 'omni-moderation-latest', 'dall-e-3', 'whisper-1', 'davinci-002', 'babbage-002', 'sora-2', 'computer-use-preview', 'gpt-5-search-api', 'gpt-4o-search-preview', 'o3-deep-research', 'chat-latest', ''):
    assert not _current('openai', hidden), hidden
    assert not _current('openai', hidden, legacy=True), hidden
for old in ('gpt-4.1', 'gpt-4o', 'gpt-3.5-turbo', 'claude-3-5-haiku-latest'):
    assert not _current('openai', old) and _current('openai', old, legacy=True), old

title: models
text:
What a picker offers
provider_models(p) returns the list a picker shows for provider p. It starts with the CATALOG ids in their order. It then adds the ids from the live listing that _current admits and that do not end in an eight-digit date, newest first by version number. No id repeats. ramabana.core.probed remembers the live answer for five minutes. If the listing fails, the result is the catalog alone. A provider that is in neither CATALOG nor LIVE returns [].
The first cell below fakes an OpenAI listing. The second makes every listing fail. The third fakes Anthropic’s endpoint and shows that claude and anthropic share one request.


source

provider_models
def provider_models(
    p, legacy:bool=False, ttl:int=300
):
Ids a picker offers for provider p: the curated ones in their order, then what live discovery adds.



from ramabana.core import forget_probes
_orig = dict(LIVE)
forget_probes()
LIVE['openai'] = lambda: ['gpt-6-astra', 'gpt-6-nova', 'gpt-6-nova-2026-09-01', 'gpt-6-audio', 'gpt-4.1']
try:
    got = provider_models('openai')
    test_eq(got[:len(CATALOG['openai'])], list(CATALOG['openai']))
    test_eq(got[len(CATALOG['openai']):], ['gpt-6-nova'])
    test_eq(got.count('gpt-6-astra'), 1)
    assert 'gpt-4.1' in provider_models('openai', legacy=True)
    # newest first, by the numbers: alphabetical put gpt-6.1 after every gpt-5
    forget_probes(); LIVE['openai'] = lambda: ['gpt-5.1', 'gpt-6.1-nova', 'gpt-5.10']
    test_eq(provider_models('openai')[len(CATALOG['openai']):], ['gpt-6.1-nova', 'gpt-5.10', 'gpt-5.1'])
finally: LIVE.clear(); LIVE.update(_orig); forget_probes()


def _boom(): raise OSError('no network')
forget_probes()
LIVE.update({p: _boom for p in LIVE})
try:
    for p in CATALOG: test_eq(provider_models(p)[:len(CATALOG[p])], list(CATALOG[p]))
finally: LIVE.clear(); LIVE.update(_orig); forget_probes()
test_eq(provider_models('nobody'), [])


_n, _key, _lst = [], os.environ.get('ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'), _listed
def _fake(*a, **kw): _n.append(1); return ['claude-sonnet-6', 'claude-sonnet-6-20270101', 'claude-sonnet-5-5']
forget_probes(); os.environ['ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'] = 'k'; _listed = _fake
try:
    got = provider_models('claude')
    test_eq(got[:len(CATALOG['claude'])], list(CATALOG['claude']))
    test_eq(got[len(CATALOG['claude']):], ['claude-sonnet-6'])
    assert 'claude-sonnet-6' in provider_models('anthropic') and len(_n) == 1
    forget_probes(); del os.environ['ANTHROPIC_API_KEY']
    test_eq(provider_models('claude'), list(CATALOG['claude']))
finally:

title: models
text:
Through available_models
ramabana.core.available_models builds its hosted rows from provider_models. It includes a provider only when runtime_available and auth_status report that the provider can be used here. Each row has a value, label, provider and source. With a fake OpenAI key and listing, the OpenAI rows are the catalog followed by the one new model:

import ramabana.models as _m
from ramabana.core import available_models
_orig_live, _key = dict(_m.LIVE), os.environ.get('OPENAI_API_KEY')
forget_probes()
_m.LIVE.update({'openai': lambda: ['gpt-6-astra', 'gpt-6-nova', 'gpt-6-nova-2026-09-01', 'gpt-6-audio'], 'anthropic': lambda: [], 'codex': lambda: []})
os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY'] = 'sk-not-a-real-key'
try:
    rows = available_models()
    test_eq({tuple(sorted(r)) for r in rows}, {('label', 'provider', 'source', 'value')})
    openai = [r['label'] for r in rows if r['provider'] == 'openai']
    test_eq(openai, [*CATALOG['openai'], 'gpt-6-nova'])
    test_eq([r['value'] for r in rows if r['provider'] == 'openai'][0], 'openai/gpt-6-astra')
finally:
    _m.LIVE.clear(); _m.LIVE.update(_orig_live); forget_probes()
    if _key is None: del os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY']
    else: os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY'] = _key

title: peer_hooks
text:
Claude Code and Codex have no control socket, as Ramabana has. They run hooks: commands that the agent starts at fixed events. Every peer hook is one command, PYTHON -m ramabana.peer_hooks KIND EVENT. PYTHON is the full path of the Python that ran ramabana setup peers, so the hook does not depend on the ramabana that is first on PATH; an older ramabana there would read the words as its own options and fail. It reads the hook input as JSON on stdin and writes what the agent expects.
Hooks must be fast and must not break the agent. They make no model call and use no network. An error goes to hooks.log in the peers folder, and the hook then does nothing. A hook never exits with code 2, which blocks the agent, except the waiter when it has messages. The module does not load the agent code.

title: peer_hooks
text:
Adapters
An Adapter holds what is different for each agent kind: its config file, the file that gets the peer-work skill, the variable that holds its session id, and whether a hook can wake it. ramabana setup peers uses them to install the hooks.


source

Adapter
def Adapter(
    kind:str, config:str, skill_path:str, session_env:str | None, wakes:bool
)->None:
What the peer hooks need to know about one agent kind.


hook_block gives the hook entries for one agent’s config, by event. Claude Code gets a second Stop hook, the waiter: async runs it in the background, and asyncRewake lets its exit code 2 wake an idle session. Claude Code stops an asyncRewake hook at its timeout, so the waiter gets a long one. Codex has no way to wake an idle session, and it names its file edit tool apply_patch.


source

hook_block
def hook_block(
    kind
):
The hook groups, by event, that agent kind needs in its config.




source

hook_cmd
def hook_cmd(
    kind, event
):
The command that runs hook event of agent kind with this Python, whatever ramabana is first on PATH.


Each event has one group. Claude Code has two Stop groups; Codex has one.

b = hook_block('claude')
test_eq(b['PreToolUse'], [{'matcher': 'Edit|Write|NotebookEdit', 'hooks': [{'type': 'command', 'command': f'{sys.executable} -m ramabana.peer_hooks claude pre-tool'}]}])
test_eq([g['hooks'][0].get('asyncRewake') for g in b['Stop']], [None, True])
test_eq(len(hook_block('codex')['Stop']), 1)

title: peer_hooks
text:
What the agent reads
_messages writes unread messages for the agent with peer_text. An ask also says who decides. Outside work together mode, the agent must ask the user first. In work together mode with that sender, it can act without the user. The ask also shows the command that answers it, as PEER_RUN: the Python the hook runs under, with -m ramabana.peers. An older ramabana first on PATH may have no tell, so the agent does not depend on it. These lines come before the <peer-message> block, as peer_text puts them. In work together mode an ask also counts against the budget: one over it gets the reply refused: budget: ... at once, and the agent does not see it. Codex does not give its session id to commands, so its commands carry --session.

title: peer_hooks
text:
Session start
_start registers the session with the git root of its folder and the agent’s process id. Only a git root is guarded: a session started outside git, for example in your home folder, shows its folder but locks nothing. Then it tells the agent who it is, which peers are live, and how to send. The brief gives PEER_RUN once as the command to use for ramabana.

title: peer_hooks
text:
The user is back
When the user types, _ended ends work together mode. It returns the start time of a mode that ended since the user last saw one, also a mode that ended while the user was away. The end of a mode waits in the small file <key>.ended, and _ended removes it, so the user sees each end once. The hook reads only that file on each prompt, not the whole log; a report_shown row in the log keeps the record. _report_note gives the saved report, or tells the agent to make it.
Claude Code also sends prompts that no human typed through UserPromptSubmit: a background task’s notification, a subagent’s hand-back, and a message from another session. The hook input has no field that tells them apart from a typed prompt; it has only the prompt text. Claude Code opens each such prompt with a frame: a hand-back or a message from another session starts with Another Claude session sent a message: and an <agent-message> or <cross-session-message> block, and a notification starts with <task-notification>. _typed looks for a line that opens with one of these frames, so a typed prompt that only mentions a tag in its text still counts as typed. _prompt ends work together mode only for a typed prompt.

title: peer_hooks
text:
Stop and wait
_stop blocks the stop while messages are unread, so the agent goes on and reads them. The reason is the messages. It blocks only for new messages, so it cannot loop: each message is taken once, the hop limit counts, and Claude Code stops after 8 blocks.
_wait is the background waiter. Only one runs for each session: it holds a lock on the .wait file and writes its process id there. A second waiter exits at once. A lock dies with its process, so a crashed waiter does not block the next one. On messages, the waiter exits with code 2 and writes them to stderr, which wakes Claude. If it cannot write the messages it took, it puts them back in the inbox. It exits with code 0 when the session ends. When work together mode expires while it waits, it saves the report first.

title: peer_hooks
section: Session end and the folder guard
text:
Session end and the folder guard
_end removes the registration, so the waiter stops. It leaves the .wait file, because the waiter can hold a lock on it. Claude Code gives SessionEnd only 1.5 s, so it does nothing more.
_pre_tool finds the paths a tool call writes. Claude Code’s file tools give file_path or notebook_path. Codex’s apply_patch gives the patch, which names each file. folder_denial checks each path. A refusal names the owner, and the agent can send it a message instead.
A patch names files to add, change, delete and move to.

test_eq(_paths({'tool_name': 'apply_patch', 'tool_input': {'command': '*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: a.py\n*** Move to: b.py\n*** Add File: /r/c.py\n*** End Patch'}}), ['a.py', 'b.py', '/r/c.py'])
test_eq(_paths({'tool_name': 'Bash', 'tool_input': {'command': '*** Add File: x'}}), [])
test_eq(_paths({'tool_input': {'notebook_path': '/r/n.ipynb'}}), ['/r/n.ipynb'])

title: peer_hooks
text:
The entry point
peer_hook runs one event and returns the exit code, stdout and stderr. An error is logged to hooks.log and gives exit code 0 with no output, so a broken hook never stops the agent. main is python -m ramabana.peer_hooks, the command in the hooks; ramabana peer-hook, the command of older setups, runs it too. Wrong words or input that is not JSON are logged and give exit code 0, never 2. The event version prints the ramabana version, so --doctor can see which code the hooks run.


source

main
def main(
    argv
):
Run python -m ramabana.peer_hooks KIND EVENT on the hook input in stdin; the exit code, which is 2 only from a waiter with messages.




source

peer_hook
def peer_hook(
    kind, event, data, d:NoneType=None, cfg:NoneType=None
):
Run hook event of agent kind on the hook input data: (exit code, stdout, stderr); an error is logged and gives (0, ’‘,’’).


A stop with nothing unread lets the agent stop. A note makes it block, once. A write into another session’s folder is refused, and a write into the session’s own folder is not. A broken input is logged.

from ramabana.peers import Envelope, post, register
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as t, patch.dict(os.environ, RAMABANA_PEERS=t):
    s1 = {'session_id': 's1', 'cwd': t}
    test_eq(peer_hook('claude', 'stop', s1, cfg=t), (0, '', ''))
    post(t, 'claude-s1', Envelope('note', 'v2 is out', {'key': 'ramabana-r1', 'name': 'leela'}))
    assert 'v2 is out' in json.loads(peer_hook('claude', 'stop', s1, cfg=t)[1])['reason']
    test_eq(peer_hook('claude', 'stop', s1, cfg=t), (0, '', ''))
    register(t, 'codex', 'c9', ['/r/abhyasa'], os.getpid())
    peer_hook('claude', 'session-start', s1, cfg=t)
    deny = json.loads(peer_hook('claude', 'pre-tool', s1 | {'tool_name': 'Edit', 'tool_input': {'file_path': '/r/abhyasa/a.py'}}, cfg=t)[1])
    test_eq(deny['hookSpecificOutput']['permissionDecision'], 'deny')
    test_eq(peer_hook('claude', 'pre-tool', s1 | {'tool_name': 'Edit', 'tool_input': {'file_path': f'{t}/a.py'}}, cfg=t), (0, '', ''))
    test_eq(peer_hook('claude', 'stop', {}, cfg=t), (0, '', ''))
    assert 'KeyError' in (Path(t)/'hooks.log').read_text()

title: hl
text:
hl_text(code, lang, theme) colours a piece of code for the terminal and returns a rich.Text. theme is a Lumis theme name. HL_THEMES maps each palette name the terminal accepts to a Lumis theme name. For example, --theme nord colours code with the Lumis theme nord. hl_text returns code unstyled when lang is 'plaintext'.
scope_style(scope, theme) returns the rich style a theme gives one scope. It returns an empty string when the theme gives the scope no foreground colour. When the theme does not name a scope, scope_style uses the longest dotted prefix of the scope that the theme does name. For example, function.builtin falls back to function.


source


def hl_text(
    code, lang, theme:str='github_dark'
):
code as a rich Text, coloured by fastpylight with Lumis theme.




source


def tokens(
    code, lang
):
fastpylight’s tokens for code; none for a lang whose tokenizer panicked in this process.




source


def scope_style(
    scope, theme:str='github_dark'
):
The rich style Lumis theme gives token scope; the longest dotted prefix it names wins.


fastpylight counts positions in UTF-8 bytes. rich counts characters. hl_text converts between them, and each coloured span starts on the character where its token starts. rich rewrites a line ending such as \r\n to \n. The spans stay on their tokens after the rewrite:

t = hl_text('a\r\nb = 1  # one', 'python')
test_eq(t.plain, 'a\nb = 1  # one')
assert any(t.plain[s.start:s.end] == '1' for s in t.spans)
t

hl_toks(code, lang) returns the tokens as data instead: one list per line, each token a (start, end, scope) tuple in characters. Use it when you draw the code yourself. A token that runs across a line break, such as a triple-quoted string, is cut at the break and appears on both lines:


source


def hl_toks(
    code, lang
):
Per line of code, its tokens as (start, end, scope) in characters; a token crossing a line break is cut at it.



t = hl_toks('é = """a\nb"""', 'python')
test_eq(t[0][0], (0, 1, 'variable'))
test_eq([k for *_, k in t[1]], ['string'])

fastpylight raises RuntimeError when its Rust code panics, for example when the grammar of a language fails to load. Rust also prints a panic message to the terminal on that call, and again on each later call for that language. tokens adds the language to FAILED_LANGS and does not call fastpylight for it again. The language then shows as plain text, and the panic message prints one time. In fastpylight 0.1.19 the Swift grammar fails to load. Swift code then has no tokens, and a second call does not call fastpylight:

ls = hl_toks('let x = nil\nlet y = 1', 'swift')
assert all(ls) or ('swift' in FAILED_LANGS and hl_toks('let z = nil', 'swift') == [[]])
ls

An unknown language is a caller error. It still raises ValueError, and it does not go into FAILED_LANGS:

test_fail(lambda: tokens('x', 'nosuchlang'), contains='unknown language')
assert 'nosuchlang' not in FAILED_LANGS
FAILED_LANGS

title: hl
text:
Diffs
diff_rich(s, palette, theme) colours a unified diff for the terminal. It also colours a diffstat, the file | 3 ++- summary git prints, and returns any other text in gray. palette maps fg1, gray, red, green, aqua and bg0 to colours. File headers are bold, hunk headers are aqua, and added and removed lines get a background tinted 15% toward green or red. The code inside each hunk is coloured with theme in its own language. The old side and the new side of a hunk are each tokenized whole, so a string that spans several lines keeps its colour on every one. is_diff says whether a text holds a unified diff at all.
The same split is available as data. diff_toks returns one entry per line of a diff: the line’s tokens, or None for a line outside a hunk body, such as a header. hunk_toks does the same for one hunk body. diff_html renders each code line as HTML through toks_html, which wraps each token in a span whose classes are its scope and every prefix of it, as in hl-function hl-function-builtin, so a stylesheet that styles only function still colours it.
diff_lang picks the language of a hunk from the path on its --- or +++ line. A notebook’s diff holds the source of its cells, so a path ending in .ipynb reads as Python. So does a single cell, written nb.ipynb#id the way edit_cell writes it. Any other path takes fastpylight’s guess from the file name. The cells below check diff_lang, then diff_html on a small diff.

title: Theory
text:
This page is one of the five skills that ship with Ramabana. A skill is a piece of markdown that the agent reads when a task calls for it, so that the guidance costs nothing in turns that do not need it. The system prompt lists every skill the session found with a one-line description, the read_skill tool returns one in full, and /skill theory prints it in a terminal session.
The skill’s text is this module’s docstring. nbdev builds it from the description line above and the exported markdown cell below, and pyproject.toml registers the module under the pyskills entry point as theory, so any agent built on shalya can find it once Ramabana is installed. To change what the agent reads, edit the exported cell.
The agent reads this skill when the user asks about the Theory of a piece of software, in Peter Naur’s sense of the word.
Read this when the user says the Theory of something, or asks to discuss, find, or capture a Theory. “Theory” is Peter Naur’s programming-as-theory-building, in the sense this team uses the word.

title: Theory
text:
The Theory
The sense is Naur’s, from his 1985 paper Programming as Theory Building. A program is not its source code and not its documentation. It is the theory held in its builders’ minds. They understand how the code maps onto the world, why it took the shape it did, and how to extend it sensibly.
Consequences Naur draws:

A developer has to hold the Theory in mind, which means expressing it in its most minimal form. There is always time for details later. When discussing the Theory, conciseness is king. That does not mean excluding important details, and it does not mean giving the developer the illusion of control. It means iterating until the core that is true is found, and anchoring into that.
The Theory cannot be fully written down. Documentation captures artifacts of the Theory, not the Theory itself, which is why “just read the docs” never fully onboards anyone.
A program whose theory-holders have all left is dead, even if it still runs. Reviving it is closer to rebuilding than to reading.
Modification quality depends on the Theory, not the code. Someone holding the Theory makes changes that fit the program’s nature. Someone without it makes patches that gradually corrode the design.

title: Theory
text:
Using it
Working in an unfamiliar codebase, find the Theory first and read the code through it. Ask what facts or constraints drove it, how the design follows from them, and which alternatives the builders rejected and why. search_code finds the pattern. The Theory says why it is the pattern.
Reviewing a change, ask what Theory the change assumes and whether that matches the Theory of the codebase. A patch can be locally correct and still violate the Theory. Line-by-line review never sees that.
When the user says “the Theory of X”, they assume this vocabulary. Do not re-explain Naur. Discussing a Theory means talking it through in conversation. Do not turn it into a process, a checklist, or markdown files unless the user asks for a written artifact.
Stating or discussing a Theory, follow the write_prose skill closely. A Theory lives in minds, and its statement has to be plain enough to hold there.

title: cli
text:
This module applies two small fixes to teleprint when it loads. Each fix checks whether the installed teleprint already has it and does nothing if so. FRAME_PATCHED and INK_PATCHED are True when the module applied the fix.
The first fix concerns rows already written to the scrollback. Teleprint keeps a mark, _ws, of how many rows of the document it has committed to the scrollback. Each frame writes only the rows past the mark. Those rows are history in the terminal and cannot be taken back. When a tool result folds, the document gets shorter. Teleprint used to lower the mark to match, and the next frame wrote earlier rows a second time. A session with many folded calls had many copies of its startup banner. The fix never lets the mark go down.
The second fix adds a hook, Compositor.on_frame, which runs after each paint. Pictures need the hook, because a picture is placed on the screen after the text is drawn. The section on pictures below explains this. The module installs the hook before the mark fix. Compositor._frame.__wrapped__ is therefore the frame without the mark fix, and the test below uses it to show the duplicated rows.
from teleprint.testing import EmuTty as _EmuTty
async def _marks_over_a_fold(frame):
    "The ink mark after growth, after a fold, and after growing again, under `frame`."
    tty = _EmuTty(40, 8)
    comp = Compositor(tty); comp._register_signals = lambda: None
    await comp.start()
    comp.put('banner', Text('BANNER'), source='BANNER')
    tall = comp.put('tall', Text('\n'.join(f'line {i}' for i in range(20))), source='x')
    out = []
    frame(comp); out.append(comp._ws)
    tall.collapsed, tall.collapse_at = True, 1
    comp._dirty(tall); frame(comp); out.append(comp._ws)
    comp.put('again', Text('\n'.join(f'again {i}' for i in range(20))), source='y')
    frame(comp); out.append(comp._ws)
    tty.close()
    return out

_marks = await _marks_over_a_fold(Compositor._frame)
assert _marks[0] > 0, 'the document has to outgrow the window for anything to be inked at all'
test_eq(_marks, sorted(_marks))

if INK_PATCHED:
    _bare = await _marks_over_a_fold(Compositor._frame.__wrapped__)
    test_eq(_bare[1], 0)
    assert _bare != sorted(_bare)
_h_tty = _EmuTty(30, 6)
_h_comp = Compositor(_h_tty); _h_comp._register_signals = lambda: None
await _h_comp.start()
_fired = []
_h_comp.on_frame = lambda: _fired.append(_h_comp._cursor)
_h_comp.put('one', Text('one'))
test_eq(len(_fired), 1)
_h_comp.paused = True
_h_comp.put('two', Text('two'))
test_eq(len(_fired), 1)
_h_tty.close()
Ramabana gives shift+enter its own meaning: it starts a new line in the composer, and plain enter sends. Leela’s terminal and a default tmux never pass shift+enter on, so there it arrives as enter and sends. By default a terminal sends the same byte for both keys, so the program has to ask the terminal for richer key reports. There are two protocols for this:
The compositor asks for both, and each terminal answers with the one it supports. ext_key turns either report into the same Key the old byte parser would have produced. Once kitty’s flag is on, esc, control letters and alt letters also arrive in the new form. The decoder covers every key and follows these rules:
ext_keys_ok decides whether to ask. It returns True only when the compositor’s terminal and standard output are both real terminals. Tests and pipes never see the escape codes. The compositor turns the modes off wherever it hands the terminal back: at stop, at borrow when another program has the terminal, before a fatal signal, and while ctrl+z has the process suspended. A ctrl+z from the transcript view also leaves the alternate screen while suspended and returns on fg. Kitty keeps a separate flag stack for the alternate screen. The transcript view sets the flag again there and clears it before leaving.

text:
Blocks and keys
Every block has a kind, and each kind has its own gutter, the mark in the left margin. GUTTERS maps the nine kinds to their marks: user for your prompts (▌), step for the agent’s narration (┆), tool for a tool call (│), reply for the answer, ask for an approval question (◆), plan for the plan checklist (▸), note for a message from Ramabana itself (·), error (×), and media for a picture.
A turn is one prompt and everything the agent does to answer it. In the transcript a turn reads as a timeline in the order the work happened: a step block for each stretch of narration, a tool block for each call that narration introduced, and one reply block with the answer at the end. A tool block folds to one summary row. Narration stays visible. The answer always sits below the narration that led to it.
The cell below also defines the palettes. Each palette is a dict of colour names (bg0, fg1, red and so on) to hex colours. THEMES maps each theme name to its palette. set_theme(name) selects the active palette. auto picks light or github-dark by the terminal’s background: first the terminal’s answer to the OSC11 query, then $COLORFGBG, then github-dark. Every name in THEMES is a valid cli.theme in config.toml, and is_light says which palettes draw on a light background. GRUVBOX is a legacy name that always holds the active palette, whatever its theme. code_theme, hl_theme and code_bg return the matching settings for highlighted code. plan_text draws the plan checklist in the active palette.

text:
Attachments
A prompt can carry files: pictures, sound or text. In the terminal you attach a file in one of three ways. You can drop the file on the window, paste its path, or write @path in the prompt. All three make the same attachment. The path parser accepts quoted paths, paths in brackets, file:// URIs and backslash-escaped spaces. It leaves a plain sentence that mentions a path alone. The tests below check this.
A picture goes to the model as an image content part, the form a model API takes images in. Every attachment also carries its absolute path. The path works when the model cannot take the content part. A model without audio support, for example, can open a .wav file through the file tools.
The attachment helpers themselves, media_paths, Attachment, media_parts and the rest, live in ramabana.tools and are imported here so the terminal and the other frontends share one parser.

Pictures, drawn where the terminal can draw
A picture can reach the screen in two ways. The model can return one in Resp.media. A tool can also write an image file during the turn and report it through on_media. On a terminal without kitty graphics, the picture is saved and its path is printed. kitty_graphics decides which kind of terminal this is. It reads the environment variables in KITTY_ENV and the $TERM substrings in KITTY_TERM, and it accepts the $TERM_PROGRAM names in KITTY_PROGRAM. The KITTY setting overrides all three.
On a terminal with kitty graphics the picture is drawn in place. Kitty positions an image by screen cell, separately from the text. The compositor redraws its document with absolute cursor moves. An image cannot move with the text the way prose does. A Picture handles this in two steps. Picture.send transfers the image bytes to the terminal once. The block holds only the blank rows the picture will cover. img_cells sizes them from png_size. Picture.place then writes a short placement command at the end of every frame, at the current position of those blank rows. Each placement reuses the picture’s image id and replaces the previous placement. Repaints never stack copies. Every frame places the picture again. A picture the terminal cleared comes back on the next frame.
picture builds a Picture for a file. It returns None when this terminal or this file cannot be drawn. Only .png files can be drawn. draw_png is for code that has no frames to hook into. It sends and places a picture at the cursor in one call. media_line returns the transcript line for a saved picture.
Kitty also offers Unicode placeholders, which anchor the image to special characters in the text. Ramabana does not use them. Kaku and at least one other terminal ignore the U=1 flag and draw at the cursor. They print U+10EEEE as a missing glyph and leave a block of boxes behind the picture.

def kitty_graphics():
Whether this terminal speaks the kitty graphics protocol.



import os as _osr, struct as _struct, zlib as _zlib

def _a_png(w, h):
    "A real noise PNG, big enough to need several APC chunks."
    def chunk(tag, data):
        return (_struct.pack('>I', len(data)) + tag + data
                + _struct.pack('>I', _zlib.crc32(tag + data) & 0xffffffff))
    raw = b''.join(b'\x00' + _osr.urandom(3 * w) for _ in range(h))
    return (b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n' + chunk(b'IHDR', _struct.pack('>IIBBBBB', w, h, 8, 2, 0, 0, 0))
            + chunk(b'IDAT', _zlib.compress(raw)) + chunk(b'IEND', b''))


import os as _os
_seen = {k: _os.environ.pop(k, None) for k in (*KITTY_ENV, 'TERM', 'TERM_PROGRAM')}
try:
    test_eq(kitty_graphics(), False)
    test_eq(picture('/tmp/nope.png'), None)
    test_eq(draw_png('/tmp/nope.png'), '')

    import tempfile
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        png = b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n' + b'x'
        p = save_media({'mime': 'image/png', 'data': png}, d)
        test_eq(p.name, 'image-1.png')
        test_eq(p.read_bytes(), png)
        test_eq(p.parent.name, 'media')
        test_eq(save_media({'mime': 'image/png', 'data': png}, d).name, 'image-2.png')
        test_eq(save_media({'mime': 'image/avif', 'data': png}, d).suffix, '.avif')

    _os.environ['RAMABANA_KITTY'] = '1'
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        p = Path(d)/'a.png'
        p.write_bytes(_a_png(1200, 600))
        pic = picture(p, 24)
        test_eq((pic.cols, pic.rows), (24, 6))
        assert len(pic.send()) > 2 * APC_CHUNK
        test_eq(pic.send().count('m=0'), 1)
        assert 'a=t' in pic.send() and 'a=p' not in pic.send()
        test_eq(pic.place(), f'\x1b_Ga=p,i={pic.id},p=1,c=24,r=6,C=1,q=2\x1b\\')
        test_eq(len(pic.gap().plain.split('\n')), 6)
finally:
    _os.environ.pop('RAMABANA_KITTY', None)
    for k, v in _seen.items():
        if v is not None: _os.environ[k] = v

text:
The turn
A turn starts when you press enter on a prompt. run_turn runs one turn and streams it into the transcript. The agent’s stream is a blocking generator. It runs on a separate model thread, and run_turn reads its chunks from a queue. The event loop stays free to handle keystrokes, approval questions and activity updates while the model works.
Some prompts get a row of choices before the turn starts. A request such as “refactor the runtime” can mean “make the change”, “propose a plan” or “say what is in scope”. Finding out afterwards which one the model chose is costly. options_for checks the typed line against the trigger words in MENUS. It returns a title and a list of Options, or None. ChoiceMenu draws the row above the input line and handles the keys that move through it and pick one. Each Option has a suffix, an instruction that the turn appends to your prompt. The model receives the choice as part of what you asked for. REFACTOR is the only menu. The examples of the menu in use come later, under the surface.
close_done_shells closes the tmux panes of run_shell_bg commands that have finished. Their output stays readable through cmd_output.

title: cli
text:
The surface
Ui is the whole terminal surface. The rest of this page builds on it. It has three jobs. It paints the tail, the status bar and the input line at the bottom of the screen. It turns tool calls and approval requests into blocks. It decides what each keystroke means. on_key returns a coroutine for the caller to start (a turn, for example), the string 'quit', or None when the key was handled.
Every method on Ui is synchronous and does no terminal I/O of its own. The examples below drive it against an emulated terminal with no mocks. Activity and approval callbacks arrive on the model’s worker thread. Only the event loop thread may touch the compositor. _post hands those callbacks to the loop.
The class is long, and later cells add to it with fastcore’s @patch. The methods a caller uses most are submit for the typed line, say to print a block, note for a one-line message, stream for reply text as it arrives, and paint to redraw.


source

Ui
def Ui(
    comp, agent, loop:NoneType=None
):
The terminal surface: a transcript of blocks, a status bar, and one line to type in.


A line that starts with /name and is not one of the agent’s slash commands is looked up as a skill or a command file. Command files are markdown files in <cfg>/commands/*.md. When the project_extensions option is on, they also come from a root’s .agents/commands/. For example, /exhash fix the loop sends the prompt “fix the loop” with the exhash skill attached. It does not report an unknown command. In a command file, $ARGUMENTS is replaced by everything after the name, $1 to $n by its separate words, and each @path by that file when the file lies inside the open folders. A command file with subtask: true in its frontmatter is sent as a task for delegate_async, which runs it in a sub-agent.
While an approval question waits, y approves and n refuses. Lowercase a approves this request and every other request for the rest of the session. Capital A approves and adds a rule that always allows requests like this one. always_allow adds the rule when the approval gate can hold rules, and ask_pattern is what the rule matches. from types import SimpleNamespace

class _QueueWork:
    def __init__(self): self.closed = False
    def close(self): self.closed = True

class _QueueTask:
    def add_done_callback(self, callback): self.callback = callback
    def done(self): return False

class _QueueComp:
    def __init__(self): self.blocks, self.started = {}, None
    def drop(self, *keys):
        for k in keys: self.blocks.pop(k)
    def spawn(self, work, name):
        self.started = work
        return _QueueTask()

class _QueueUi:
    agent = SimpleNamespace(leftovers=lambda: [])
    _echo, _retract, _replay = Ui._echo, Ui._retract, Ui._replay
    _turn_over, start_turn, _next_queued, take_back = Ui._turn_over, Ui.start_turn, Ui._next_queued, Ui.take_back
    _queued_prompt = Ui._queued_prompt
    flash, mark_read, kind = Ui.flash, Ui.mark_read, Ui.kind
    def __init__(self, turn=None):
        self.comp, self.turn = _QueueComp(), turn
        self._queued, self._queued_echo, self._echoed = None, [], []
        self._steered, self._queued_typed = [], ''
        self._steer_drafts = {}
        self._queued_text, self._typed, self._prompt, self._flash = [], '', None, None
        self.buf = SimpleNamespace(text='', cursor=0)
        self.notes, self.painted, self.attachments, self.kinds = [], False, [], {}
    def say(self, body, kind='reply', **kw):
        block = type('Block', (), {'key': len(self.comp.blocks) + 1, 'body': str(body)})()
        self.comp.blocks[block.key], self.kinds[block.key] = block, kind
        return block
    def note(self, text, kind='note'):
        self.notes.append((text, kind))
        return self.say(text, kind)
    def paint(self): self.painted = True

Shell lines
A line that starts with ! runs as a shell command in the first open folder, with no approval question, because you typed it yourself. run_shell_line runs it. Its output prints as one block, followed by the exit code, and a non-zero exit code prints as an error. The model never sees the command or its output.
So that the model knows this exists, main adds SHELL_NOTE to an interactive session’s extra_sp, the extra text appended to the agent’s briefing, before a resumed session builds its briefing. The note tells the model it can ask you to run a command with !. A one-turn run from the command line never gets the note.
The command runs in its own process group with stdin from /dev/null, so a command that tries to read from the terminal gets end of file instead of hanging. Ui.shell_proc holds the process while it runs, which is how ctrl+c reaches it (see stop further down).

Folding
A block taller than FOLD (12 rows) starts folded. A four-hundred-line result takes one row until you open it. ctrl+o opens all the working of the latest turn, every step and call. A second press folds it again. alt+o does the same for every turn. alt+1 to alt+9 open a single entry, newest first. The main screen leaves the mouse to the terminal, and selecting and copying work as in any scrollback. In the transcript view, a block opens and closes under the block cursor or with a click.

A one-line block has nothing to fold, so toggling it does nothing and raises no error.

A tool call folds to its own summary line. It does not wait for FOLD rows. A turn of thirty calls reads as thirty lines, and you can open any one result with a keystroke.
_act decides the fold when the result arrives. Ramabana prints a tool block when the call starts, one row tall. When the call returns, it puts the result into the same block. Teleprint’s put folds a block once, when the block first grows past collapse_at. A call needs a different rule. _act applies _folded again when the result arrives.

While the reply is still arriving its block is tagged reply. /copy copies the final answer; the tool calls are the foldable trace above it.

class _FakePlan:

A delegation is a call where the agent hands a question to a sub-agent. It shows as one entry with the sub-agent’s calls grouped under it. A sub-agent is a second agent that the main agent starts for a piece of work, here through delegate_search. It uses the same recorded tool wrappers as its caller, and its calls arrive in the same Activity feed. Each call has a parent_action_id. Agent sets it from a per-thread stack of the delegate calls in flight. Ui uses it to put the call under its parent. Without the grouping, the calls of several sub-agents would appear among the caller’s own calls.
_folded decides whether a call folds. A finished call that succeeded folds to its summary when it has sub-agent calls or when opens is false for it (see above). A failed call never folds. A running call folds only while FOLD_RUNNING is True and the call has no sub-agent calls. drillable lists the turn’s foldable calls, newest first. drill(n) opens or folds the nth of them. alt+1 to alt+9 call drill.

parent = tl_acts.start('delegate_search', {'question': 'who reads the threshold?'})

title: cli
text:
Copying and browsing
There are two ways to copy out of the transcript, and both use the system clipboard. On the main screen the mouse belongs to the terminal. You select and copy as in any scrollback. The transcript view, opened with ctrl+r or up, takes the mouse only while it is open (enter_transcript and leave_transcript). /copy and the view’s y key send the text over OSC 52, a terminal escape code for setting the clipboard, which works through ssh and tmux.
/copy and the y key copy a block’s source text, not what is drawn. The source is the Markdown the model wrote, or the arguments a tool got. Text taken off the screen would be wrapped at the terminal’s width, indented by the gutter and missing the code fences. Every block therefore records its source when it is printed. transcript.block_text returns it, as the examples show.
The last three examples attach files: attach adds a picture once and refuses a duplicate, paste turns a pasted path into an attachment, and submit sends the attachments with the prompt and clears them.

md = 'Here is the fix.\n\n```python\nthreshold = 42\n```\n\nCall it from `runtime.py`.'
rblk = ui.stream(None, md[:20])
rblk = ui.stream(rblk, md[20:])
test_eq(ui.transcript.block_text(rblk), md)
rendered = '\n'.join(''.join(s.text for s in l) for l in comp._content_lines(rblk))
assert '```' not in rendered
assert '```python' in ui.transcript.block_text(rblk)


u = ui.say(Text('where is the threshold?'), 'user')
test_eq(ui.transcript.block_text(u), 'where is the threshold?')
wrapped = ui.say('x' * 200, 'note')
test_eq(ui.transcript.block_text(wrapped), 'x' * 200)
test_eq(wrapped.height > 1, True)
ui.copy_last('reply')


ui.enter_transcript()
test_eq((ui.transcript.active, ui.transcript.follow), (True, True))
ui.say(Text('search_code("threshold") landed while browsing'), 'tool')
assert 'landed while browsing' in tty.term.text()
sblk = ui.stream(None, 'and a reply streamed ')
sblk = ui.stream(sblk, 'in behind it')
ui.touch(now=True)
assert 'in behind it' in tty.term.text()
ui.transcript.move(-1)
test_eq(ui.transcript.follow, False)
ui.leave_transcript()
test_eq((ui.transcript.active, comp.paused), (False, False))


ui.attach(shot); ui.attach(shot); ui.attach(snd_path)
test_eq([a.name for a in ui.attachments], ['shot.png', 'note.wav'])
assert 'shot.png' in ui.attach_row().plain
ui.detach('2')
test_eq([a.name for a in ui.attachments], ['shot.png'])
ui.detach(); ui.detach()
ui.attach(media_dir / 'gone.png')
test_eq(len(ui.attachments), 0)
test_eq(ui.attach_row(), None)

test_eq([a.name for a in ui.attachments], ['shot.png'])
test_eq(ui.buf.text, '')
ui.paste('and this is ordinary text')
test_eq(ui.buf.text, 'and this is ordinary text')
long_text = 'copied text ' * 100 + 'image.png'
ui.paste(long_text)
test_eq(ui.buf.text, 'and this is ordinary text' + long_text)

test_eq(ui.attachments, [])

title: cli
text:
Approvals in a terminal
An approval is the question Ramabana asks before a tool with an effect runs: a file write, a shell command, a git commit and so on. The approval gate, Approvals, holds the model’s worker thread until a person answers. The request arrives on that thread and the answer comes from the event loop thread. While a question waits, the input line is where you answer it: y, n, a for the rest of the session, or n: followed by a reason.
Here a write is requested from another thread, the way a tool call does it:

tty2 = EmuTty(72, 12)
comp2 = Compositor(tty2)
comp2._register_signals = lambda: None
await comp2.start()
gated, _ = fake_agent(replies=['done'])
gated.approvals = Approvals(tools=WRITE_TOOLS, host=gated.host)
ui2 = Ui(comp2, gated)
comp2.on_key = ui2.on_key
ui2.paint()
threading.Thread(target=lambda: gated.approvals.request(
    'create_file', {'path': '/proj/notes.md', 'text': '# notes\n'}), daemon=True).start()
await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
print(tty2.term.text())

The question block shows what you need to decide: the path, whether the write overwrites a file, and the start of what would be written. The input line now holds the approval question.

test_eq(ui2.ask.tool, 'create_file')
tty2.term.text().splitlines()[-1]

parse_answer reads a typed answer. A line that is not an answer, such as a prompt typed at the wrong moment, does not count as a refusal. The question is shown again with a hint and keeps waiting. A waiting question also shows itself again every REASK_EVERY seconds.

test_eq([parse_answer(t) for t in ('y', 'YES', 'n', 'no: too broad', 'n:', 'continue.', 'y: and add a test', 'approve', 'deny', 'ok')],
        [(True, ''), (True, ''), (False, ''), (False, 'too broad'), (False, ''), None, (True, 'and add a test'), (True, ''), (False, ''), None])

ui2.buf.insert('continue.')
ui2.on_key(Key('enter'))
assert ui2.ask is not None and ui2.ask.pending
test_eq(ui2.buf.text, '')

rang = []
_write = tty2.write
tty2.write = lambda s: rang.append(s) if s == '\a' else _write(s)
ui2._asked_at -= REASK_EVERY; ui2._key_at -= BELL_IDLE + 1
test_eq(ui2.nudge(), True)
test_eq(rang, ['\a'])
test_eq(ui2.nudge(), False)

ui2.buf.insert('n: beca')
ui2._asked_at -= REASK_EVERY; ui2._key_at = time.monotonic()
test_eq(ui2.nudge(), False)
test_eq((ui2.buf.text, rang), ('n: beca', ['\a']))
ui2._asked_at -= REASK_EVERY; ui2._key_at -= BELL_IDLE + 1
test_eq(ui2.nudge(), False)
test_eq((ui2.buf.text, rang), ('n: beca', ['\a', '\a']))
ui2.buf.clear()
tty2.write = _write

The question takes the input line, so what you type is read as the answer and never sent to the model.
y and a answer at once when nothing has been typed. n waits for enter, and a reason can follow it. n and enter refuses. n: put it in docs/ instead refuses with that reason, and the model receives the reason instead of the word “denied”.

comp2.on_bytes(b'n: put it in docs/ instead')
tty2.term.text().splitlines()[-1]


comp2.on_bytes(b'\r')
await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
ui2.ask, gated.approvals.history[-1].reply()

There are two histories, kept apart. The composer keeps your past prompts, and teleprint’s blocks are the history of the transcript. up and down recall a past prompt only when the cursor cannot move further inside a prompt of several lines. ctrl+r opens teleprint’s transcript view, where you can search old blocks, open them and copy them.

test_eq(bool(gated.approvals.history[-1]), False)
test_eq(tty2.term.text().splitlines()[-1], '▌')
[ui2.kind(b) for b in comp2.blocks.values()][-2:]

a approves the current request and sets the approval mode to auto for the rest of the session.

threading.Thread(target=lambda: gated.approvals.request('create_file', {'path': '/proj/b.md'}), daemon=True).start()
await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
comp2.on_bytes(b'a')
await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
gated.approvals.mode, gated.approvals.history[-1].note

Commands
The agent answers slash commands such as /model, /tools and /cost. The terminal does not. Each command has one implementation, and every frontend shares it. The terminal answers /help itself, because the keys it describes belong to the terminal. An unknown command prints an error block.

ui.buf.insert('/tools')
ui.submit()
[l for l in str(comp.blocks[max(comp.blocks)].body[0]).splitlines()[:4]]


ui.buf.insert('/nope')
test_eq(ui.submit(), None)
ui.kind(comp.blocks[max(comp.blocks)])

Commands are recognised before the options row, so /tools refactor runs the command and opens no menu.

ui.buf.insert('/tools refactor')
test_eq(ui.submit(), None)
test_eq(ui.menu, None)
ui.kind(comp.blocks[max(comp.blocks)])

An empty line does nothing; no empty turn goes to the model.

test_eq(ui.submit(), None)
ui.buf.text

title: cli
text:
Running it
mk_agent from ramabana.agent builds what the terminal runs. It makes a WorkspaceHost over the folders named on the command line, an Agent over that host, and an approval gate connected to both. A host is the object that supplies the agent’s tools and decides what they may touch: which folders, whether the network is reachable, and which writes need approval. mk_host builds the host alone. amain is the terminal loop that runs the Ui.
The prompt appears before the model is ready. begin builds the system prompt and tools and starts the model on a thread. The status bar says starting model… until the model is ready. A line sent before the model is up waits in the queue, like a line sent during a turn. It runs when the model is ready.
start_agent starts the turn model and then the code index, the search index behind search_code. The index never delays the model. sync_index decides whether the index needs rebuilding. It rebuilds when a package or an open folder changed since the last good build. Otherwise it reopens the saved index. It logs which one it did to <cfg>/kosha.log. warm_up runs start_agent off the loop with off_loop. It prints a note that gives the reason when no model starts.


source

Ui.begin
def begin():
Start the model behind the prompt; lines sent meanwhile wait in the queue.




source

Ui.warm_up
async def warm_up():
Start the model off the loop; a start that fails says why in a note.




source

off_loop
async def off_loop(
    fn
):
fn() on a daemon thread, so quitting never waits for it.




source

start_agent
def start_agent(
    agent, closed:function=<lambda>, note:NoneType=None
):
Try the turn model, then start the code index search reads, whether the model came up or not; the backend, or None with agent.note saying why.




source

sync_index
def sync_index(
    host, cfg:NoneType=None, dirs:NoneType=None
):
Sync the code index when a package or root changed since the last good sync, else reopen it; run or skip, logged to <cfg>/kosha.log.


amain is the interactive loop. It uses one terminal, one event loop and one owner of the keyboard. It starts the compositor and connects keys, pastes, resizes and mouse events to the Ui. It starts the model with begin. On exit it restores the terminal and shuts down the agent.
Three helpers keep a broken terminal from breaking the session. AppTty is teleprint’s RealTty with two changes. A write waits for a full terminal to drain and sends the whole frame. When the terminal hangs up, reading stops and writes are dropped, and the session quits instead of spinning. loop_error shows an exception from a key handler or a posted notice as an error in the session. stderr_to sends Python’s stderr to a file while the screen belongs to the compositor. A warning written straight to the terminal would scroll the transcript under the compositor’s frames. stderr_to also points faulthandler at that file, and a hard crash leaves its stack trace there. stderr_log names the file, inside the session’s own run folder.
For --resume, pick_session lists the newest saved sessions and asks which to open. show_resumed draws the last RESUME_SHOWN turns of the reopened session before the first prompt.


source

amain
async def amain(
    agent, hint:str='', bell:bool=True, pane:str='auto',
    resumed:bool=False, # draw the resumed session's turns before the first prompt
    first:str='', # what the session says before anything else: the welcome, or the model it moved to
    cold:bool=False, # no model runs here, so none is warmed
    hints:bool=True, # the hint row under the status bar
    tips:bool=True, # the tip under the working rows
    theme:str='auto', # `auto` asks the terminal for its background before the first frame
):
The tty loop: one terminal, one event loop, one keyboard owner.




source

can_ask_background
def can_ask_background():
Whether to ask the terminal for its background: stdin and stdout are a terminal, and not under tmux, whose answer need not be the outer terminal’s.




source

query_background
async def query_background(
    comp, timeout:float=0.2
):
The terminal’s reply to OSC11, read through comp‘s parser; b’’ when nothing answers within timeout seconds.




source

Ui.show_resumed

    n:int=10
):
Draw the resumed session’s last n turns: each request, what was sent during it, and its reply.




source

loop_error
def loop_error(
    ui
):
An event-loop exception handler that keeps asyncio’s report in stderr.log and shows the error in the session, which carries on.




source

pick_session

    agent, all_folders:bool=False, # list every folder's sessions, not only those that ran in these folders
    ask:function=_no_stdin, out:builtin_function_or_method=print, n:int=20

The id of the saved session the person picks from the newest n, or ’’ for a new session.




source

    agent

Where a session’s stderr goes: its own run folder, so the next start cannot overwrite a crash’s trace.




source

stderr_to

    path
):
Append Python’s sys.stderr and faulthandler crash traces to path while the TUI owns the screen.




source

AppTty
def AppTty():
RealTty that waits out a full terminal, and stops reading and drops writes once it hangs up.


A terminal that another process left non-blocking takes only part of a large frame. It then refuses the next write until it drains. AppTty waits for it and writes the rest. Only a real hangup marks the terminal gone. A gone terminal freezes the screen and quits the session on the next key:

import pty, types
def _drain(m, got, n):
    while sum(map(len, got)) < n: got.append(os.read(m, 1 << 16))

def _pty():
    m, s = pty.openpty()
    a = termios.tcgetattr(s); a[1] &= ~termios.OPOST; termios.tcsetattr(s, termios.TCSANOW, a)
    os.set_blocking(s, False)
    t = object.__new__(AppTty); t.fd = s
    return m, s, t

out, wait = sys.__stdout__, WRITE_WAIT
m, s, t = _pty()
sys.__stdout__ = types.SimpleNamespace(fileno=lambda: s, flush=lambda: None)
try:
    got = []
    th = threading.Thread(target=_drain, args=(m, got, 400_000), daemon=True); th.start()
    t.write(b'a' * 200_000); t.write('b' * 200_000)
    th.join(5)
    assert not (t.gone or t.dropped)
    test_eq(b''.join(got), b'a' * 200_000 + b'b' * 200_000)
    test_eq(t.read(timeout=0), b'')
    assert not t.gone
    WRITE_WAIT = 0.05
    t.write(b'x' * 200_000); t.write(b'y' * 200_000)
    assert t.dropped and not t.gone
    os.close(m)
    t.write(b'after the hangup')
    assert t.gone
finally: sys.__stdout__, WRITE_WAIT = out, wait
os.close(s)

An exception from a key handler or a notice posted from another thread reaches the event loop’s exception handler, which shows it as an error and leaves the session running:

import io
class _Ui:
    closed, painted, notes = False, 0, []
    def note(self, text, kind='note'): self.notes.append((text, kind))
    def paint(self): self.painted += 1

async def _raises():
    u, loop = _Ui(), asyncio.get_running_loop()
    loop.set_exception_handler(loop_error(u))
    def bad(): raise ValueError('a key handler broke')
    loop.call_soon(bad)
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    loop.set_exception_handler(None)
    return u

with contextlib.redirect_stderr(io.StringIO()) as err: u = await _raises()
test_eq(u.notes[0][1], 'error')
assert 'a key handler broke' in u.notes[0][0] and u.painted == 1 and 'a key handler broke' in err.getvalue()

read_outside and vault stay off in the function signature. The positive flags remain available to scripts that do not read config.toml. The check below reads the exported entry point.

import inspect
import ramabana.cli as _cli_defaults
from fastcore.script import anno_parser

The parser keeps the positive flags available while both function defaults stay off:

_signature_defaults = inspect.signature(_cli_defaults.main.__wrapped__).parameters
assert _signature_defaults['read_outside'].default is False
assert _signature_defaults['vault'].default is False
_script_flags = anno_parser(_cli_defaults.main.__wrapped__, pos=['prompt']).parse_args(['--read-outside', 'x'])
test_eq((_script_flags.read_outside, _script_flags.prompt), (True, 'x'))
(_script_flags.read_outside, _script_flags.vault)

The agent the terminal gets is a real one, over real folders, with writes behind the approval gate. approve='none' builds it with no gate at all:

tempdir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
cli_agent, cli_host = mk_agent([tempdir], approve='ask', web=False)
cli_host.roots, sorted(WRITE_TOOLS & set(t.__name__ for t in cli_agent.tools))


test_eq(cli_agent.approvals.mode, 'ask')
test_eq(cli_agent.approvals.timeout, None)
test_eq(mk_agent([tempdir], approve='none')[0].approvals, None)
cli_agent.routing.name_for()

Without a terminal, ramabana runs one turn, which suits a pipe or a script. main is the entry point behind the ramabana command. It parses the options, builds the agent with mk_agent, and then either runs one turn with ask_once or starts the interactive session with amain. headless_prompt picks the one-turn prompt: the argument, or stdin when the argument is - or empty and stdin is a pipe. host_kw holds the host options the terminal adds. Outside tmux, an interactive session first starts itself again inside a tmux server of Ramabana’s own, as setup explains.


source

ask_once
def ask_once(
    agent, prompt, as_json:bool=False
):
Run one turn without a terminal and return the exit code.




source

headless_prompt
def headless_prompt(
    prompt
):
The one-shot prompt: the argument, or stdin for - or an empty piped run.




source

main
def main(
    prompt:str='', # one turn and exit; omit for interactive
    root:str='.', # comma-separated folders: .,~/notes,/srv/app
    model:str=None, # turn model; omit for the routing default
    approve:str='ask', # ask | edits | auto | off | none (no gate)
    web:bool=True, # --no-web takes the web tools offline
    read_outside:bool=False, # reads reach any path; writes need --root
    subagent_writes:bool=True, # --no-subagent-writes restricts delegates to read-only tools
    vault:bool=False, # vishalakshi vault for reads
    pii:str='off', # off | redact | refuse PII from the vault, and from shell, Python and web reads a hosted model gets
    pii_ner:bool=False, # --pii also gates titled names
    spec:bool=False, # enable OpenAPI, Azure and Google Discovery tools
    theme:str='auto', # auto follows the terminal's background; /theme lists the palettes
    max_tool_calls:str='auto', # auto | 20..400 tool calls per turn
    max_steps:str='auto', # auto | 8..80 model/tool-loop steps per turn
    max_cost:float=None, # stop the turn once it has cost this many dollars
    cfg:str='~/.config/ramabana', # config dir: skills, extensions, resumable history
    resume:str='', # saved session id/prefix, or 'latest'; bare --resume lists this folder's sessions to pick from
    all_folders:bool=False, # with a bare --resume, list sessions from every folder
    json:bool=False, # with a prompt: print the full result as JSON
    bell:bool=True, # --no-bell silences turn-end and approval bells

Ui.stop
def stop():
Escalate repeated Ctrl-C from cancellation to termination to exit.


stop is what ctrl+c does, and repeated presses escalate. During a turn, the first press cancels the turn’s run, the second terminates it, and the third quits; presses count as repeats only while they come within the agent’s cancel_grace seconds of each other. Each press also takes queued lines back into the composer, so nothing you typed is lost.
For a ! command, stop signals the command’s process group. The first ctrl+c sends SIGINT, and the next sends SIGKILL, however long after the first it comes. A command ended by a signal prints stopped, and the prompt is free once the process exits. Quitting kills a command that is still running.
on_key is patched once more so that ctrl+c stops a turn without clearing the composer, and alt+up pulls queued text back into the composer for editing.

    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
assert armed.exists()
sh_ui.stop()
await asyncio.sleep(0.6)   # longer than `cancel_grace`, and the command ignores SIGINT
test_eq(sh_running.done(), False)
sh_ui.stop()
await asyncio.wait_for(sh_running, 5)
sh_comp.stop()
test_eq((sh_ui.turn, sh_ui.shell_proc), (None, None))
sh_last = sh_ui.transcript.block_text(list(sh_comp.blocks.values())[-1])

title: cli
text:
The now pane
The now pane is a small live view, in a tmux split beside the chat, of what the main agent and each sub-agent are doing at this moment: the turn, the call it is on, and each sub-agent run with its own calls. The surface writes a snapshot, now_snapshot, to <runs_dir>/now.json from its own loop: at most every PANE_EVERY seconds while calls change or a turn runs, and once more when the turn ends. ramabana-pane, from pane, reads that file and draws it.

/pane opens it with open_pane and /pane off closes it with close_pane.
--pane auto|on|off decides whether a session starts with it, through start_pane; auto opens it only inside tmux.
pane_cmd is the shell line that runs the viewer for a given file.

When the viewer crashes rather than quits, the surface reopens it, a limited number of times.
