title: cli
text:
Peers
Each terminal session listens on a control socket from ramabana.control, so another session can steer it, prompt it and read its events. amain starts it with start_control once the Ui exists, and closes it however the session ends. The session writes its events to EVENT_FILE in its run folder, where events reads them, and its agent gets the peers and tell tools.
UiControl keeps one owner of the turn. A peer’s prompt goes to the event loop and through start_turn, as a typed line does: it starts a turn, or it waits behind the running one in the queue and joins a line already waiting there. The transcript shows it as from a peer. A peer’s cancel is stop, which ctrl+c calls, so the lines waiting behind the turn come back to the composer and nothing is lost. status reports the Ui’s turn and queue.
The user reaches other sessions too. /peers lists them, numbered, the most recently active first, with no run ids. /tell N TEXT steers session N of that list, and /tell N --prompt TEXT starts or queues a turn there. /tell N alone aims the lines typed next at that session, as /talk does for a sub-agent, until /tell or /tell main. What the user sends this way asks for no approval, since the user typed it. A /tell whose first word is neither a number, main nor a listed session id is the agent’s own /tell RUN TEXT to a sub-agent.

Background tasks
ctrl+l (TASKS_KEY) and /tasks open a list of what runs outside the turn: background sub-agents, run_shell_bg shells and folder watches. The rows come from background_rows in ramabana.pane, the same source the now pane reads. title: vault
text:
LocalHost is the host the terminal runs on. It can read web pages and index the repository, but it keeps neither after the process ends. A page read in one session is gone in the next. The code index and the pages read live in separate stores that never meet.
A vishalakshi Vault is one SQLite file that holds documents of every kind: notes, web pages and research. VaultHost puts a vault behind the host. This adds three abilities.

Memory. LocalHost does not provide the memory group, and tools_for builds no memory tools for it. With a vault, the memory tools appear (memory_search, memory_read, remember, memory_forget) together with ask_memory. They answer from everything the vault has stored.
One search over everything. search_code asks three indexes at once: the vault for prose, kosha for identifiers and ripgrep for literal text. The three score results on unrelated scales. Vault.federate merges them by rank and ignores the scores.
Watches. A watch is a standing request that the vault stores. A scheduled watch is a job the vault runs on a schedule, such as re-reading a page every week or filing a reminder. A folder watch is a request to review changes under a folder, and Monitors carries it out. With a vault, the watch tools appear too (watch, list_watches, cancel_watch).

title: vault
text:
The host
VaultHost is a LocalHost with a vishalakshi vault. The constructor opens the vault in a background thread. Building the tool list never waits for an embedding model to load. The constructor declares the memory, ask and watch groups by taking them out of without, the set of groups a host switches off.
vault is a Vault, a path to one, or None for the shared default at ~/.vishalakshi/vault.db. shelf names a separate store inside the vault for this host’s writes. remember_reads files every page that read_url fetches. federate turns on the merged search. pii and pii_ner gate personal data and are covered below. mk_chat builds the chats that the vault uses to answer questions. graph_chat is the chat that builds the vault’s entity graph.
WorkspaceHost, in the same cell, is the host that mk_agent builds. It is both a VaultHost and a SpecHost. Both providers are off unless requested. vault=True (or a path, or a Vault) turns memory on. spec=True turns on the API tools from the spec notebook. When a provider is off, its groups stay switched off and calls fall through to LocalHost. WorkspaceHost adds two calls. add_worktree(repo, branch) makes a git worktree for a job and opens it as a root. run_cmd_bg starts a background command that logs to a file. It does not open a tmux pane.


source

WorkspaceHost
def WorkspaceHost(
    roots:tuple=('.',), vault:bool=False, # False, True (default vault), a path, or a Vault
    spec:bool=False, # whether Ramabana's API provider is available
    pii:NoneType=None, pii_ner:NoneType=None, warm:bool=True, **kwargs
):
One workspace host configured with optional memory and API providers.

poll and connect work on a second connection to the vault file. _worker_vault opens it. A background job never shares the connection that a turn uses. The next two cells check that poll gets a connection of its own.

from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as d:

    worker = host._worker_vault()

    assert worker is not host.vault
    assert worker.db is not host.vault.db
    assert worker.doc('report')

    worker.db.conn.close()

The vault builds its entity graph with graph_chat only. When graph_chat is None, the host builds no graph unless $VISHALAKSHI_MODEL names a model. vishalakshi’s own default would load a local model. mk_chat answers the session’s questions and can be a hosted model. Every chunk in the vault is private material. mk_chat never sees the graph build, and the next cell checks this.

from ramabana.testing import no_model

def _connect_arg(**kw):
    "What `Vault.connect` was handed as `chat`, by a host built with `kw`."
    with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        h = VaultHost(vault=Path(d)/'vault.db', warm=False, **kw)
        h.vault.add('A report about polonium.', title='report')
        got = []
        original = h._worker_vault
        def worker():
            v = original()
            v.connect = lambda *a, **k: got.append(k.get('chat'))
            return v
        h._worker_vault = worker
        h.connect(wait=True)
        return got

test_eq(_connect_arg(mk_chat=lambda model=None, **kw: None), [None])
quiet = no_model()
test_eq(_connect_arg(graph_chat=quiet), [quiet])

title: vault
text:
Memory
Memory search returns whole sections of stored documents, plus related sections found through the vault’s graph. Each section carries its age in seconds and whether it is stale. memory_tree lists the heading tree of each stored document, memory_read returns one section by its node id, and memory_forget deletes a document. These pass straight through to the vault.
remember stores a note. Notes are ordinary documents in the same store as everything else. A conclusion the agent reached comes back in the same search results as the evidence for it. The example stores two notes. A search in different words finds them.

host.remember('The weekly Coles order is milk, sourdough, eggs, baby spinach and olive oil.',
              title='weekly Coles order', tags=['groceries'])
host.remember('Ceres Fair Food delivers a mixed seasonal fruit box on Thursdays.',
              title='Ceres fruit box', tags=['groceries'])

r = host.memory_search('what do I need from the supermarket', limit=2)
[s['title'] for s in r['results']], {k: r['results'][0][k] for k in ('age', 'stale')}


test_eq(len(host.memory_tree()), 2)
test_eq(len(host.memory_tree('ceres')), 1)

node = r['results'][0]['node_id']
'olive oil' in host.memory_read(node)['text'] or 'fruit box' in host.memory_read(node)['text']

With a vault behind the host, tools_for offers the memory group. NullHost has no memory group.

from ramabana.tools import tools_for, NullHost
have = lambda h: {getattr(t, '__name__', '') for t in tools_for(h)}
test_eq('memory_search' in have(NullHost()), False)
test_eq('memory_search' in have(host), True)

title: vault
text:
Gating what memory returns
Some of what a vault holds is personal data: names, emails and phone numbers. pii sets what happens when a section that the vault returns contains such data. off is the default and returns the section as stored. redact masks the personal parts. refuse withholds the section. pii_ner=True also catches titled names in addition to the pattern matches. vishalakshi does the gating. The host passes the setting into every vault read:

memory_search
memory_read
memory_tree
search
research

Either setting can be a function instead of a value. The host calls the function on every read. A settings panel can therefore change the setting during a session. A function that raises counts as off. The hidden cells check each mode against a note that contains an email address and a phone number.

title: vault
text:
Federated search
search, the host call behind search_code, asks the vault for prose, kosha for identifiers and ripgrep for literal text, and merges the three lists with litesearch.rrf_all through Vault.federate. If the vault fails to open, the host falls back to LocalHost.search.
In an empty temporary folder only the vault has anything to find. There is no kosha index, and there is no text file for ripgrep to match. search_note reports how many hits each index returned.

hits = host.search('seasonal fruit box', limit=5)
host.search_note

A prose hit’s symbol is its section’s node id. memory_read(hit.symbol) reads the whole section. A repository hit’s symbol is its module name, for use with symbols. One field serves the follow-up call for either kind of hit.

prose = [h for h in hits if h.symbol.count('#') == 1]
prose and host.memory_read(prose[0].symbol)['text'][:60]

federate=False turns the merging off and keeps LocalHost’s own search. A host also falls back to that search when its vault will not open.

plain = VaultHost(roots=[tmp], vault=tmp/'vault.db', index=False, web=False,
                  federate=False, warm=False)

title: vault
text:
Watches and reminders
Watches live in the vault, so they survive between sessions. poll runs the watches that are due. It does not rebuild the entity graph while a turn waits; when something ran, it starts connect, which rebuilds the graph in the background.
Each watch has an action and an interval. The simplest action is remind. When a reminder comes due, the vault files the reminder text back into itself as a note. A memory search finds the reminder together with everything else. The reminder does not wait in a notification queue that the harness does not own.

w = host.watch('Add the weekly groceries to the Coles trolley, and a Ceres fruit box.',
               action='remind', every='1w', note='weekly shop')
[(x['id'], x['action'], int(x['every'])) for x in host.watches()]

A new watch is first due at the moment it is created. A poll at any earlier time finds nothing to run.

test_eq(host.vault.poll(at=w['next_run'] - 1, connect=False)['ran'], 0)

A poll after that moment runs it, and a memory search then finds what it filed.

fired = host.vault.poll(at=w['next_run'] + 1, connect=False)
test_eq(fired['ran'], 1)
test_eq(fired['results'][0]['status'], 'ok')

hit = host.memory_search('what am I supposed to be doing about groceries', limit=3)
[s['title'] for s in hit['results']]

One failing watch must not stop the others. vishalakshi’s run_watch records a failure on the watch and returns it instead of raising. A poll over five due watches therefore runs all five. The vault runs each watch by calling its method named after the action. Replacing host.vault.url with a function that always fails makes every url watch fail. The example below puts one such watch next to a working reminder.

def _down(target, **kw): raise ConnectionError('name not resolved')
host.vault.url = _down

dead = host.watch('https://example.invalid/x', action='url', every='1d')
live = host.watch('check which day the Ceres box arrives', action='remind', every='1d')
out = host.vault.poll(at=max(dead['next_run'], live['next_run']) + 1, connect=False)
sorted(r['status'] for r in out['results'])

The failed watch is still there, rescheduled, with its last status recorded. A single failure does not delete a watch. The cleanup cancels both watches by hand.

host.unwatch(dead['id'])
host.unwatch(live['id'])
test_eq(len(host.watches()), 1)

The watch tools appear when the host provides the watch capability, as the memory tools do for the memory capability.

tools = have(host)
test_eq({'remember', 'watch', 'list_watches', 'cancel_watch'} <= tools, True)
test_eq(any(t.startswith('watch') for t in have(NullHost())), False)

watch is one tool for every kind of watch. Its kind is url for a page, remind for a reminder, search for a web query and folder for a path. The harness polls watches. The model does not. At the start of each turn, Agent.poll_watches calls host.poll() in a background thread, at most once every poll_every seconds, and reports what fired. The host returns failures instead of raising. A turn that starts by asking what is outstanding therefore does not end on an error.

from ramabana.tools import watch_tools
watch = next(t for t in watch_tools(host) if t.__name__ == 'watch')
print(watch('renew the domain', kind='remind', every='1w'))
host.poll()

title: vault
text:
Using it
from ramabana import Agent
from ramabana.vault import VaultHost

host = VaultHost(roots=['~/code/myproject'])     # the shared ~/.vishalakshi/vault.db
agent = Agent(host, model='gpt-mini')
This agent has eight tools that a LocalHost agent does not have: the four memory tools, ask_memory and the three watch tools. Its search_code also answers from everything the vault has read. Agent needs no change. The tools appear because the host declares the groups they belong to.

title: vault
section: Answering from material the model must not see
text:
Answering from material the model must not see
memory_search returns whole sections to the model. This suits research. It does not suit a bank statement. To answer from a section, the model that runs the turn must hold the section in its context. That model often runs on someone else’s servers.
ask, which the ask_memory tool calls, works in reverse. The vault answers and the caller receives only the answer. vishalakshi.pii detects personal information by pattern. It does not ask a model to read the sections first. When the retrieved sections hold personal information, the vault answers with a local model under a briefing that forbids repeating any personal detail. These cells are marked eval: false, and the test suite skips them.
In a real session, Agent.lend_model supplies mk_chat, and mk_chat honours the model it is asked for. The vault asks for its local model. It then checks that the returned chat runs on this machine. Without this check, a factory could send a statement to a hosted API. In the example, the factory returns a chat that claims a remote runtime. The vault refuses and sends nothing.

_h.mk_chat = _chat('remote', 'THIS MUST NEVER BE SENT')
_sent.clear()
r = _h.ask('what is on invoice 4471?')
test_eq(_sent, [])
test_eq(r.refused, True)
r.answer

A chat on a local runtime receives the question under a different briefing. It returns an answer that withholds the personal details.

_h.mk_chat = _chat('litert', 'One invoice, 240.00 GBP, due in September. Holding back the name, '
                             'email, phone and card. Tell me if you need a total, a date, or a yes/no.')
_sent.clear()
print(ask_memory('what is on invoice 4471?'))

That reply is half of a two-step exchange. The model that reads the reply decides what it needs and sends an instruction back. The instruction runs the local model again over the same sections. The model receives a useful answer, and the private material never leaves the machine.

_h.mk_chat = _chat('litert', 'Total 240.00 GBP, due 2026-09-01.')
_sent.clear()
out = ask_memory('what is on invoice 4471?', instruction='Give me the total and the due date only.')
test_eq('Give me the total and the due date only.' in _sent[0][1], True)
out

title: ramabana
text:
Ramabana runs a language model as a coding assistant. You describe a task in plain words. The model searches the code, reads and edits files, runs commands and Python, and tells you what it did. Ramabana runs that loop, decides which tools the model may call, keeps every write inside the folders you opened, and stops to ask you before anything changes.
The same agent runs in three places: a terminal session, an MCP server that lends its tools to another assistant, and your own Python program. Each of them builds the same Agent over the same tools. A behaviour in one appears in the others.
Start with one folder. Ramabana writes only inside the folders that --root names, and its reads stay inside them too unless you pass --read-outside.

title: ramabana
text:
How the pieces fit
A few words recur on every page of these docs.
A turn is one prompt from you and everything the agent does to answer it. During a turn Ramabana calls the model, runs the tools the model asked for, sends back their results, and calls the model again. A step is one model call and the tool calls it makes. The turn ends when the model answers without asking for a tool, or when it runs out of one of its budgets.
A tool is a Python function the model may call. Its name, arguments and docstring are what the model sees. Tools come in groups: code search, files, notebooks, the web, memory, shell commands, git, Python, and a few more. The toolset itself lives in shalya, and Ramabana imports it.
A host is the object that sets what the tools can reach: which folders they may read and write, whether the network is on, where memory is kept, and which approval gate guards a write. A host lists the groups it supports by inheriting one class per group, such as CodeHost or WebHost, and the agent offers only the tools of those groups. The terminal runs on shalya’s LocalHost. The tests run on an in-memory host from ramabana.testing.
The approval gate sits between the model and any tool with an effect, such as editing a file, running a command or making a git commit. In the default mode it asks you about each one. The Approvals section lists the other modes.
The briefing is the system prompt Ramabana writes for each session. It names the open folders, sets out how to work, lists the skills it found, and adds the project’s own instructions from files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md in each open folder.
A skill is a markdown file of guidance the agent reads only when the work calls for it. The briefing lists each skill in one line and the read_skill tool returns one in full.
A sub-agent is a second agent that the running one starts for a piece of the work, through the delegate tools. It has its own steps and transcript, works under the same approval gate, and reports back to the turn that started it.
A job is a kind of model call other than the turn itself, such as a completion, a summary or a sub-agent. Ramabana routes each job to a model suited to it, as Point it at a model explains.

title: ramabana
text:
Install
Ramabana needs Python 3.12 or newer. The core package holds the agent, its hosts, and the file, code, shell and git tools, which is enough to build an agent into your own program. Each extra adds one way of using it:
pip install ramabana           # the core, to build an agent or an app on
pip install 'ramabana[cli]'    # the terminal session, with search
pip install 'ramabana[all]'    # every extra







extra
adds




[search]
semantic code search, the vault’s memory and watches, the web tools


[serve]
ramabana-mcp


[dhrona]
--warm, which starts a chat with example rounds from dhrona


[cli]
the terminal session, plus [search]



A program that embeds Ramabana installs only the extras it needs, such as ramabana[search,serve]. When an extra is missing, the tools that need it are left out of what the model is offered, and any command that needs it names the extra to install.
The core install already brings in the packages shalya depends on: dhrishti, jupyter-client, fossick, litesearch and vishalakshi, which in turn brings in mcp. The extras add the terminal, the MCP server and the search pieces on top.
To use the terminal on its own, run uv tool install 'ramabana[cli]' and then ramabana. The first interactive run starts inside a tmux server that belongs to Ramabana. That server needs no setup from you. It gives you the now pane, a live view of what the agent is doing in a split beside the session. It also passes the alt keys and shift+enter through to Ramabana as keys of their own. shift+enter arrives only from a terminal that sends it. Inside a tmux server of your own, Ramabana turns extended-keys on for that server when it is off. When tmux is missing, Ramabana offers the install command once. ramabana --doctor checks tmux, extended keys, the config and ramabana-pane. --tmux off or RAMABANA_TMUX=off keeps the session in the terminal you started it in. Detaching or closing the window ends the session, and --resume latest reopens it.







command
what it is




ramabana
the terminal session, drawn with teleprint. Needs [cli]


ramabana-mcp
the MCP server. Needs [serve]


ramabana-tick
one beat of the schedules, run on a timer by pobblebonk

title: ramabana
text:
Point it at a model
--model names the model that this session’s turns run on, called the turn model. Without it the turn model is $RAMABANA_MODEL, then $LEELA_MODEL, then [jobs] turn in config.toml, then claude-opus-5-5 through Claude Code. When that model cannot run here and neither --model nor $RAMABANA_MODEL named it, a session runs on the first model that is ready (see Set up a provider). A turn runs on this machine only when you name a local model.
ramabana --root . --model sonnet
export RAMABANA_MODEL=sonnet    # the same choice in every session

the ollama daemon
none



/models lists what this machine can reach and marks the one running. /model NAME changes model without ending the session. /model alone prints the routing summary.
Not every model call needs the turn model. Ramabana sorts the smaller calls into jobs and sends each job to a cheaper or faster model. Completions and classification run on claude-haiku-5-5. Inline edits, summaries and other one-shot work run on gpt-6-luna through your Codex login. Delegated sub-agents run on claude-sonnet-5-5. When the turn model is local, every job without a model of its own stays on it. When a job’s default model cannot run, the job runs on the turn model and says nothing. When a model you gave a job cannot run, the job moves to another cloud route and the session says so once. A cloud model whose one-shot answer fails or comes back empty is set aside for five minutes, and its jobs move the same way. With no cloud route left, a job runs on gemma-e4b on the device, and the turn never moves. The session reports each fallback once. With nothing left at all, the error names the job, the model and the key or CLI it needs.
$RAMABANA_MODEL_<JOB> overrides one job. <JOB> is ONESHOT, INLINE, COMPLETION, CLASSIFY, SUMMARY or SUBAGENT. $RAMABANA_MODEL_IMAGE and $RAMABANA_MODEL_VIDEO set the models that generate_image and generate_video use. The turn model uses $RAMABANA_MODEL and has no _TURN variable. /model JOB NAME sets one job inside a session:
export RAMABANA_MODEL_SUBAGENT=gpt-5.6-luna

title: ramabana
text:
Settings for this machine
~/.config/ramabana/config.toml holds the settings you would otherwise repeat in every shell: the model for each job, the window guard’s numbers, compaction, learning, and the defaults of the terminal’s flags. Every Ramabana on the machine reads it, including one embedded in Leela (a notebook editor), another editor or an MCP client. A flag beats an env var, an env var beats the file, and the file beats the built-in default.
ramabana config init    # write the file, every key commented out beside its default
ramabana config show    # each value in effect, and whether it came from an env var, the file or the default
[jobs]
turn = "gpt-5.4"          # what $RAMABANA_MODEL and --model beat
subagent = "gpt-5.6-luna"

[window]
margin = 1.2              # charge estimated token counts 20% more

[model."openai/gpt-5.4"]  # correct a number fastllm's table has wrong
max_input_tokens = 272000

[model."claude-opus-5-5"] # a Claude Code turn silent this long is ended and tried once more
timeout = 300
Ramabana reports an entry it cannot use and applies the default. A bad entry never stops a session from starting.
ramabana config set KEY VALUE writes one key, such as subagents.effort high, runtime.tool_channel text or model."openai/gpt-5.4".tool_channel native. Quote a model name that holds a dot. ramabana config models prints the models this machine can reach, as /models does.
Tool schemas travel on one of two channels: native, the model API’s own tool field, or tags (also written text), in the system prompt. A local runtime always uses native. For every other runtime, the first of these that sets a channel decides: $RAMABANA_TOOL_CHANNEL; tags for a model whose wire refused its schemas this session; /model tools for the turn or /subagents tools for sub-agents; [model."NAME"] tool_channel; runtime.tool_channel, or for sub-agents $RAMABANA_SUBAGENT_TOOL_CHANNEL and then subagents.tool_channel; then the runtime’s default. Claude Code’s default is tags. Every other runtime’s is native. Claude Code takes native through an in-process MCP server. A managed Claude Code configuration that forbids MCP servers refuses it, and the turn goes on with tags and a note.
[subagents]
effort = "high"            # what a sub-agent asks for; $RAMABANA_SUBAGENT_EFFORT beats it
tool_channel = "native"    # how a sub-agent's tools travel; empty follows runtime.tool_channel

[model."claude-sonnet-5-5"]
tool_channel = "native"    # this model only
effort = "medium"          # when nothing else names a level

Set up a provider
A session opens whatever this machine has. When the turn’s model cannot run here, and neither --model nor $RAMABANA_MODEL named it, the session runs on the first provider that is ready, in this order: a Claude Code sign-in, a Codex sign-in, a GitHub Copilot sign-in, then an Anthropic, OpenAI or Gemini key. It never picks Azure, Bedrock or a custom endpoint, because each needs a name only you know. A job whose default model cannot run here runs on the turn model. One provider is enough. A one-shot run, ramabana 'PROMPT' or a piped prompt, with nothing ready prints the providers and exits 1.
With nothing ready, the session opens on a welcome. Inside tmux, a Getting started pane beside it lists what this machine has and what to do next, and redraws as each item is done. On WSL it says that logins, programs and variables set in Windows do not reach Linux. ramabana --doctor prints the same list.
/login                  the providers, and which are ready
/login claude           Claude Code's own sign-in, in this terminal; codex and copilot work the same way
/login openai           asks for OPENAI_API_KEY without echoing it, and keeps it in keys.env
/login bedrock          the endpoint questions, then the key
/config                 each setting in effect and where it came from
/config set KEY VALUE   writes one key and applies it to this session
/config edit            opens config.toml in $VISUAL, $EDITOR, nano or vi, and applies it on exit
/config reset           writes the commented template, keeping the old file as config.toml.bak
/model NAME --save      switches model and keeps it as [jobs] turn
A change made with /config applies to the running session. After editing config.toml by hand, /config reload applies it. A job set with /model in this session keeps its model.
~/.config/ramabana/keys.env holds the keys /login asks for. Only you can read it. Ramabana refuses a keys.env that other users can read. A variable already in the environment wins over the file. A value that starts with ! is a command, and its output is the key. A key can then stay in a password manager:
OPENAI_API_KEY=!security find-generic-password -ws openai
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=!op read op://vault/anthropic/key
From a shell, ramabana setup asks the endpoint questions:
ramabana setup                         # pick a provider and answer its questions
ramabana setup --provider azure --model-id gpt-5.4 --endpoint https://NAME.openai.azure.com --jobs turn,summary
It writes a [model."NAME"] table into config.toml. The new model becomes [jobs] turn when config.toml names no turn and no provider is ready here. --jobs names other jobs. ramabana setup never writes a key. ramabana config show prints what is in effect.

gpt-5.4

this machine

Azure OpenAI, by hand:
[azure]
endpoint = "https://NAME.openai.azure.com"   # or $AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT; the key stays in $AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY

[model."az-image"]                            # an Azure deployment of gpt-image-1, for generate_image
model_id = "gpt-image-1"
base_url = "https://NAME.openai.azure.com/openai/v1"

[jobs]
turn = "azure/gpt-5.4"                        # a deployment, named by its deployment name
completion = "azure/gpt-5.4-mini"
classify = "azure/gpt-5.4-mini"
image = "az-image"
video = "gemini/veo-3.0-generate-001"        # generate_video; or an Azure sora-2 [model."NAME"]

[model."azure/prod-chat"]                     # a deployment named for no known model needs its window
max_input_tokens = 200000
Requests go to https://NAME.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/responses with the deployment name as the model. No api-version is needed. A deployment named for a model, such as gpt-5.4, gets that model’s window and briefing. Any other name runs with a 128k window until max_input_tokens corrects it, and its cost reads as $0, because prices are looked up by model name.
AWS Bedrock, by hand, through its OpenAI-compatible Mantle endpoint:
[model."bedrock-gpt"]
model_id = "openai.gpt-5.4"                   # Bedrock's model id
base_url = "https://bedrock-mantle.us-east-1.api.aws/v1"
api_key_env = "AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK"      # a Bedrock API key; short-lived keys need renewing
api_name = "openai"                           # Responses; openai_chat for the models that offer only chat completions

[jobs]
turn = "bedrock-gpt"
Claude on Bedrock, and anything else that needs Bedrock’s native Converse API, AWS profiles or SigV4 signing, is not supported yet: fastllm, which makes the requests, implements none of them. The Mantle endpoint has no images endpoint. generate_image needs another [jobs] image.
A [model."NAME"] table with model_id defines a hosted model of any OpenAI-compatible kind under a name of your own: model_id, base_url, api_key_env (the env var, never the key), api_name (openai for Responses, openai_chat for chat completions; openai is the default on an Azure host), vendor_name, runtime and ctx. Saved model aliases live in ~/.config/ramabana/models.json (Leela keeps its own in ~/.config/leela/models.json). Every Ramabana process loads them, and config.toml’s definitions, on first use. A name defined in both places belongs to config.toml. A scheduled job, such as Dhrona’s nightly batch, sees the environment it was started with, beat.env and keys.env. A key exported only in a shell profile does not reach it.
A message too large for the window still goes out. A huge paste, a screenshot too many or a giant tool result is cut to its head and its end, the whole kept in a file under the session’s run folder, and the note in its place tells the model where the file is and to read it in pieces.

title: ramabana
text:
Your first session
ramabana --root .
This opens the current folder, asks before every write, and runs on the default model. Type a task and press enter. /help prints the key card and /guide the longer tour. ctrl+c stops a running turn and ctrl+d quits.
Pass a prompt instead and Ramabana runs one turn, prints the answer on stdout, and exits:
ramabana --root . 'Find where request timeouts are configured.'
ramabana --root . 'Summarise the open TODOs' > todos.md
The one-turn form prints each problem on stderr and exits 1 when the turn model was not up. A script or a git hook can test that exit code.

Inside a session

title: ramabana
text:
Approvals
An approval gate guards the write tools. --approve sets its mode.



mode
what happens




ask
every write waits for you. The default


edits
file and notebook edits run; other writes wait


auto
writes run unattended for the rest of the process


off
the gate refuses every write


none
no gate at all



At an approval prompt:

y approves.
n refuses.
a approves everything for the rest of the session.
ctrl+y approves with a note.
A typed reason and enter refuses with that reason.

shift+tab cycles ask, edits, auto and back to ask. From off it comes back in at ask. ctrl+g moves one step stricter, from auto to edits to ask to off, and never the other way. /approve MODE moves in either direction and answers any prompt already waiting.
The gate covers every tool with an effect:

files: replace_text, create_file, edit_cell, add_cell, and edit_file when --optin exhash offers it
code: run_python, run_shell, run_shell_bg
git: git_commit, git_checkout, git_stash, git_remote, git_sync, git_conflicts
the rest: memory_forget, create_skill, cancel_watch, add_root

Git goes through those tools. Merge or rebase with git_sync, not run_shell. Settle conflicts with git_conflicts, and git_status shows the plan. run_shell refuses git commit|push|pull|fetch|stash|switch|checkout|merge|rebase and names the tool to use. Ramabana snapshots every git write so /rewind can undo it. When the same gated call comes three times running, Ramabana asks you rather than run or refuse it again, whatever the mode.

title: ramabana
text:
The folders it can touch
--root is the file policy. Name every folder, comma separated:
ramabana --root .,~/notes,/srv/app
Writes reach those folders and nowhere else. Reads start out in the same folders. --read-outside widens reads to any path on the machine and leaves writes where they were. /root prints the open folders, and /root add PATH opens another mid-session for reading and writing.
Sub-agents, started through the delegate tools, may write, run commands and run Python by default. Every write remains behind this session’s approvals. --no-subagent-writes or /subagents off restricts them to read-only tools. A read-only session refuses delegate_async(writes=True). delegate_search hands its sub-agents read tools only unless the model passes writes=True. Several read-only questions then run at once.
A sub-agent runs on the subagent job’s model, claude-sonnet-5-5 by default. /subagents model NAME changes it for this session, and /subagents model default goes back to config.toml’s. The model may also name a model per delegation: delegate_search(questions, model=...) takes one name for every question or a list with one per question. A named model that is unknown or not set up here fails that question with the setup message, and no other model answers in its place. Read-only questions on different cloud models run at once. Questions on the session’s local engine run one after another. Writes run one at a time.
effort is low, medium, high, xhigh or max. A delegation’s own effort comes first, then /subagents effort, then $RAMABANA_SUBAGENT_EFFORT, then config.toml’s [subagents] effort, then the model’s default. Claude Code takes the level as its effort. A hosted model takes it as its reasoning effort. OpenAI and Azure take max as xhigh. A local model takes no effort level. It runs at its default and the answer says so. A provider that refuses the level is asked once more without it, and the answer says so. Sub-agents do not take the turn’s own reasoning level.
A sub-agent takes at most 80 steps and runs for at most 1800 seconds by default. /subagents steps N and /subagents timeout S change those limits. timeout 0 removes the time limit. A delegation’s max_steps stays within the session cap and has a floor of 20 steps unless the session cap is lower. Two levels of sub-agents may delegate again by default. /subagents nest 0 disables nesting. A nested sub-agent gets only delegate_search. The sub-agents under one turn share one tool-call budget the size of the turn’s own. At most four run at once.
Every run keeps a transcript under <cfg>/runs/<session>/. Inside tmux:

/watch RUN opens a pane that tails the transcript.
/watch monitors tails the folder reviews.
/tell RUN TEXT sends a running sub-agent a message. It gets the message with its next tool result.
read_terminal reads the sibling panes.
run_shell_bg logs to a file rather than opening a pane. The side pane’s Background rows show its output, and p on one follows it in a tmux pane.

/pane opens the now pane in a split on the right. It shows the turn, the call it is on, and each sub-agent run with its own calls. The split needs tmux 3.1 or later, and --pane on opens it at startup. Without tmux, or with --tmux off, /pane prints the ramabana-pane command to run in another terminal instead.

title: ramabana
text:
Budgets, cost and history
A turn runs until the model stops calling tools. --max-tool-calls caps the tool calls. --max-steps caps the steps, each one model call and the tools it runs. Both take auto or a number: 20 to 400 calls, 8 to 80 steps. /tool-budget and /steps change them mid-session and print what the last turn ran under.
/cost prints:

the tokens in and out
the cached share
the reasoning tokens
the spend, when the backend reports one

/compact summarises the history so far and carries on with the shorter context. /compact NOTE tells the compactor what to keep.
Ramabana saves every session with a completed turn under --cfg, which defaults to ~/.config/ramabana. /sessions lists them with their turn counts and models. /resume ID reopens one from a full id or a unique prefix. From the shell:
ramabana --root . --resume latest
A resumed session brings back its history and its plan. It prints on stderr any other folder that session had open, and /root add PATH opens it again.

title: ramabana
section: Memory, API specifications and a beat
text:
Memory, API specifications and a beat
--vault keeps what the agent reads in a vishalakshi vault, for the next session to retrieve. --pii redact masks personal data on the way back out of the vault, and in the shell, Python and web reads sent to a hosted model; file reads keep it, because edits match text exactly. --pii refuse refuses those reads instead. API keys and tokens are masked as [SECRET] in every read whatever --pii says, and commands that print the environment are refused. --pii-ner extends either mode to titled names, not only patterns. Either mode needs --vault. Without it the command exits 2 and does not ignore the flag; a cli.pii in config.toml is skipped instead.
--spec adds api_load, api_ops and api_call. Point api_load at an OpenAPI, Azure or Google Discovery document and the agent can call the operations it describes.
Some work should happen on a timer even when no session is open. A schedule is a callback that pobblebonk fires at set times. A package registers one under the ramabana.ticks entry point, as dhrona does, and Python code registers one with ramabana.monitor.on_tick(name). A beat is one pass that runs every schedule that has come due. ramabana-tick runs one beat and leaves what the schedules found as notes, which the next session reads. --install registers the command with cron, launchd or schtasks. Beats then run while no session is open:
ramabana-tick --install --every 300    # a beat every five minutes
ramabana-tick                          # one beat now
ramabana-tick --uninstall

title: ramabana
text:
Skills and extensions
A skill is markdown the agent reads when the work calls for it. Ramabana looks for skills in these folders, in order:

<cfg>/learned/skills
<cfg>/skills
~/.agents/skills
.leela/skills and .agents/skills under each open folder

When two skills share a name, the later folder wins. In each folder, a skill is a subfolder holding a SKILL.md. Five skills ship inside the package as Python modules: coding_patterns, debugging, theory, write_prose and write_docs. Any folder above overrides them. /skills lists what this session found, and /skill NAME prints one.
<cfg>/learned holds what dhrona, a separate package that learns from past sessions, kept from earlier sessions. Its skills override the packaged ones and lose to every folder you write. Its AGENTS.md goes in the briefing after Ramabana’s own rules and before the project instructions, and the project instructions outrank it. A learned skill is listed like any other and read when a task needs it. A learned skill that replaces an inlined skill is clipped in the briefing to the same cap as AGENTS.md. No proposal from dhrona reaches a session until you accept it. Each proposal waits on a pending/ branch of the folder’s own git repository. /learned in a session, or ramabana-learned from a shell, lists them, and diff ID, accept ID and reject ID act on one. Ramabana refuses an accept that would take AGENTS.md past the 2,000 characters dhrona allows. /learned compact ID then asks dhrona to merge and shorten the paragraphs it wrote, with that proposal folded in. Your own paragraphs stay as they are. The shorter file waits for review like any proposal. Accepting a proposal moves the other proposals onto it, and a proposal that no longer applies is marked stale. ramabana.learned offers the same to a host. --no-learned starts a session without the folder. /learned off, or ramabana-learned off, sets learning = false in config.toml and turns learning off for every session on this machine. Nothing learned is briefed, no lessons are kept or read, and the nightly batch does nothing until /learned on.
An extension adds behaviour without changing Ramabana. It is a Python file in <cfg>/extensions with a setup(reg) function, and through reg it can:

add a tool
add a slash command
register a skill
hook the turn
replace the approval policy

def setup(reg):
    @reg.tool
    def deploy_status() -> str:
        "What is deployed right now."
        return open('/var/run/deploy').read()

    reg.command('deploys', lambda agent, arg: deploy_status(), help='what is deployed')
    reg.on('after_tool', lambda agent, name, out: print(name, file=open('/tmp/tools.log', 'a')))
The hook events are before_turn(agent, prompt), after_turn(agent, text), before_tool(agent, name, args), after_tool(agent, name, out), compact(agent, text) and approval. reg.approval(fn) replaces the approval policy, and the last registration wins. /extensions prints one line per extension: loaded, or why not. /reload loads skills, extensions and tools again after an edit.

title: ramabana
text:
Talk between sessions
Claude Code, Codex and Ramabana sessions on one Mac can send each other messages. A note shares news. An ask requests work. A reply returns the result with proof.
Set up the hooks once. This step edits the Claude Code hook settings and gives the session the peer-work skill:
ramabana setup peers --agent claude
Plain ramabana setup does not install these hooks. The command shows the diff of ~/.claude/settings.json and asks before it writes. Add --yes to write without the question. Use --agent codex for Codex, or --agent all for both. --remove takes the hooks out again.
A Claude Code session registers when it starts. A session that was already running before the setup does not appear in ramabana peers. Restart it, or resume it with claude --resume. ramabana --doctor shows whether each agent has the hooks.
List the live sessions:
ramabana peers
Send a note to a session. Add --ask to request work, and --wait 120 to wait for the reply:
ramabana tell sanketa "The Card API moved to v2"
ramabana tell --ask --wait 120 sanketa "Add a Card part"
Work together mode lets the named sessions send you asks without a question to the user. Each session keeps its own permission mode. The mode ends at the set time, after 12 hours if you set no time, or with ramabana together off. In a Claude Code or Codex session it also ends when you type. In a Ramabana session, /together on starts it, and so does telling the agent to work with peers: the agent calls its work_together tool. In auto permission mode the tool runs without a question; ask and edits ask you. A turn that a peer message reached cannot call it:
ramabana together on --with abhyasa,leela --until 07:00
A thread carries at most 6 messages: the ask and 5 replies. Each session sends at most 40 notes and asks in 12 hours; replies do not count. So two sessions cannot loop all night. When the mode ends, Ramabana saves a morning report. It lists each thread, its changes, its proof and the actions left for you:
ramabana report

title: ramabana
section: Serve the tools to another assistant
text:
Serve the tools to another assistant
ramabana-mcp serves one host’s tools over MCP:
ramabana-mcp --root .
By default the server mounts only the read tools, because the client cannot reach this process’s approval gate. --write mounts the write tools too. --model NAME adds one further tool, ask, which runs a whole Ramabana turn and returns only its answer. --model also builds the agent. The mounted tools are then the same objects a turn gets, and they record into the same activity log. The server offers skills as resources rather than tools: an index, plus one per skill. A client lists them and fetches the one it needs.



option
default
what it does




--root A,B
.
the folders to serve


--model NAME
none
adds the ask tool, running on this model


--write
off
mount the write tools too


--no-web
web on
takes the network away from the web tools


--read-outside
off
reads may name any path. Writes stay inside


--vault, --pii MODE, --pii-ner
off
as in the terminal


--transport NAME
stdio
stdio, sse or streamable-http


--cfg DIR
none
skills and extensions, with --model



A model-less server still finds skills in the served folders and in ~/.agents/skills. The server loads --cfg and its extensions only when --model builds the agent.
A client that launches its own servers takes the command:
{"mcpServers": {"ramabana": {"command": "ramabana-mcp", "args": ["--root", "/srv/app"]}}}

title: ramabana
text:
Drive it from Python
ramabana.agent.mk_agent builds what the terminal runs: a host over the folders you name, and an Agent whose approval gate works the way approve says. agent.ask(prompt) runs one turn and returns the answer.
The example below goes through the same Agent.ask path with fake_agent from ramabana.testing. Instead of a real model it uses a backend that returns the replies you give it, and instead of your disk it uses a small in-memory project. It needs no credentials or downloads and writes nothing.
A long-running program, such as a web app that runs agent jobs, uses the same calls with these options:

Read roots: mk_agent(read_roots=[...]) opens folders that the read tools search and no write touches. The system prompt names them.
Many asks: an ask is one approval request waiting for an answer. Approvals holds every waiting ask. answer(id, ok) resolves any of them, and waiting lists them oldest first. Each ask appears through on_activity as an awaiting row with its ask_id before its call runs.
A policy: Approvals(policy=fn) is consulted before rules and modes. fn(name, args) returns 'allow', 'deny', 'ask' or None.
Waiting and timeouts: no_listener='wait' holds an ask until a page listens, and that page is shown the asks already waiting. on_timeout='allow' lets an unanswered ask through, except one that the policy or the loop guard put to a person.
A typed result: agent.ask(prompt, schema=Model) returns a TurnResult whose result is a validated Model.
Sessions: Agent(session_id=...) names the session. A turn in a session another live process holds raises SessionBusy.
Budgets: max_cost, max_tokens, session_max_cost and session_max_tokens stop a turn that passes them. The turn is recorded with state budget.
An event file: agent.events_to(path) writes one JSON line per call, ask, plan change, turn start and end, and steering delivered. A file past max_bytes rolls over to <name>.1.
A queue: agent.queue(prompt) holds a prompt, and agent.run_queued() runs what is held, in order. Steering a turn never read joins the next turn.
A full resume: resume_session(id, full=True) restores the conversation as its last turn left it, every tool result whole. A stop that leaves a backend running hands its conversation to the next one.
Defaults for a host: mk_agent(python='off') withholds Python. mk_agent(global_skills=False) leaves ~/.agents/skills out. rules_path= names the job’s own rules file. Agent(extra_sp=...) adds to the briefing.
A worktree: host.add_worktree(repo, branch) makes a git worktree for the job and opens it as a root.
A control socket: ramabana.control.Control(agent).start() listens on a socket in the session’s run folder, and control_call(path, method, ...) prompts, steers, cancels and answers it from another process, and takes messages from peer sessions.

examples/embed_host.py runs one such job end to end.

from ramabana.testing import fake_agent

agent, backend = fake_agent(replies=['The threshold is defined in `pkg/sizes.py`.'])
answer = agent.ask('Where is the threshold defined?')
answer

'The threshold is defined in `pkg/sizes.py`.'



assert agent.history[-1]['prompt'] == 'Where is the threshold defined?'

agent.turn_lines(), repr(agent.turn_use)

title: ramabana
text:
Read the implementation
Start with the page for the contract you need:

core: errors, routing, model budgets, and shared values
models: the model catalog, curated and discovered
runtime: backends, usage, runs, and compaction
tools: hosts, tool construction, and delegation
agent: turns, approvals, activity, plans, history, and branching
testing: in-memory hosts and deterministic backends
terminal and MCP: frontend adapters, the now pane beside the terminal, and the first-run setup that starts it in tmux
vault, API specifications, and folder monitoring: optional capabilities
control: a local socket a detached job runner listens on
learned: the review queue for what Dhrona proposes for the learned folder
coding patterns, debugging, theory, prose, and documentation: bundled agent skills

The toolset itself is shalya, the git plumbing is gheasy, and the scheduler is pobblebonk.

title: learned
text:
Dhrona is the optional package (the dhrona extra) that learns from past sessions. The learned folder is <cfg>/learned, a git repository. Dhrona’s nightly batch never changes the files that Ramabana briefs from. It commits each candidate it keeps on its own pending/<id> branch of that repository. The briefing and skill discovery read only the folder’s files, which are its HEAD. A pending candidate therefore has no effect until a person accepts it. --no-learned leaves out the folder whatever it holds.
pending lists what waits, diff shows one candidate’s change, accept moves it onto HEAD, and reject drops it. Each of diff, accept and reject returns a dict with ok and id, and with error when ok is False. A client application can display the returned dict directly. accept and reject take the lock that a Dhrona batch holds, and refuse while a batch runs. diff takes no lock. accept refuses only when the learned folder has an uncommitted change to a file that the candidate also changes. A hand edit to another file stays as it is, unstaged. Dhrona keeps each lesson as an entry in a dated file, dhrona-<date>.md. Two lessons on the same day give two candidates that change the same file, and the newer one holds both entries. pending lists only the newest, with the older ids in includes. accept on the newest deletes the older candidates. reject on the newest lists the older ones again. accept refuses a candidate that would take AGENTS.md past LEARNED_MAX. LEARNED_MAX is the 2,000 characters that Dhrona allows one candidate. Accepted rounds add up. accept keeps HEAD within the limit too.
compact asks Dhrona for a shorter AGENTS.md when accepted lessons crowd it. Dhrona’s editor model merges and shortens the paragraphs that Dhrona proposed. It keeps every paragraph that a person wrote byte for byte. It commits the result as one more pending candidate. diff, accept and reject act on that candidate like any other.
compact(folder, id) also folds in pending candidate id. This is the case that accept refuses for size. The refusal returns length and names /learned compact ID. Accepting that compaction accepts the candidate with it.
compact returns {ok, id, before, after}, where before and after are the file’s length in characters. On failure it returns {ok: False, error}. It needs the dhrona extra and says so when Dhrona is missing. It runs one model turn and takes as long as that turn.

    folder, id

Move pending candidate id onto HEAD, then restack the other candidates onto it. The next briefing reads HEAD. Returns {ok, id, commit, moved, stale}.

    folder

Each candidate waiting for review, oldest first, as {id, at, subject, files, stale, includes}; at is when it was proposed, in epoch seconds, and stale why it cannot be accepted or None. A candidate that holds the entries of older candidates for the same dated file lists them in includes, and they are left out.

Move each pending candidate proposed on an older HEAD onto HEAD where it picks cleanly; returns (moved, stale) ids.

# git gets end of input, and a line waiting on the session's terminal stays there
import os, pty, subprocess, sys
m, s = pty.openpty(); os.write(m, b'x\n')
probe = "import os, select, tempfile; from ramabana.learned import _git; print(_git(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'hash-object', '--stdin').stdout.strip(), os.read(0, 9) if select.select([0], [], [], 1)[0] else b'')"
got = subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-c', probe], stdin=s, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=60).stdout.split()
os.close(s); os.close(m)
test_eq(got, ['e69de29bb2d1d6434b8b29ae775ad8c2e48c5391', "b'x\\n'"])

accept first applies a candidate in a throwaway git worktree. A conflict never leaves markers in the files that a running session briefs from. HEAD moves only when the pick is clean. After HEAD moves, restack moves every other candidate proposed on an older HEAD onto the new HEAD where it picks cleanly. accept returns those ids as moved. A candidate that no longer picks cleanly is listed as stale. An example is a candidate that edits a line that a compaction rewrote. accept returns those ids as stale, and pending gives the reason in each candidate’s stale field. A host can show the reason beside the candidate. Ids sort by when Dhrona proposed them, and moving a candidate does not change its id. A candidate whose change HEAD already holds is accepted with commit set to None. The commit keeps Dhrona as its author. Its commit time is the moment of acceptance, and Dhrona’s 30-day expiry clock starts there.

import os, json, time
def git(d, *a): return subprocess.run(['git', '-C', str(d), *a], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
def propose(folder, files, id):
    "What Dhrona's `keep` does: a commit on `pending/<id>` off HEAD, the folder's files untouched."
    wt = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'wt'
    git(folder, 'worktree', 'add', '-q', '-b', PENDING + id, str(wt), 'HEAD')
    for rel, text in files.items(): (wt/rel).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); (wt/rel).write_text(text)
    git(wt, 'add', '-A'); git(wt, '-c', 'user.name=Dhrona', '-c', 'user.email=d@x', 'commit', '-qm', f'Lesson from a replay: {id}')
    git(folder, 'worktree', 'remove', '--force', str(wt))

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    f = Path(d)/'learned'; f.mkdir()
    (f/'AGENTS.md').write_text('A rule a person wrote.\n')
    git(f, 'init', '-q'); git(f, 'add', '-A'); git(f, '-c', 'user.name=t', '-c', 'user.email=t@x', 'commit', '-qm', 'first')
    a, b, c = '20261019-010101-aaaaaa', '20261019-020202-bbbbbb', '20261019-030303-cccccc'
    propose(f, {'skills/sizes/SKILL.md': '---\nname: sizes\ndescription: x\n---\nuse ls\n'}, a)
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': 'Something else entirely.\n'}, b)
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': 'A third view.\n'}, c)
    test_eq([(p['id'], p['files']) for p in pending(f)], [(a, ['skills/sizes/SKILL.md']), (b, ['AGENTS.md']), (c, ['AGENTS.md'])])
    test_eq((f/'AGENTS.md').read_text(), 'A rule a person wrote.\n')
    assert not (f/'skills').exists()
    assert '+use ls' in diff(f, a)['diff']
    r = accept(f, a)
    test_eq(r['moved'], [b, c])
    assert r['ok'] and r['commit'] and (f/'skills'/'sizes'/'SKILL.md').exists() and a not in [p['id'] for p in pending(f)]
    test_eq(git(f, 'log', '-1', '--format=%an'), 'Dhrona')
    test_eq(accept(f, b)['ok'], True)
    test_eq([p['stale'] for p in pending(f)], [STALE])     # `c` rewrites the line `b` changed
    head, text = git(f, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD'), (f/'AGENTS.md').read_text()
    r = accept(f, c)
    assert not r['ok'], r
    test_eq((git(f, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD'), (f/'AGENTS.md').read_text()), (head, text))
    assert '<<<<' not in text and git(f, 'status', '--porcelain') == ''
    test_eq(reject(f, c), dict(ok=True, id=c))
    test_eq(pending(f), [])
    test_eq(accept(f, c)['ok'], False)
    test_eq(accept(f, '--force')['ok'], False)             # not an id, never an option
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': 'Hand edit pending.\n'}, a)
    (f/'AGENTS.md').write_text('an uncommitted edit\n')
    test_eq(accept(f, a)['ok'], False)                      # a hand edit blocks it
    git(f, 'checkout', '-q', '--', '.')
    with _locked(f) as held:                                # a batch holds it
        assert held and not accept(f, a)['ok'] and not reject(f, a)['ok']
    test_eq(len(git(f, 'worktree', 'list').splitlines()), 1)
    test_eq(pending(Path(d)/'none'), [])
    git(f, 'checkout', '-q', '--', '.'); reject(f, a)
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': 'A rule a person wrote.\n' + 'x' * LEARNED_MAX}, a)   # past Dhrona's limit
    head, r = git(f, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD'), accept(f, a)
    assert not r['ok'] and r['length'] > LEARNED_MAX and git(f, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD') == head, r
    assert a in learned_command(f)
    test_eq(learned_command(f, f'reject {a}'), f'rejected {a}')
    test_eq(learned_command(f), 'nothing is pending')


with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    f = Path(d)/'learned'; f.mkdir()
    (f/'AGENTS.md').write_text('A rule a person wrote.\n')
    git(f, 'init', '-q'); git(f, 'add', '-A'); git(f, '-c', 'user.name=t', '-c', 'user.email=t@x', 'commit', '-qm', 'first')
    a = '20261019-010101-aaaaaa'
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': 'A rule a person wrote.\n\n' + 'Read sizes with ls -l. ' * 40 + '\n'}, a); accept(f, a)
    r = compact(f, chat=lambda prompt: '[kept 1]\n\nRead sizes with ls -l.')
    assert r['ok'] and r['before'] > r['after'] and r['id'] in learned_command(f), r
    test_eq(git(f, 'show', f"{PENDING}{r['id']}:AGENTS.md"), 'A rule a person wrote.\n\nRead sizes with ls -l.')
    assert not compact(f)['ok']                            # the pending compaction stands in the way
    import sys; mod = sys.modules.pop('dhrona.improve'); sys.modules['dhrona.improve'] = None   # dhrona not installed
    try: assert not compact(f)['ok']
    finally: sys.modules['dhrona.improve'] = mod


with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    f = Path(d)/'learned'; f.mkdir()
    (f/'AGENTS.md').write_text('A rule a person wrote.\n')
    git(f, 'init', '-q'); git(f, 'add', '-A'); git(f, '-c', 'user.name=t', '-c', 'user.email=t@x', 'commit', '-qm', 'first')
    a, big, x, y = '20261019-010101-aaaaaa', '20261019-020202-bbbbbb', '20261019-030303-cccccc', '20261019-040404-dddddd'
    lessons = 'A rule a person wrote.\n\n' + 'Read sizes with ls -l. ' * 40 + '\n'
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': lessons}, a); accept(f, a)
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': lessons + '\n' + 'Run pytest -q before a commit. ' * 40 + '\n'}, big)
    propose(f, {'skills/rg/SKILL.md': '---\nname: rg\ndescription: x\n---\nuse rg\n'}, x)
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': lessons.replace('Read sizes', 'Read file sizes', 1)}, y)
    r = accept(f, big)
    assert not r['ok'] and r['length'] > LEARNED_MAX, r
    r = compact(f, big, chat=lambda prompt: '[kept 1]\n\nRead sizes with ls -l.\n\nRun pytest -q before a commit.')
    assert r['ok'] and r['before'] > LEARNED_MAX >= r['after'], r
    assert not compact(f, '20990101-000000-abcdef')['ok']
    r = accept(f, r['id'])                                  # the compaction carries `big` with it
    assert r['ok'] and (f/'AGENTS.md').read_text() == 'A rule a person wrote.\n\nRead sizes with ls -l.\n\nRun pytest -q before a commit.\n', r
    test_eq((r['moved'], r['stale']), ([x], [y]))           # `x` moved onto the compacted file; `y` edits a line it rewrote
    test_eq([(p['id'], p['stale']) for p in pending(f)], [(x, None), (y, STALE)])
    assert f'{y}  AGENTS.md' in learned_command(f)
    test_eq(git(f, 'rev-parse', f'{PENDING}{x}^'), git(f, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD'))
    assert accept(f, x)['ok'] and accept(f, y)['error'] == STALE

learned_command is the text form a terminal shows. /learned in a session and ramabana-learned from a shell both use it: with no argument it lists what is pending, diff ID, accept ID and reject ID act on one, and compact proposes a shorter AGENTS.md.
Learning is one setting per machine: learning in config.toml (see setup). It is on unless set off. set_enabled(cfg, False), /learned off in a session and ramabana-learned off in a shell turn it off for every session on this machine, whatever its config folder. When learning is off:

The briefing leaves out the learned AGENTS.md and the learned skills.
The briefing drops its rule to record lessons.
remember keeps plain notes only.
Agent.lessons() returns none.
The session writes no start.json.
Dhrona’s nightly schedule returns “learning is off” and does not touch the learned folder.

Lessons already kept stay where they are, unread. The review queue still works, and a person can clear it. Agent(learned=False) and the CLI’s --no-learned turn learning off for one session only.
Ramabana 0.2.44 kept the switch in each config folder’s settings.json. When config.toml does not set learning, enabled(cfg) reads the value from <cfg>/settings.json and writes it into config.toml. A choice made there survives. If the write fails, enabled keeps answering from settings.json. Ramabana never writes the settings.json that an embedding app shares. Ramabana never rewrites a config.toml that is not valid TOML. set_enabled raises ValueError saying so, and /learned on returns that message:

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    os.environ['RAMABANA_CONFIG'] = str(toml := Path(d)/'config.toml')
    try:
        assert enabled(d)
        test_eq(learned_command(learned_folder(d), 'off'), 'learning is off')
        test_eq((enabled(d), (Path(d)/SETTINGS).exists()), (False, False))
        assert '\nlearning = false\n' in toml.read_text()
        test_eq(set_enabled(d, True), True)
        toml.unlink(); (Path(d)/SETTINGS).write_text(json.dumps({'editor': {'tabSize': 2}, 'learning': 'off'}))
        test_eq(enabled(d), False)
        assert 'learning = false' in toml.read_text() and json.loads((Path(d)/SETTINGS).read_text())['learning'] == 'off'
        toml.write_text('learning = [')
        learned_command(learned_folder(d), 'on')
        test_eq(toml.read_text(), 'learning = [')
    finally: os.environ.pop('RAMABANA_CONFIG')

title: Debugging
text:
This page is one of the five skills that ship with Ramabana, built the way theory is: the exported markdown cell below is the module’s docstring, and pyproject.toml registers ramabana.debugging under the pyskills entry point as debugging.
It exists because of one comparison. An agent on Ramabana and Claude Code, on the same model, worked through the same failed Dhrona night and the same set of harness faults. Ramabana’s agent found the launchd PATH cause about as fast, but it then said two things about code it had not read, one of which another commit had already fixed that day, and it did not know where its own launcher, plist and source live. Earlier it had taken a grep that returned “no matches” for text it had just read as the tool working as designed, and a sub-agent that noticed the same fault mentioned it only in passing. The briefing already says not to work around a broken tool. What was missing was how to tell that a tool is broken, how to check a claim before making it, and a map of Ramabana’s own files. Those cost nothing in a turn that is not debugging, so they live here rather than in the system prompt.
Read this before explaining why something failed: a test, a command, a scheduled job, a sub-agent, one of your own tools, or Ramabana itself.

title: Debugging
text:
Find the root cause

Read the raw error first. Open the failing component’s own record (its log, summary file or transcript) and quote the line that names the failure. A count such as “3 failed” points to that record. It is not the cause.
Reproduce the failure in the environment it ran in. A scheduled job does not run in your shell, so rerun the failing step with the scheduler’s environment before blaming or clearing it.
Check a claim about code in that code before making it. “X has no timeout” and “Y already writes Z” are both claims; read or grep the code first. Check the version that ran as well as the checkout, because an installed package can predate a fix in its repository.
Name the cause and the evidence for it before changing anything. A fix that cannot be tied to the quoted error is a guess, and a workaround leaves the cause in place for the next run.
When an earlier claim turns out to be wrong, say so in the reply.

title: Debugging
text:
A tool that misbehaves
A result that contradicts what you have already seen is a tool fault until shown otherwise. Examples:

grep or search_code reports no matches for text you have just read.
ls lists nothing in a folder that exists.
A schema reaches a model without the fields you declared.
The user refers to a message you never received.
A tool reports success and the file or state is unchanged.

Confirm the fault once by a second route, such as rg through run_shell, or view_file. Do not explain it away as how the tool is meant to work unless its description says so. Then:

record it with remember, with component='tool' and the call and its result as evidence
say in the reply, beside the work it affected, which tool failed and how
carry on by the second route

The fault belongs to the harness and is fixed there. The second route keeps this turn going and nothing more.
A sub-agent whose answer says its tool-call budget ran out has returned part of an answer, and its saved answer names what it did not read. Delegate that remainder as narrower questions, or read it yourself, before relying on anything in the gap.

title: Debugging
section: Where Ramabana keeps its own state
text:
Where Ramabana keeps its own state
The running code is the installed package. With the interpreter that “On this machine” lists as this process, python -c 'import ramabana; print(ramabana.__file__, ramabana.__version__)' names it, and uv tool list shows the installed tool’s version. A source checkout, if the user has one, is an nbdev repository whose notebooks under nbs/ are the source. A fix goes there, and the running copy changes only once a release is installed. An editable install runs the checkout’s code, but its entry points (pyskills, ramabana.ticks, scripts) change only on reinstall.
The config folder is ~/.config/ramabana unless --cfg names another:

config.toml holds models, jobs and settings, and models.json the saved model aliases.
agent-history.jsonl has one line per finished turn, with its model, usage, error and the lines the user sent while it ran (steered). A tool result over 600 characters is clipped there; the whole result is in agent-details/<session>.jsonl, named by the row’s details.
runs/<session>/ has one folder per session. run_<id>.log is one run’s transcript, the turn’s or a sub-agent’s. answer_<id>.txt is a sub-agent’s whole answer. stderr.log is the process’s error output, where a backend crash can appear and nowhere else. start.json records each open folder’s repository state at the first turn.
learned/ is a git repository of the rules, skills and extensions that learning keeps.

A turn on a Claude model runs through Claude Code. Its transcripts are under ~/.claude/projects/, in the folder named after ~/.rishi-claude, one .jsonl per conversation, sub-agents included. Each holds the system prompt, model, effort and every tool result exactly as the model received them.
The beat runs scheduled jobs while no session is open:

ramabana-tick runs one beat, and ramabana-tick --install --every 300 schedules it and prints the PATH each beat runs on.
~/.pobblebonk/ramabana.sh is the launcher the scheduler starts, ~/.pobblebonk/ramabana.log holds its output, and ~/.pobblebonk/pob.db holds the schedules, their fires and the notes a session shows inside <beat>.
The scheduler entry is ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ramabana.plist on macOS, a line in the user crontab on Linux, and a Task Scheduler task named ramabana on Windows.
Dhrona’s nightly batch writes ~/.cache/dhrona/nightly/<time>/summary.json, one row per round with its error, beside one folder per round.

title: Debugging
text:
A scheduled job that fails
launchd and cron start a job with PATH=/usr/bin:/bin and none of the exports in a shell profile. When a beat fails with “not found”, “not on PATH” or a missing key:

Read the launcher with cat ~/.pobblebonk/ramabana.sh. Since Ramabana 0.2.52 it starts with /usr/bin/env PATH=…, the PATH of the shell that installed it.
Read what the scheduler gives it: launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/ramabana on macOS shows its environment, and crontab -l on Linux.
Reproduce it: env -i HOME="$HOME" PATH='<that PATH>' /bin/sh -c 'command -v claude git-lfs uv'.
Running ramabana-tick --install again from a shell that finds the tools rewrites the launcher with that shell’s PATH. A key exported in a shell profile still does not reach the beat.

The skill names files that other modules decide. The test below finds the skill the way an agent does, through shalya’s discovery of installed entry points, and checks that every such name in it still matches the code that writes it, so the map cannot drift from the files. The skill is only found once the package is installed, so after adding the entry point an editable install needs reinstalling.

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from shalya.skills import discover
from pobblebonk.heartbeat import LaunchdBeat
from rishi.claude import CLAUDE_WORK_DIR
from ramabana.monitor import BEAT_TAG, _pob_home
from ramabana.agent import Agent
from ramabana.testing import MemHost

s = next(s for s in discover() if s.name == 'debugging')
text, home = s.text(), Path.home()
def tilde(p): return '~/' + str(Path(p).expanduser().relative_to(home))
a = Agent(MemHost(), cfg=Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()), extensions=False, profile='full')
POB_HOME = _pob_home()   # not `monitor.POB_HOME`, which another notebook in this test worker may point at a temp folder
for p in (tilde(POB_HOME/f'{BEAT_TAG}.sh'), tilde(POB_HOME/f'{BEAT_TAG}.log'), tilde(POB_HOME/'pob.db'),
          tilde(LaunchdBeat()._p(BEAT_TAG)), tilde(CLAUDE_WORK_DIR), a.history_path.name,

Act is one row of the feed. It is one tool call, and it exists from the moment the call starts. A frontend can show ⏳ Web fetch: ... while the fetch is still running. kind comes from the tool’s group and selects the icon. line returns the one-line text.

def Act(
    tool:str, args:dict=<factory>, summary:str='', detail:str='', ok:bool=True, done:bool=False, secs:float=0.0,
    started:float=<factory>, id:str=<factory>, turn_id:str='', revision:int=0, branch_id:str='main',
    parent_action_id:str='', run_id:str='', state:str='running', kind:str='', ask_id:str=''
)->None:
One tool call, from the moment it starts to whatever it returned.



a = Act('read_url', {'url': 'https://nbdev.fast.ai/api/export.html'},
        summarise(tool['read_url'], {'url': 'https://nbdev.fast.ai/api/export.html'}))
a.kind, a.icon, a.line()

finish records the outcome, the time taken and the result. state becomes complete or failed. A frontend can use state to choose a colour. The line of a failed call starts with a warning sign, as the second example below shows.

a.finish('# Exporting a notebook to a library\n\nnb_export(...)')
a.line(), a.state

md renders the row as markdown. The result is folded under a <details> tag. A notebook cell that saves an answer can keep the tool work one click away and does not print every result above the answer.

print(a.md())


bad = Act('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'}, 'Edit a.py').finish('edit failed: stale address', ok=False)
test_eq(bad.state, 'failed')
bad.line()

Activity is the whole feed for a session. It calls on_change when a row starts and when it finishes, which is twice per call. A frontend redraws from this callback. rows returns the feed as dicts, lines returns one string per call, and md returns folded markdown. The feed keeps at most max_acts rows (MAX_ACTS, 500) and drops the oldest first.


source


def Activity(
    on_change:NoneType=None, max_acts:int=500
):
The calls of a session, and the on_change callback a frontend uses to redraw.



seen = []
feed = Activity(on_change=lambda act: seen.append((act.tool, act.done)))
act = feed.start('search_code', {'query': 'compaction'})
feed.finish(act, 'nbs/01_runtime.ipynb:88  threshold')
seen

Activity calls on_change outside its lock. It discards any exception the callback raises. A broken frontend cannot stop the model’s turn. The callback below divides by zero, and the row is still recorded.

noisy = Activity(on_change=lambda act: 1/0)
noisy.finish(noisy.start('outline', {'path': 'a.py'}), 'ok')
len(noisy)

mark(turn_id) records where the current turn begins and sets turn_id on every new row. rows, lines and md accept a mark= position and then return only the rows after it. Without mark=, they return every row in the feed.

feed.mark('turn_000002')
feed.finish(feed.start('view_file', {'path': 'a.py'}), 'def a(): return 1')
feed.lines(), feed.lines(mark=feed._mark)


test_eq(len(feed.rows()), 2)
test_eq(len(feed.rows(mark=feed._mark)), 1)
feed.rows(mark=feed._mark)[0]['turn_id']
