title: runtime
text:
Sizing a conversation
These functions decide when a conversation has grown too big for its model. Each limit is a fraction of the context window and not a fixed number of tokens. The same code then works for a 4k-token local model and a 200k-token hosted one. A fixed reserve fails on the small window. With 16k tokens held back from a 4k window, every turn is due for compaction, and the agent compacts a two-message conversation forever.
estimate_tokens counts the tokens in a text. threshold gives the token count at which compaction becomes due, and should_compact compares a count with it. halvings returns the original budget followed by successively halved budgets. Use it to retry a request whose size was only estimated. No value is larger than the original budget. halvings(0) returns [0].








Parameter
Default
Meaning




tries
3
Number of values returned


floor
256
Minimum for each value after the first, unless the original budget is smaller





source

done_items
def done_items(
    summary
):
The lines under a summary’s ### Done heading, up to the next heading, or ''.




source

should_compact
def should_compact(
    used, ctx, reserve:NoneType=None
):
Whether used tokens against a ctx window has crossed the line.




source

threshold
def threshold(
    ctx, reserve:NoneType=None
):
The token count at which a conversation should be compacted, or None when there is no window. reserve is config.toml’s window.reserve, else RESERVE.




source

halvings
def halvings(
    budget, tries:int=3, floor:int=256
):
A budget and its halvings, to retry a prompt whose fit was only estimated.




source

estimate_tokens
def estimate_tokens(
    text, count:NoneType=None
):
Tokens in text: exact via count when a tokenizer is at hand, CHARS_PER_TOKEN otherwise.


estimate_tokens uses the model’s own tokenizer when you pass one as count, and otherwise divides the length of the text by CHARS_PER_TOKEN (3.25). The estimate is rough, and close enough for budgeting.

estimate_tokens('the exporter writes one module per notebook'), estimate_tokens('', ), estimate_tokens('x' * 400)

threshold(ctx) holds back a reserve below the window. The reserve is the full RESERVE of 16,384 tokens for a large window and at most a quarter of the window for a smaller one. Without the quarter-window cap, a 4k model is due for compaction before its first turn. The reserve argument overrides the default, which is config.toml’s window.reserve when set. threshold returns None when the window size is 0 or unknown.
A large window is rarely the limit. A model works best well below its window, and every call re-reads what the conversation holds. Compactor therefore adds two absolute lines in tokens:









line
default
config key
what happens past it




soft
SOFT_LINE, 150,000
compaction.soft
the next turn that starts at a clean boundary hands off to a fresh context


hard
HARD_LINE, 250,000
compaction.hard
the conversation is compacted, or at the window’s threshold when that is lower



done_items reads the Done list out of a summary, which a handoff keeps as a memory note.

threshold(200_000), threshold(32_768), threshold(4096)


test_eq(threshold(4096), 3072)
test_eq((halvings(4000), halvings(128), halvings(0)), ([4000, 2000, 1000], [128, 128, 128], [0]))   # no retry is larger than the first budget
test_eq(threshold(0), None)
should_compact(3000, 4096), should_compact(3072, 4096)

title: runtime
text:
Reading a conversation
A backend stores its conversation as a list of message dictionaries in urai’s format, which is the same for every model. Each message has a role (user, assistant or tool) and content. An assistant message that calls tools also carries tool_calls, and the result of each call comes back as a tool message. Compaction reads this list directly, using urai’s resp_text for a message’s text and tool_rows for its tool calls.
The examples below use this four-message conversation: a request, a tool call, the tool’s result, and the reply.

hist = [
    {'role': 'user', 'content': 'the exporter duplicates cells, please fix it'},
    {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'Reading the exporter.',
     'tool_calls': [{'function': {'name': 'view_file', 'arguments': {'path': 'nbdev/maker.py'}}}]},
    {'role': 'tool', 'content': 'def _make_exists(self, cells):\n    with self.fname.open("a") as f: ...'},
    {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'It appends, so a second export duplicates every named cell.'},
]
[(m.get('role', '?'), resp_text(m)[:40], [name for name, _ in tool_rows(m)]) for m in hist]

serialise writes a list of messages as the text a summarizing model reads. Each message goes in a <message> tag, with its tool calls named in a <tool-calls> tag. Each text is clipped to mx characters (2,000 by default), and a clipped text ends with an ellipsis. An empty list gives (no new messages).


source

split_previous
def split_previous(
    msgs
):
Split off a leading summary: (previous_summary_or_None, remaining_msgs).




source

serialise
def serialise(
    msgs, mx:int=2000
):
Messages as the tagged block the summarizer reads, each text clipped to mx.



print(serialise(hist))

Once a conversation has been compacted, its first message is a user message that starts with SUMMARY_PREFIX and holds the summary. split_previous separates that summary from the messages after it. The next compaction can then update the existing summary with the new messages, instead of summarising the old summary as if it were ordinary conversation.

prev, rest = split_previous([{'role': 'user', 'content': SUMMARY_PREFIX + '## Goal\nfix the exporter'}] + hist)
prev, len(rest)


test_eq(split_previous(hist), (None, hist))
split_previous([])

summarise_prompt builds the request sent to the summarizing model. With no earlier summary it asks for a new one in a fixed format: goal, constraints, progress, key decisions, next steps and critical context. When split_previous finds an earlier summary, it asks for that summary to be updated with the new messages instead. extra adds a line saying what the summary should focus on.
The summary is usually written by a cheaper model with a smaller window, so max_tokens caps the size of the request. When the whole request does not fit, the earlier summary is cut to a quarter of the budget, and the messages after it fill what is left, cut from the end. The instructions come last and are kept whole while the budget can hold them.


source

fold_summary
def fold_summary(
    msgs, summariser, extra:str='', max_tokens:NoneType=None, count:NoneType=None
):
Summarise msgs in runs that each fit max_tokens, every summary updated with the next run; ’’ when a step answers nothing.




source

transcript_runs
def transcript_runs(
    msgs, budget, count:NoneType=None
):
msgs in consecutive runs whose transcript fits budget tokens; a message that alone is larger makes a run of its own.




source

summarise_prompt
def summarise_prompt(
    msgs, extra:str='', max_tokens:NoneType=None, count:NoneType=None
):
The bounded prompt handed to the summarizer, choosing fresh or update instructions.


With no budget the request holds the whole conversation, one <message> per message, followed by the format instructions:

p = summarise_prompt(hist)
test_eq(p.count('<message'), len(hist))
estimate_tokens(p)

With a budget, the request always fits. When the budget is too small to hold the instructions as well, they are cut too, as at 120 and 30 tokens below. A request with cut instructions still gets an answer. The engine refuses a request over the limit.

[estimate_tokens(summarise_prompt(hist, max_tokens=n)) for n in (2000, 400, 120, 30)]


for n in (2000, 400, 120, 30): assert estimate_tokens(summarise_prompt(hist, max_tokens=n)) <= n
summarise_prompt(hist, max_tokens=30)

Summarising needs a second model call. Sometimes no summarizing model is available, or its summary cannot be trusted. Surgical compaction needs no model. surgical_history rewrites old messages as short lines, one per request, reply, tool call and tool result. Each line is cut to a token budget for its role. The request, the calls, the results and the conclusion all remain, at a fraction of the size.
truncate_middle does the cutting. It keeps the start and end of a text and replaces the middle with …. Paths, error messages and diffs carry most of their meaning at the ends. Cut to 12 tokens, this long name keeps its file and its last function:


source

truncate_middle
def truncate_middle(
    text, budget, count:NoneType=None, mark:str=' … '
):
Keep both ends of text inside a token budget.




source

surgical_history
def surgical_history(
    msgs, policy:NoneType=None, count:NoneType=None
):
Render old history as a compact, readable DSL while preserving tool evidence.



truncate_middle('nbs/01_runtime.ipynb::Compactor.compact::summarise_prompt', 12)

Each role has its own marker: § for the user, » for the assistant’s text, ▶ for a tool call and > for its result. User and assistant lines end with the same marker. The lines of a tool result are joined with ¶.

print(surgical_history(hist))

SURGICAL_POLICY sets the budgets: 2,000 tokens for a user message, 150 for the assistant’s text, 60 for a tool call and 35 for a result. The user’s own words are kept nearly whole, and tool results are cut hardest. policy overrides any of them:

print(surgical_history(hist, policy={'result': 8, 'assistant': 20}))

title: runtime
text:
Reorienting the model
After compaction the model sees a summary where its conversation used to be. reorient writes the reminder placed after the summary. The reminder says whether the Python kernel survived. The model then knows whether its variables still exist. The reminder tells the model that skill text it read earlier is no longer in context and has to be read again with read_skill. It names the skills when skills is given. The reminder also tells the model not to answer a finished request a second time. If the latest request is complete, the model replies in one line and waits. REORIENT is the reminder with the default arguments.


source

reorient
def reorient(
    kernel_alive:bool=True, skills:tuple=()
):
The system reminder placed after a compacted or otherwise rewritten conversation.



print(reorient(skills=('nbdev', 'fossick')))

When the kernel restarted, the reminder says the namespace is empty and tells the model to rebuild its variables. When the kernel survived, the reminder tells the model to inspect its variables with inspect_python() and not to rebuild them.

assert reorient(kernel_alive=False) != reorient()
print(reorient(kernel_alive=False)[:180])


assert 'inspect_python' in reorient() and 'list_vars' not in reorient()

title: runtime
text:
Notices on the way in
Before a prompt reaches the model, prompt_notices checks it with a few string tests and returns notices: short instructions that tell the model how to treat the prompt. They follow the UserPromptSubmit hook in Answer.AI’s aai-coding prompts, and each one prevents a mistake models often make.

A prompt ending in ? is a question. The model answers it and stops, without starting the work it implies (Q_NOTICE).
A prompt containing “please read”, “read the” or “have a look at” asks the model to read the target in full before answering (READ_NOTICE).
A bare approval such as “go”, “ok” or “do it” approves only what the user explicitly agreed to, not everything the model proposed earlier (APPROVAL_NOTICE).
A prompt starting with “BTW” is a side request. The model answers it and then goes back to the task it was on (BTW_NOTICE).
A prompt starting with a verb such as fix, add, run or rename, or ending in as NAME, asks for action. The model does the work and checks it before replying (ACTION_NOTICE).

Three one-character prompts are shortcuts and get only their own notice: . continues the agreed task, ; asks for the last answer in simpler words, and , asks what the user needs to answer next.


source

notices_block
def notices_block(
    prompt
):
The notices for prompt as one reminder to append to it, or ''.




source

prompt_notices
def prompt_notices(
    prompt
):
Notices a submitted prompt earns, from aai-coding’s UserPromptSubmit hook.


The question below gets Q_NOTICE and nothing else. A bare “go” gets APPROVAL_NOTICE:

test_eq(prompt_notices('can you fix the exporter?'), [Q_NOTICE])
prompt_notices('go')

A prompt can earn several notices. Here an imperative gets one, a side request that asks for a read gets two, and “thanks” gets none:

[len(prompt_notices(p)) for p in ('fix the exporter', 'BTW please read nbs/01_runtime.ipynb', 'thanks')]

notices_block is the function the agent calls. It wraps the notices in one <system-reminder> block, ready to append to the prompt, or returns '' when there are none.

print(notices_block('ok'))


test_eq(notices_block('thanks'), '')
notices_block('thanks')

title: runtime
section: Fitting a notebook into the prompt
text:
Fitting a notebook into the prompt
A prompt can carry the user’s open notebook inside a <notebook> tag, one <cell> per cell. Each cell has a compact attribute that the user sets: keep, auto or discard. compact_notebook_context leaves the prompt alone when it fits. When it does not, it removes discard cells, then auto cells, each in notebook order, until the prompt fits. It never removes a keep cell. A <context-compacted> tag records how many cells were left out.
fits is a function that says whether a prompt fits. The agent passes the backend’s fits, so the decision is made against the real window of the model in use.


source

compact_notebook_context
def compact_notebook_context(
    prompt, fits
):
Reduce a tagged notebook only when prompt does not fit. A keep cell is never removed.


The notebook below has three cells, one with each setting, and a question about it. When everything fits, the prompt comes back unchanged:

nb = '''<notebook path=analysis.ipynb>
<cell id=1 compact="discard">print(load_everything())  # 900 lines of output</cell>
<cell id=2 compact="auto">df = read_csv('sales.csv')</cell>
<cell id=3 compact="keep">model.fit(df)  # the cell the question is about</cell>
</notebook>

why did the fit fail?'''
print(compact_notebook_context(nb, fits=lambda s: True))

With a lower limit the discard cell goes first, and <context-compacted> records it:

out = compact_notebook_context(nb, fits=lambda s: len(s) < 270)
print(out)

A lower limit still removes the auto cell as well. The keep cell stays, even though the result is still over the limit, because the user chose to keep it.

tight = compact_notebook_context(nb, fits=lambda s: len(s) < 150)
test_eq('compact="keep"' in tight, True)
test_eq('load_everything' in tight, False)
print(tight)

title: runtime
text:
The compactor
Compactor decides when a backend’s conversation is due for compaction, and carries it out. It keeps the most recent messages as they are. It replaces everything older with a summary, followed by the reorient reminder. The summary comes from a second model call, made through the summariser(prompt, sp) function you pass to compact. With strategy='surgical' it uses surgical_history instead and calls no model.
due(backend) says whether the backend has crossed its threshold. compact returns the summary, or '' when it did nothing, and note says what happened either way. on_compact, when given, is called with each new summary. If the summarizer fails or returns nothing, the conversation is left alone. When you give the summarizer’s window as summary_ctx, no request is larger than it. fold_summary splits a history that is too large for one request into runs that each fit (transcript_runs). It summarises the first run and updates that summary with each run after it. A history of any length can compact this way. A failed or empty call is retried at half and then a quarter of the request size.
Compaction has its own class and is not a rishi callback. It needs a second model call and then replaces the first model’s history. A callback does not do both.


source

Compactor
def Compactor(
    reserve:NoneType=None, # None reads config.toml's `window.reserve`, else `RESERVE`, each time
    keep_recent:NoneType=None, # None reads `window.keep_recent`, else `KEEP_RECENT`
    auto:bool=True, # the agent compacts on crossing the threshold only when true; `Compactor` itself ignores it
    kernel_alive:bool=True, # whether the kernel survived; passed to `reorient`
    on_compact:NoneType=None, # called with each new summary
    strategy:str='summary', # 'summary' or 'surgical'; 'surgical' calls no model
    soft:NoneType=None, # None reads `compaction.soft`, else `SOFT_LINE`
    hard:NoneType=None, # None reads `compaction.hard`, else `HARD_LINE`
):
Decide when to compact, and do it.


budget(ctx) is how many tokens of recent conversation survive compaction: KEEP_RECENT (20,000), capped at half of what the window holds besides the system prompt and tools (overhead). Without the cap, a 4k model would count its whole conversation as recent, find nothing older to summarise, and report everything is recent; nothing to compact until the engine refused the turn. compact also keeps at most about half of the conversation, and the part it keeps always starts at a user message.

c = Compactor()
c.budget(200_000), c.budget(32_768), c.budget(4096)


test_eq(c.budget(4096), 2048)
test_eq(c.note, 'not compacted')
class _Held:
    def __init__(self, used, ctx): self.used_tokens, self.spec = used, type('Spec', (), {'ctx': ctx})()
lines = Compactor(soft=150_000, hard=250_000)
test_eq([lines.due(_Held(u, 1_000_000)) for u in (100_000, 200_000, 260_000)], [False, False, True])
test_eq([lines.soft_due(_Held(u, 1_000_000)) for u in (100_000, 200_000, 260_000)], [False, True, False])
assert lines.due(_Held(190_000, 200_000)), 'a small window keeps its own threshold'
test_eq(done_items('## Progress\n### Done\n- [x] export fixed\n- [x] tests green\n\n### In Progress\n- [ ] docs'), '- [x] export fixed\n- [x] tests green')
test_eq(done_items('## Goal\nnothing finished'), '')
c.strategy

Compacting needs a running backend and a summarizer. testing defines doubles for both and runs a compaction end to end.

title: runtime
text:
Answers, without the thinking
Reasoning models think before they answer. Some runtimes return the thinking in a separate channel. Others leave it in the reply, wrapped in <think>...</think>. The agent’s one-shot jobs read the reply as data, such as a label, a summary or a completion to insert. The thinking has to come off first. A classifier that returned the model’s reasoning would return no label.
answer_only removes the thinking from a finished reply, using urai’s split_think.


source

answer_only
def answer_only(
    text
):
A one-shot reply with the model’s thinking removed, however the runtime left it.


In the simple case the thinking is wrapped in a pair of tags:

answer_only('<think>7 times 6. Six sevens are 42.</think>\n\n42')

Some chat templates open the <think> block in the prompt itself, so the reply starts inside the thinking and only the closing tag appears. answer_only handles that too. A reply that opens a block and never closes it, because it hit the output cap, has no answer and gives ''. A reply with no tags comes back as it is.

answer_only('Six sevens are 42. They asked for only the number.\n</think>\n\n42')


test_eq(answer_only('<think>cut off at the cap and never closed'), '')
test_eq(answer_only('thinking, and then the cap hit\n'), 'thinking, and then the cap hit')
test_eq(answer_only('42'), '42')
answer_only('<think>a</think>yes')

A model whose template opens the thinking block does so at every step of a turn. After each tool call, the next reply begins inside a new thought. prefills_think tells whether a model’s template does this. It renders a one-message prompt and looks for an unclosed <think>. For such a model RishiBackend passes the stream through a ThinkFilter. The filter drops text until it sees </think>, lets the rest through, and starts dropping again after each tool call. Use answer_only on a finished reply and ThinkFilter on a stream. The filter also counts the characters of thinking (thought) and of answer (answer). The backend uses the counts to report a turn that spent all its output thinking. One-shot jobs avoid the problem by asking the model not to think.


source

ThinkFilter
def ThinkFilter():
Drop a template-opened thinking block out of a raw chunk stream. A tool call re-arms it.




source

prefills_think
def prefills_think(
    chat
):
Whether this model’s chat template opens a <think> block and leaves the model to close it.


The closing tag can be split across chunks, and the filter still finds it. The answer comes through whole:

def chunks(*texts): return [{'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': t}]} for t in texts]
def texts(chunks): return ''.join(resp_text(c) for c in chunks)
f = ThinkFilter()
texts(f(chunks('Six sevens', ' are 42.\n</th', 'ink>\n\n', '42')))


test_eq(texts(ThinkFilter()(chunks('deliberating', '</think>', 'yes'))), 'yes')

tool = {'content': [{'type': 'tool_call', 'name': 'search_code', 'arguments': {}}]}
out = list(ThinkFilter()(chunks('think 1', '</think>', 'calling ') + [tool] + chunks('think 2', '</think>', 'done')))
test_eq(texts(out), 'calling done')
test_eq(out[1], tool)

f = ThinkFilter()
test_eq(texts(f(chunks('cut off at the cap'))), '')
test_eq((f.thinking, f.thought, f.answer), (True, 18, 0))

f = ThinkFilter()
test_eq(texts(f(chunks('deliberating', '</think>\n\n'))), '')
test_eq((f.thinking, f.answer), (False, 0))

title: runtime
text:
Usage
Usage holds the token counts and cost of a turn: tokens in and out, cached tokens, tokens written to the cache, reasoning tokens, the cost in dollars, and the number of turns. Two Usage values add up. A session’s total is sum of its turns. Subtracting an earlier running total from a later one gives what was used in between, and no field goes below 0. Its repr is a one-line summary.


source

Usage
def Usage(
    model:str='', input:int=0, output:int=0, total:int=0, cached:int=0, cache_write:int=0, reasoning:int=0,
    cost:float=0.0, turns:int=0, estimated:bool=False
)->None:
Token counts and cost for a turn or a session; values add up. estimated marks a cost that holds an estimate from the tokens.




source

oneshot_tokens
def oneshot_tokens(
    ctx
):
The default reply budget for a one-shot call in a window of ctx tokens.



a = Usage(model='anthropic/claude-sonnet-5', input=12_000, output=800, total=12_800, cached=9_000, cost=0.041, turns=1); a

The sum takes the model name from the right-hand value. A session that switched models reports the model it uses now:

b = Usage(model='openai/gpt-5.6-terra', input=3_000, output=200, total=3_200, cost=0.008, turns=1)
sum([a, b], None)


test_eq((a + None).total, a.total)
test_eq(sum([a, b], None).turns, 2)
a.dict()['cached']

title: runtime
text:
Backend
Backend is the contract the agent uses to talk to a model. One backend holds one conversation. It starts the model on first use, sends a message with send or streams the reply with stream, asks one-shot questions with oneshot, counts tokens, and replaces or restores the conversation’s history. Subclasses supply the engine-specific methods whose names start with an underscore. RishiBackend, further down, is the one the agent uses.
send, stream and oneshot do not raise when the model fails. A model that cannot start, a stream that breaks and an empty reply all become text: note holds the latest status, problems keeps the last 20 problem lines, and turn_error says why the last turn failed. A caller can always show the user what the backend returned.
The examples below run the base class itself, which has no engine, to show these rules.


source

fit_content
def fit_content(
    c, room, save, how:str='', count:NoneType=None, tail:int=0
):
Message content c within room tokens: the newest pictures that fit stay and the rest are saved and named, then text past the room becomes an excerpt. The last tail characters of the last text part are always kept.




source

excerpt
def excerpt(
    text, room, save, how:str='', count:NoneType=None, tail:int=0
):
text cut to its head and its end within room tokens, the last tail characters always kept; the whole goes to save(data, suffix) and the note names the file.




source

omitted
def omitted(
    n, path, how:str=''
):
The note an excerpt carries where n characters were cut: where the whole is, and how to read it.




source

trim_hist
def trim_hist(
    hist, need, count:NoneType=None, keep:int=2, save:NoneType=None, how:str=''
):
Free about need tokens from hist in place, the oldest tool results first and then the oldest pictures; the last keep messages stay whole. With save, a trimmed result is kept in a file its note names. Returns what was freed.




source

msg_tokens
def msg_tokens(
    m, count:NoneType=None
):
One history message’s tokens: its text, its tool calls’ arguments, and img_tokens() for each picture.




source

img_tokens
def img_tokens():




source

margin
def margin():




source

Backend
def Backend(
    spec, sp:str='', tools:tuple=(), approve:NoneType=None, tool_max_len:NoneType=None, shared:bool=False, **kw
):
The contract a model engine meets: start, send or stream a turn, count tokens, and replace history.




source

cap_breach
def cap_breach(
    rows, at:bool=False
):
The first of rows, each (cap, limit, spent, ...), whose spent is past its limit, or with at has reached it. A limit of None is never passed. None when no row is.




source

BudgetExceeded
def BudgetExceeded(
    cap, limit, spent, estimated:bool=False, stopped:bool=True
):
A one-shot began at, or ended past, a budget. cap is ‘max_cost’ or ‘max_tokens’, limit that budget, spent what the agent had spent, estimated whether spent holds an estimate, and stopped is False when the provider call may still finish and spend. This is a soft spend cap, not a billing ceiling. Parallel calls can overshoot by the calls already in flight.




source

StreamUnsupported
def StreamUnsupported(
    *args, **kwargs
):
A one-shot stream asked of a backend that cannot stream one. Nothing was sent, and no whole reply was buffered in its place.




source

cancel_hit
def cancel_hit(
    e
):
Whether e is rishi’s OneShotCancelled: a one-shot that cancel() ended, or whose stream would not close. Only a loaded rishi can have raised one, so nothing is imported here.




source

deadline_hit
def deadline_hit(
    e
):
Whether e is a call that outran its deadline: a TimeoutError that says whether the call stopped, as rishi’s ClaudeDeadline does.




source

OneshotTimeout
def OneshotTimeout(
    route, elapsed, stopped
):
A one-shot outran its deadline. route names the model it ran on, elapsed is the seconds since the one-shot began, and stopped is False when the provider call may still finish and spend.




source

DeadlineUnsupported
def DeadlineUnsupported(
    *args, **kwargs
):
A one-shot asked for a deadline of a backend that cannot hold one. Nothing was sent.


The base class has no engine, so start fails. It returns None and records the NotImplementedError in note instead of raising it:

b = Backend(resolve('gemma-e4b'))
b.start(), b.note

send on a backend that could not start returns the same note, and the failure is in problems. A caller that never checks for errors still shows the user something true:

test_eq(b.send('hello'), b.note)
b.problems

pending_tokens(msg) estimates what a message will add to the conversation. Each image or audio part counts as img_tokens(), which is config.toml’s window.image_tokens or else IMG_TOKENS (1,600). A 120 KB image does not count as the tokens of its bytes:

test_eq(b.pending_tokens([bytes(120_000), 'what is this?']),
        b.pending_tokens('what is this?') + IMG_TOKENS)

problem adds a line to problems. It skips a line identical to the one before it and keeps the latest 20:

for _ in range(30): b.problem('ERROR: oom')
len(b.problems), b.problems[-1]

Before the model has started there is no tokenizer, so count_tokens falls back to estimate_tokens. used_tokens is the size of the conversation so far, and pct_full is that size as a share of the window:

b.count_tokens('a prompt of some length'), b.used_tokens, round(b.pct_full, 3)

fits(msg) says whether the conversation plus msg still fits in the window, keeping back a quarter of the window for the reply, but no less than 128 and no more than 1,024 tokens. This is the fits that compact_notebook_context receives. The gemma-e4b spec used here has a 16,384-token window, and a spec with no window (ctx=0) fits anything:

big = 'x' * 200_000
b.fits('a short prompt'), b.fits(big)


test_eq(Backend(ModelSpec('unbounded', 'remote', 'v/m', ctx=0)).fits(big), True)
b.spec.ctx

fits charges the pending message margin() more than its estimate, config.toml’s window.margin or EST_MARGIN (1.15), because a count from characters runs short on code and escapes. A hosted chat’s token_count is what its last step reported. After replace_hist or restore_hist, used_tokens gives window_tokens until the chat reports again. window_tokens estimates the briefing, the tool schemas and every message. Without it, the old count stays after a compaction, fits keeps failing and each retry compacts again. A hosted chat that has not reported a step yet also gives window_tokens. A backend that has not started gives the estimate for the conversation it will restore. The first turn after a resume is measured before it goes out.
trim(need) frees tokens from the oldest tool results first, then the oldest pictures, and leaves the newest two messages whole. With spill set, a trimmed result is written whole to a file first, and its note names the file and says how to read it (how). shrink_recent(need) cuts the newest two messages that a person or a tool wrote, largest first. trim leaves those messages whole. fit_content(content, room, save) does the cutting. It keeps the newest pictures that fit and saves and names the rest. Text past the room becomes an excerpt: its head and its end around a note such as …[52,000 characters omitted; full text at <path>; read it in pieces with view_file(path, start=N)]. Nothing is lost. The whole is in the file:

from urai import mk_msgs
t = trim_hist(h := mk_msgs(['look at this', 'done']) + [{'role': 'tool', 'tool_call_id': 'c', 'content': 'r' * 9000}] + mk_msgs(['and now', 'ok']), 100)
test_eq(h[2]['content'], TRIMMED)
assert t > 100 and h[-1]['content'] == 'ok'


saved = []
def save(data, suffix): saved.append(data); return Path(f'/tmp/full{len(saved)}{suffix}')
cut = fit_content('head ' + 'x' * 20_000 + ' end', 200, save, 'read it in pieces with view_file(path, start=N)')
assert cut.startswith('head') and cut.endswith(' end') and saved[0].endswith(b' end')
pics = fit_content([b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n1', b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n2', b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n3', 'which?'], 2 * IMG_TOKENS, save)
test_eq(pics[0], b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n3')
assert 'which?' in pics
print(cut[:60] + ' ... ' + cut[-160:])

oneshot(prompt) asks one question in a throwaway conversation and returns the answer with any thinking removed. It cuts the prompt to fit the window, keeping its end, and returns if_busy (by default '') while another call is using the backend. It returns '' and records a problem when the call fails. This subclass stands in for a model that leaves its thinking in the reply:

class Thinker(Backend):
    def _start(self): return self
    def _oneshot(self, prompt, sp, max_tokens): return 'They want one label.\n</think>\n\nsuccess'

test_eq(Thinker(resolve('gemma-e4b')).oneshot('the tests pass'), 'success')
Thinker(resolve('gemma-e4b')).oneshot('the tests pass')

replace_hist, restore_hist and revise_last_assistant raise when no model is running. There is no conversation to change. replace_hist(summary, keep) is what Compactor calls. snapshot_hist and restore_hist save and restore a conversation, for branching. resume_hist hands a saved conversation to a backend that has not started yet, and applies it when the model starts.

test_fail(lambda: b.replace_hist('summary'))
test_fail(lambda: b.restore_hist([]))
test_fail(lambda: b.revise_last_assistant('...'))

title: runtime
text:
RishiBackend
RishiBackend is the only implementation of Backend, because rishi runs every model, local or hosted. It turns a ModelSpec (a model’s name, runtime, id and window, from core) into a rishi Chat, converts rishi’s usage into Usage, and handles what differs between runtimes:

The window goes to LiteRT as the engine’s token ceiling, max_num_tokens, and to llama.cpp and ollama as n_ctx.
A Claude model is asked for high reasoning effort (CLAUDE_EFFORT) unless a higher-precedence source names another level. In order of precedence these are an effort argument to the backend, RAMABANA_EFFORT, the model’s effort setting and runtime.effort.
On MLX, one-shot questions run in a separate conversation on the same engine, so a completion never sees earlier completions.
A local model’s window is set from the window it was trained for, capped by Ramabana’s limit for that model, and narrowed again if the engine reports a smaller one.
When a hosted service refuses the tool schemas, the backend moves that model to the tags channel and retries once. On that channel the schemas travel in the system prompt and calls come back as <tool_call> blocks in the text.
When a reply on the tags channel describes a tool call instead of making one, the backend sends one reminder (TAG_REMINDER) asking the model to make the call.

rishi adds two callbacks to a chat by default: a reminder on every message, and a sliding window that forgets old messages without summarising them. RishiBackend removes both (ROUTINE_CBS). Compactor does that job. LiteRT runs the tool loop inside the engine. The text a model writes before a tool call never reaches Ramabana. QUIET_RUNTIMES lists such runtimes, and narrates is False for them.
LiteRT models run on the GPU by default. rishi asks for the GPU, and falls back to the CPU with a warning when the build has no GPU support. RAMABANA_LITERT_BACKEND=cpu pins a model to the CPU, and gpu asks for the GPU explicitly. The runtime.litert_backend setting does the same. A backend= argument, or eng_kw={'backend': ...}, takes precedence over the variable. RISHI_LITERT_GPU=0 stops rishi asking for the GPU at all.


source

make_backend
def make_backend(
    spec, **kw
):




source

getattr
def __getattr__(
    name
):




source

RishiBackend
def RishiBackend(
    *a, max_steps:int=40, **kw
):
The Backend that runs every model, local or hosted, through rishi’s Chat.




source

use_chat
def use_chat(
    f
):
Build model conversations with f for the duration, instead of rishi’s Chat.


use_chat(f) makes backends build their conversations with f instead of rishi’s Chat, for the duration of a with block. testing uses it to install urai’s CachedChat, which replays a real model’s recorded answers with no weights and no network. Here f is a stub chat that answers from a script. Nothing is downloaded:

from ramabana.core import ModelSpec

built = []
class StubChat:
    def __init__(self, model, **kw): built.append((model, kw)); self.hist = []
    def oneshot(self, prompt, sp='', think=None, max_tokens=None): return 'replayed'
    def close(self): pass

with use_chat(StubChat):
    be = make_backend(ModelSpec('stub', 'remote', 'openai/gpt-x', 8000))
    assert be.start() is not None
    test_eq(built[0][0], 'openai/gpt-x')
    test_eq(be.oneshot('a cheap job'), 'replayed')
    test_eq(be._usage().total, 0)
test_eq(_MK_CHAT, None)

Ramabana does not set LiteRT’s constrained decoding, since rishi turns it on itself when there are tools. A conv_kw you pass goes through unchanged:

def _a_tool(query: str) -> str:
    "A tool."
    return ''
kw = make_backend(resolve('gemma-e4b'), tools=[_a_tool])._runtime_kw()
assert 'enable_constrained_decoding' not in kw.get('conv_kw', {})
assert 'constrained_decoding_config' not in kw.get('conv_kw', {})
mine = dict(constrained_decoding_config='mine')
test_eq(make_backend(resolve('gemma-e4b'), tools=[_a_tool], conv_kw=mine)._runtime_kw()['conv_kw'], mine)

title: runtime
text:
Runs
A run is one piece of model work that can be cancelled: the turn the user started (kind='root'), or a sub-agent that the turn delegated to (kind='child', made with child). Runs form a tree. Cancelling a run cancels everything under it, and the tool calls of the whole tree count against one budget, through draw.
A run starts pending, becomes running with start, and ends completed, failed, cancelled, detached or terminated. cancel asks the backend to stop and waits up to grace seconds. A run whose backend does not stop in time is detached: the caller treats it as over and ignores anything the model sends later. terminate closes the backend outright.
A run also keeps what the user should see while it works. status is the last line the model wrote before its latest tool call. notes keeps up to 100 such messages for the now pane, the live view beside the terminal (pane), and write appends a line to the run’s transcript file when it has one. tell queues a message from the user for a running sub-agent, and drain_inbox hands the queued messages over. air returns a reminder to tell the user where the work stands once 8 tool calls in a row have gone by with less than 100 characters said before them. repeated counts identical calls with identical results in a row, so the agent can tell a model that it is looping.


source

Run

    id:str, kind:str='root', question:str='', model:str='', parent:object=None, grace:float=0.25,
    state:str='pending', started:float=0.0, ended:float=0.0, backend:object=None, log:object=None, status:str='',
    answer:str=''

A foreground or delegated model call with bounded cancellation.

    hist

The text of the message that made the latest tool call in hist, or ’’.




source

status_line
def status_line(
    text, n:int=80
):
The last line of text worth showing as a status, without bullet or bold, clipped to n chars.


A Run is one foreground or delegated model call. It has a state: pending, running, cancelling, cancelled, detached, terminated, completed or failed. It also has a one-line status, a list of children (the runs of its sub-agents) and an inbox of user messages. tell(text) queues a message in the inbox and drain_inbox takes the queued messages. cancel(grace) asks the backend to stop, then waits up to grace seconds (default 0.25) for the run and its children to finish.
A run’s status comes from the text streamed since the last tool call (hear). When nothing was streamed, it comes from the message in the backend’s history that made the call. status_line takes the last line worth showing, without list markers or bold, cut to 80 characters:

class _Said:
    hist = [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'go'},
            {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'Thought about it.\nReading the loader.', 'tool_calls': [{'id': '1'}]}]

r = Run('run_status')
r.start(_Said())
test_eq(r.on_call().status, 'Reading the loader.')
r.hear('Checking the '); r.hear('tests.\n> 🧠 hmm')
test_eq(r.on_call().status, 'Checking the tests.')
test_eq(status_line('x ' * 60), ('x ' * 40).strip())
test_eq(status_line('- **Reading** it.\n```'), 'Reading it.')

A run whose backend stops when asked ends cancelled. A run whose backend cannot stop ends detached when its grace period runs out:

import threading, time

class _Blocking:
    def __init__(self, stoppable=True): self.stoppable, self.released = stoppable, threading.Event()
    def cancel(self):
        if self.stoppable: self.released.set()

r = Run('run_cancelled', grace=.05)
r.start(_Blocking())
threading.Thread(target=lambda: (r.backend.released.wait(), r.finish()), daemon=True).start()
test_eq(r.cancel().state, 'cancelled')

r = Run('run_detached', grace=.01)
r.start(_Blocking(False))
test_eq(r.cancel().state, 'detached')

current_run() returns the run that the current thread or async task is working for, and run_context(run) sets it for a with block. The agent sets it around each turn and each sub-agent. Code deep inside a tool call can then find its run without receiving it as an argument.

    run

Make run the current run inside a with block.

current_run
def current_run():


Once its run is cancelled, a backend’s stream stops yielding, drops what the model sends later, and does not retry:

class _CancelStream(Backend):
    def __init__(self):
        from ramabana.core import ModelSpec
        super().__init__(ModelSpec('cancel-test', 'fake', 'fake/cancel', ctx=1000))
        self.first, self.release, self.calls, self.recoveries = threading.Event(), threading.Event(), 0, 0
    def _start(self): return self
    def _stream(self, msg, **kw):
        self.calls += 1
        yield 'first'
        self.first.set(); self.release.wait()
        yield 'late'
    def cancel(self): self.release.set(); return True
    def _usage(self): return Usage()
    def _recover(self, e): self.recoveries += 1; return True

be, run, chunks = _CancelStream(), Run('run_late', grace=.05), []
run.start(be)
t = threading.Thread(target=lambda: chunks.extend(be.stream('x', run=run)), daemon=True)
t.start(); assert be.first.wait(.2)
run.cancel(); t.join(.2)
test_eq(chunks, ['first'])
test_eq((be.calls, be.recoveries), (1, 0))

terminate ends a run even after it was detached, and closes its backend:

class _Closable:
    def __init__(self): self.closed = threading.Event()
    def close(self): self.closed.set()

r = Run('run_terminated', grace=0)
r.start(_Closable()); r.detach(); r.terminate()
test_eq(r.state, 'terminated')
assert r.backend.closed.wait(.2)

title: Coding patterns
text:
This page is one of the five skills that ship with Ramabana. A skill is a piece of markdown that the agent reads when a task calls for it, so that the guidance costs nothing in turns that do not need it. The system prompt lists every skill the session found with a one-line description, the read_skill tool returns one in full, and /skill coding_patterns prints it in a terminal session.
The skill’s text is this module’s docstring. nbdev builds it from the description line above and the exported markdown cell below, and pyproject.toml registers the module under the pyskills entry point as coding_patterns, so any agent built on shalya can find it once Ramabana is installed. To change what the agent reads, edit the exported cell.
The agent reads this skill before it writes, reviews or refactors code. When the skill is present, the system prompt tells it to.
Read this before writing, reviewing, refactoring, or assessing code. These are Answer.AI’s coding standards adapted to Ramabana’s tools and nbdev workflow.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Improve shared tooling
A finished task helps once. A better tool helps every later task, every later session and every agent, and ergonomics count as much as capability. Most code you have read was written by people who put up with tool friction rather than fix it. The workaround is your default. Here the tools are ours and one edit away. When repository-owned tooling grates, fix it or say so. Never quietly work around it, and do not expand the current task without the user’s agreement.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Read before writing
Use search_code before writing non-trivial code: the answer or the established pattern is usually already in the repository or an installed package. Read the exact source before editing it. Use grep for exhaustive literal audits such as call sites and renames. Match the surrounding design unless the request is specifically to change it.

title: Coding patterns
section: Every construct must earn its place
text:
Every construct must earn its place
Readers assume everything present is necessary. Seeing str(x) on something already a str, they stop and wonder what it guards against. When the answer is nothing, they paid for a mystery with no payoff. The same goes for defensive copies, speculative exception handling, redundant coercions, unused parameters, abstractions and compatibility branches. Know why a construct is needed before adding it, and leave it out when you cannot say. The cost doubles in nbdev projects, where the examples are the documentation.
Knowing why you need a construct does not mean waiting for someone to ask for it. A user who finds a gap concludes the library cannot do it and moves on. Judge a library feature by whether the design calls for it and users would expect it.
Comments state constraints the code cannot express. Never write one to say where a change came from, what the next line does, or why the change is correct. That comment addresses the reviewer, not the next reader. It becomes noise the moment the change is merged. Add type hints, docstrings and abstractions only where they improve the public contract or the surrounding code consistently uses them. Prefer concise readable code over verbose enterprise boilerplate.
Make the requested change and no unrelated cleanup. Never discard edits already in the working tree.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Prefer the fastcore ecosystem
When choosing dependencies, first check whether fastcore or another existing project dependency already provides the capability. Do not add a dependency where the repository already has an adequate primitive, and do not hand-roll what a dependency already does.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Plain commands are the contract
The bare invocation is the contract: pytest -q, nbdev-export. Project configuration exists precisely so the plain command does the right thing, and then every invocation is short, identical and instantly readable. Use the command the repository documents in its README, pyproject.toml or Makefile.
A flag, redirect or pipe states that this one call has a requirement the defaults do not cover. Used that way it carries information. The reader stops, asks why, and finds an answer. Sprinkled defensively on every call, decorations destroy that signal. Every command looks exceptional so none is, and the one deliberate flag is indistinguishable from habit. Transcripts compound the damage, since each decorated call teaches later calls to decorate too.

Wanting the same flag on every run means a missing configuration line. Promote it and go back to the bare command: pytest --timeout 300 on every run becomes timeout = 300 under [tool.pytest.ini_options].
Do not check-then-apply when applying is the goal. Apply formatters when formatting is the goal, and reserve check-only modes for final verification and CI.
Run commands and read their complete output. Never pipe diagnostics through head, tail or any filter that hides failures. The truncation is decided before the output exists. It hides the surprises worth seeing. Never merge stderr into stdout with 2>&1. Separated, a crash is unmissable.
Where output genuinely cannot come back inline, redirect stdout and stderr to separate files and read both.
A real one-off requirement gets its flag once, with the reason stated alongside, and disappears again on the next call.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Preserve docments and delegation
Docments are trailing parameter comments used as API documentation, and they are the house signature style here. Never remove them while refactoring. For a signature with docments or many parameters, keep the opening parenthesis on the definition line, put one parameter on each indented line, and put the closing ): alone at definition indentation.
Where **kwargs passes through to a known callable with useful named parameters, use @delegates(callee) and name the collector kwargs, which is what delegates requires. Do not use @delegates where the callee itself exposes only **kwargs.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Raw strings by default
Write any non-trivial string literal as a raw string: regexes, prompt and skill text, code or markup inside strings, paths with escapes, and anything multi-line. In a plain string a stray backslash-n or backslash-d either errors or silently corrupts. Each miss costs a round trip to diagnose and another to fix. The r costs nothing when no escapes are present. Make it the default rather than the exception.
The exception is a skill body, which is an exported markdown cell and reaches the module as a plain docstring that nbdev writes without the r. Spell escapes out in words there rather than showing them literally.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Tests earn their place
All code costs something to write, maintain and read. Tests cost most. Every test has to keep passing forever, is read by every future contributor, and has to be revised whenever the behaviour it pins changes. Never write a test as a reflex, and do not aim anywhere near full coverage. A test earns its place only when one of three things is true.

It documents an idea. In nbdev notebooks the examples are the documentation.
The logic is intricate enough that you had to think carefully to get it right: edge cases, parsing, arithmetic, tricky conditionals, the places a future change could silently break it.
The code assumes something about an external system, such as a file format, an API’s response shape or another tool’s behaviour, that could change one day and that we want to hear about when it does. These have to exercise the real thing, because a mock merely restates our assumption.

Wiring and orchestration get no tests: re-exports, delegations, one-line glue, and functions that only sequence calls to other tools. A test there asserts that Python works and pins down internals we may want to change. The strong tell is a test that needs recording fakes or mock collaborators to reach the code, which tests a transcript of the implementation rather than logic. Extract the logic into a small pure function and test that, or do not test at all.
For a behaviour change, work red-green: write the test first, run it to see it fail, make the change, run it again to see it pass. A regression test has to fail for the reported bug before the fix and pass after it. In notebooks there are no separate test cells. The red-green check applies to the assertion you actually added or revised.

Prefer as few tests as possible. One test that walks through many checks is more readable and faster than many small ones.
A check worth keeping goes in a test file or a notebook cell, never left as an ad-hoc command. In a notebook the checks made while exploring often are the narrative. They stay as example cells.
Assert the logic, not incidentals. Check what the behaviour guarantees, never byte-exact renderings, exact reprs or field order. A test comparing a whole output string locks in formatting decisions that were never the point. Never use a test to lock in behaviour unless that exact behaviour is part of the contract.
Do not run slow or network-touching suites until finishing a session, or after a change likely to affect them. Run the fast checks while you work; a final verification still runs every slow check the change could affect.

In nbdev projects the notebook is source, documentation, examples and tests at once. Edit the source notebook rather than the generated Python, preserve docments and explanatory structure, export with the project’s nbdev command, and run the documented tests.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Configuration and versioning
Read from standard locations rather than duplicating configuration: project settings from pyproject.toml under the package’s own table, release notes from .github/release.yml. Infer what can be inferred, such as the package name from [project].name. Bundle data files inside the package and read them with importlib.resources.
Version bumps belong to a release, never to a change. Bump immediately after releasing. The tree then always carries the next release’s version. A downstream pin is different. It belongs to the change that creates the dependency. When a change makes one package consume another’s new behaviour, stamp the consumer’s pin in the same session. A pin deferred to release time is a forgotten pin.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Handoffs, events, and honest state

Treat acceptance of background work as a lifecycle boundary. Register ownership atomically, under the same lock as competing starts and shutdown. Wake both sides on timeout, rejection and shutdown. A worker that registers after a rejection stops and emits no accepted-work event.
Make replay or terminal completion an explicit state, not a guess from the latest event. A later bookkeeping event must not erase a terminal sequence. Reset it only when the next unit of work is accepted. Keep application errors separate from transport errors, so an application failure does not trigger connection recovery.
When you move work or response ownership between layers, audit the old producer, every consumer, and both the success and failure paths. Keep every response field callers read. Find and update all callers and tests that expect the old contract.
Keep the plan truthful. Mark done steps done, keep one step active, and leave the rest pending. A [done] note inside a pending step does not complete it.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Ramabana workflow
Use Ramabana’s native tools rather than instructions written for another harness:

search_code finds repository and installed-package behaviour.
view_file or the notebook cell tools read the exact source before editing.
replace_text or edit_cell make narrow, auditable changes (edit_file when the exhash group is on).
edits is a list of {"oldText", "newText"} objects and commands a list of lists: send them as structured values, not as a JSON string. A refused edit means nothing changed: fix the payload rather than resending it.
inspect_python reads live state without mutation. run_python performs requested transformations in new bindings.
run_shell verifies edits with the repository’s own commands.
read_skill loads specialized workflows before using them. Read write_docs for the prose that ships with code, write_prose for narrative writing, and theory for the design a codebase is derived from.

Writing the code does not complete the task. Run the relevant tests or checks, read the result, fix failures, and report exactly what you verified. Never claim a file changed or a check passed without tool evidence from the current session. Before reporting a behaviour change, have an independent subagent review the exact changed files and tests, and check its findings against the real diff and test output.

title: Write docs
text:
This page is one of the five skills that ship with Ramabana. A skill is a piece of markdown that the agent reads when a task calls for it, so that the guidance costs nothing in turns that do not need it. The system prompt lists every skill the session found with a one-line description, the read_skill tool returns one in full, and /skill write_docs prints it in a terminal session.
The skill’s text is this module’s docstring. nbdev builds it from the description line above and the exported markdown cell below, and pyproject.toml registers the module under the pyskills entry point as write_docs, so any agent built on shalya can find it once Ramabana is installed. To change what the agent reads, edit the exported cell.
The agent reads this skill before it writes the prose that ships with code: docstrings, comments, READMEs, changelogs, commit messages and pull request descriptions. Its companion write_prose covers narrative writing.
Read this before writing the prose that ships with code: docstrings, code comments, READMEs, API and reference docs, changelogs, PR descriptions, commit messages, and messages to a colleague. The register is GOV.UK/GDS house style with ASD-STE100’s discipline. Very plain, very direct, no author’s voice. Narrative prose has an author on the page; reference prose has only the contract. For blog posts, essays and announcements read write_prose instead.
Here is a passage from a design doc, written in this register:
Write like that. Each sentence states one fact and stops. Each guarantee is its own sentence. The negative guarantee is stated too: what the gateway never does. Every status is named by its real identifier. Sentences this uniform would read as monotone in an essay. In reference prose they are correct. Readers scan, take the fact they came for, and leave.
Here is the same passage before editing:
Do NOT write like that. Nothing in it is false. In a blog post it might pass. As reference prose it fails. Each sentence carries several facts. The key guarantee is an aside. The final state gets a flourish instead of its name. The opener announces the section instead of starting it. A question delays a fact the reader came for.
The numbers refer to the [bracketed] markers in both passages. Where a number appears in each, the pair is the failing and the working version of the same thing.
Entries 7 to 12, 14, 17, 22 and 24 to 26 are tells the passage pair is too short to show.
Instructions address the reader as “you”, in the imperative: “Run the tests”, not “The tests should be run”. Prefer active voice everywhere. A passive that hides the actor usually hides part of the contract with it.

title: Write docs
text:
Banned words
Always use the plainest word that is still correct: use, not “utilize” or “leverage”; improve, not “enhance” or “optimize” unless something is literally being optimized; complete, not “comprehensive”; strong, not “robust”; help, not “facilitate”.
Kill on sight: seamless, streamline, empower, foster, pivotal, “a testament to”, realm, landscape (metaphorical), navigate (metaphorical), delve, myriad, plethora, paradigm, synergy, holistic, catalyze, juxtapose, tapestry, embark, endeavor, encompass, multifaceted, elucidate, nuanced (as filler), minted (metaphorical). For “land”/“landed” say what happened: merged, committed, released, appears. For metaphorical “shape”/“shaped” say structure, format, or the actual event. “Invariant” is usually “rule” or “guarantee”. Compounds in “-bearing”, such as load-bearing, have plainer forms.

title: Write docs
text:
Doc types

Docstrings: the first line states what the function does, and for most functions it is the whole docstring. Parameter detail goes in docments, never repeated in prose. State inputs, outputs, errors raised and guarantees. Never restate the signature.
Code comments: only a constraint the code cannot show, per coding_patterns. Almost never.
READMEs: read like docstrings, not like blogs. The first paragraph says what the package does and for whom. Then install, then a minimal example. No journey, no sales language.
API docs and changelogs: the contract or the change, one entry per behaviour. Rationale goes in design docs.
PR descriptions and commit messages: lead with the behaviour change, name who did what, and give reviewers what they need to judge the diff.
Messages to a colleague: the answer first, support after. No softening preamble, no closing offer of further help.

title: Write docs
text:
Summaries
A summary of a conversation, a diff, a review thread or a paper has to say what is now true. It does not shorten the source in the source’s own order. Write from the situation the source describes. Six failures cover nearly all bad summaries.

Walking the source: reporting turn by turn, file by file, section by section. Order by subject instead. The reader never needed to know when something was said.
Topics without content: “we discussed the migration”, “this PR refactors the auth module”. A sentence that could have been written before reading the source says nothing about it. Cash every topic out in specifics or drop it.
Pointers to nowhere: “the approach discussed earlier”, “the second reviewer’s concern”. Every reference has to resolve inside the summary itself.
Claims with no owner: the reader cannot tell a fact from someone’s position from your own inference. Give every claim its owner, name people rather than anonymizing them, and mark your inferences as yours.
No status and no why: a thread reported without its current state, or a conclusion kept while the reason that supports it is dropped. State means decided, dropped or still open; merged, blocked or awaiting review. Gathering the reasons scattered across a long source is most of the work of summarizing, which is why lazy summaries lose them first.
Space by bulk and buried lede: length tracks the size of the source material instead of how much it changed the situation, and the biggest change arrives last because that is where the source got to it. Weight by importance. Put the largest change first.

A summary has to still work a week later with the source gone. Naming what the source introduced is part of that; reciting background the reader already holds is not.
Never hard-wrap prose. Write each paragraph as one continuous line and let the display soft-wrap it. Put code symbols in backticks: function names, parameters, file paths, module and package names, and literal syntax.
To have a draft checked, send these rules and the draft to a subagent with delegate_search. Name the audience, so tell 12 can be judged. Ask for flagged spans rather than a rewrite. Only do this when the user asks for a docs check.

title: testing
text:
A ModelSpec describes one model: its name, the runtime that serves it, the model id and the context window in tokens (ctx). The two specs here differ mainly in that window. SPEC has 1,000 tokens, small enough that compaction arithmetic can be checked by hand. Compaction is how the agent keeps a long conversation inside the window: it replaces older messages with a summary. SCRIPTED has 8,000 tokens. Compaction does not fire in the middle of a recorded demo.

SPEC, SCRIPTED.ctx
