title: testing
text:
A host in memory
MemHost is a test host that keeps project files in a dict keyed by absolute path. The file and search tools read and write that dict. They do not touch the disk.
A host declares its abilities through the classes it inherits. Each capability class, such as CodeHost for code search or ShellHost for running commands, names one capability group. tools_for(host) builds the tools of every group the host declares. Every host has the file group from Host. MemHost inherits from NullHost, CodeHost and ShellHost. It declares the file group and the groups of those two capability classes. It declares no other group. The live Python session group is one of the groups it lacks, and host.can('session') is False. A test uses this class to check that a missing group removes its tools.
MemHost sets writes = True. NullHost sets it to False, and file_tools then withholds the editing tools.
commands scripts the shell. It maps a command string to (exit_code, output). A command not in the dict exits with code 0 and no output. Every command that runs is appended to host.cmds as (command, cwd, timeout). The cell below builds a host with two files.


source

MemHost
def MemHost(
    files:NoneType=None, root:str='/proj', commands:NoneType=None
):
A host whose folders live in a dict. The file tools never touch disk.



host = MemHost({'/proj/a.py': 'def a(): return 1\n', '/proj/b.py': 'def b(): return a() + 1\n'})
host.roots, host.walk()

search returns every file whose text contains the query as a substring, up to limit files. It returns Hit objects, the type a real code index returns. Each hit reports line 1 and the first line of the file, not the line that matched. search_note is 'memory'.

host.search('return a'), host.search_note

write stores text in the dict and returns the path. text_at reads it back and returns an empty string for a file that does not exist. Agent.changes() reads files through text_at. A test can check which files a turn edited against this host.

host.write('/proj/c.py', 'def c(): pass\n')
host.text_at('/proj/c.py'), host.text_at('/proj/never.py')

run_python appends the code to host.ran and returns 'ok'. It starts no kernel. A test can check what the agent tried to run. A test must call the method directly, because MemHost does not declare the session group and tools_for builds no run_python tool for it. The cell after the example checks this. host.provides lists the groups the host declares.

host.run_python('df2 = df.dropna()'), host.ran


test_eq(host.can('session'), False)
test_eq(names(tools_for(host)) & {'run_python', 'list_vars', 'inspect_python'}, set())
sorted(host.provides)

title: testing
text:
A host with everything
LocalHost is the host the terminal session runs on. It has real folders on disk, a real shell and a real Python kernel. Some of its groups need something a test does not have. Memory and watches need a vault, the web tools need the network, and its inspect_python has only the isolated scope. A test cannot exercise those tools on a LocalHost.
FullHost is a LocalHost that fills each gap with a small implementation over in-process state. Its web is a dict of pages you pass in. Its memory stores the pages it reads and searches them. Its terminal is a transcript you pass in. Nothing reaches the network. It works in a new temporary folder unless you pass root. A test or a docs page can write files there freely. Three groups stay off because they need a model, an API specification or a vault: ask, api and watch.


source

FullHost
def FullHost(
    files:NoneType=None, pages:NoneType=None, root:NoneType=None, terminal:str='', **kw
):
Every host capability in process over a temporary folder, never the network.


Here it is seeded with one file, one web page and a terminal that has already printed a test run. The cell lists every tool tools_for builds for it, and the next cell checks that this is a strict superset of what NullHost gets.

host = FullHost(
    files={'pkg/sizes.py': 'RESERVE = 16_384\n\ndef threshold(ctx):\n    return max(1, ctx - min(RESERVE, ctx // 4))\n'},
    pages={'https://nbdev.fast.ai/api/export.html': (
        '# Exporting a notebook to a library\n\n'
        '## nb_export\n\n'
        'Named exports append to a module another notebook owns, so a second run duplicates them.\n\n'
        '## default_exp\n\n'
        'One module per notebook, named by the default_exp directive.\n')},
    terminal='$ pytest -q\n3 failed, 66 passed')
[t.__name__ for t in tools_for(host)]


names = {t.__name__ for t in tools_for(host)}
assert 'run_shell' in names
test_eq({t.__name__ for t in tools_for(NullHost())} < names, True)
host.kernel_kind, host.concurrent, host.scopes

Underneath it is a real LocalHost. The sandbox that keeps every path inside the open folders, the file tools and the Python namespace are the production code. The next cells view a file through the real view_file tool, show a path outside the folder being refused, and run Python in the live namespace.

view_file, replace_text, create_file, add_root = file_tools(host)
print(view_file('pkg/sizes.py'))


test_fail(lambda: host.check('/etc/passwd'))
host.run_python('total = threshold_calls = 0\ntotal'), host.list_vars().splitlines()

The web is the dict of pages passed in. web_search matches the query against each page’s url and text. read_url returns a page. Unless remember=False is passed, read_url also stores the page in memory. The memory tools below search those stored pages.

web_search, read_url = web_tools(host)
print(web_search('nbdev'))
print(read_url('https://nbdev.fast.ai/api/export.html')[:80])

Memory is where the agent keeps pages and notes beyond the current conversation. A memory search returns sections of a stored document, each with a breadcrumb naming the document and heading it came from, rather than loose snippets. FullHost makes those sections by splitting a page at its headings, and memory_tree lists the headings of each stored document.

memory_search, memory_read, remember, memory_forget = memory_tools(host)
host.memory_search('duplicates')


test_eq(len(host.remembered), 1)
host.memory_tree()[0]['headings']

memory_forget deletes a stored document and its sections. The same search then finds nothing.

doc_id = next(iter(host.remembered))
memory_forget(doc_id), host.memory_search('duplicates')

research searches the web, reads every page that matches and returns them as one digest, with a source line under each page. It belongs to an opt-in tool group: tools_for(host) leaves it out and tools_for(host, optin='research') includes it. This cell builds the tool directly with shalya.research_tools.

from shalya import research_tools


research, = research_tools(host)
print(research('export')[:220])

inspect_python lets the agent look at the user’s live Python namespace. It has two scopes. The isolated scope runs the code against a copy of the namespace. The overlay scope runs it against the real namespace and sees every object as it is. FullHost runs the overlay scope, then restores every name that existed before the run.
Restoring bindings undoes an assignment such as kept = None. It does not undo a change made inside an existing object. The cell below defines kept, a list in the live namespace. The next cell appends to it from the isolated scope.

host.run_python('kept = [1, 2, 3]')
host.inspect_python('kept.append(99)\nlen(kept)', scope='overlay'), host.run_python('len(kept)')

The isolated scope copies the namespace dict, not the objects in it. A new name defined there disappears. kept is the same list in both scopes. The append changes the real list. The output shows the length of the real list after the append.

host.inspect_python('kept.append(4)\nlen(kept)', scope='isolated'), host.run_python('len(kept)')

read_terminal reads the terminal beside the agent. On FullHost it returns the transcript passed as terminal. note is how a host leaves a message for the agent, such as a report that compaction ran. FullHost also appends every note to host.notes. A test can check that list.

read_terminal = {t.__name__: t for t in session_tools(host)}['read_terminal']
print(read_terminal())


host.note('compacted 12 messages')
host.notes

title: testing
text:
A backend with no model
FakeBackend replies from a list of strings, in order, and replies (done) once the list runs out. It subclasses the real Backend. These parts are production code:

the lock that serialises calls
the usage accounting
the list of problems shown to the user
the history replacement that compaction uses

Only the replies are made up. sent holds every message sent, and spawned holds every sub-agent backend that spawn made. A one-shot call is a single call for a short job such as a summary. On FakeBackend it returns ONESHOT: followed by the first 40 characters of the prompt.


source

FakeBackend
def FakeBackend(
    spec:ramabana.core.ModelSpec=ModelSpec(name='fake', runtime='fake', model_id='fake/model', ctx=1000, note='', opts={}, missing=''),
    replies:tuple=(), **kw
):
A backend over a scripted list of replies, for turns with no model.



be = FakeBackend(replies=['the first answer', 'the second'])
be.send('a question'), be.send('another'), be.send('one more than were scripted')

hist holds both the user messages and the assistant replies. Compaction has a real conversation to shorten.

be.hist[:2]

stream yields the same reply one word at a time. Each chunk is a word followed by a space. A test can use it to check a frontend that draws text as it arrives.

''.join(FakeBackend(replies=['streamed one word at a time']).stream('go'))

use is a Usage record of tokens in and out. A live backend reports the same type. Two Usage records add with +. FakeBackend counts 10 input tokens and 5 output tokens for each message sent, as a running total.

be.use, be.use + be.use

fake_agent builds a real Agent and routes all of its jobs to one FakeBackend. A job is one kind of model call the agent makes: the turn itself, a summary, a classification, a sub-agent. Normally each job can go to a different model. With every job routed to the fake, no call reaches a real model. The routing applies only when you pass neither model nor routing. The agent leaves out the user’s ~/.agents/skills and has no beat, so a test briefs and prompts the same on every machine. Pass global_skills=True to read the skills.
The host is a MemHost with one file unless you pass host. Other keyword arguments go to Agent. fake_agent returns (agent, backend). A test scripts the replies and then reads what the backend received. Use fake_agent when a test needs a whole turn. Use FakeBackend alone when a test needs only a backend.


source

fake_agent
def fake_agent(
    host:NoneType=None, replies:tuple=(), **kw
):
Build an Agent whose every job runs on one FakeBackend, and return (agent, backend).



agent, backend = fake_agent(replies=['`threshold` lives in `ramabana/runtime.py`.'])
agent.ask('where is the compaction threshold?')

The turn ran through the real agent: it built the tools, recorded the activity lines a frontend shows, and counted the tokens.

len(agent.tools), agent.turn_lines(), repr(agent.use)

title: testing
text:
A real model, recorded
The doubles above run the agent with no model. A docs page that shows what a real model does needs another tool. A multi-gigabyte model is too slow in CI, and a pasted transcript is never checked. recorded stores real answers and replays them.
Inside with recorded(): every chat the agent opens is urai’s CachedChat. A CachedChat stores the model’s answer the first time. The stored answer is keyed by the model, the briefing, the tools and the conversation so far. Later runs replay the stored answer and start no model. Every runtime counts as available inside the block. A page can replay Claude’s answers on a machine without Claude Code.
Answers are stored in CHATS, the chatcache folder next to the ramabana package folder, unless you pass path. record=False only replays. record=True sends a miss to the real model and stores the answer. With record=None the URAI_RECORD_CHAT environment variable decides.
The key leaves out two kinds of chat option. The first kind is a value that keyable rejects, such as a callable, whose repr holds an address that changes between runs. The second kind is the UNKEYED options, timeout_hint and api_key. Recorder passes both kinds to the live chat only.
The example uses an empty cache with record=False. The one-shot call returns an empty string, and the backend’s problems say that no recording was found.


source

recorded
def recorded(
    path:NoneType=None, record:NoneType=None
):
Replay recorded model answers for the duration, instead of calling a model; every runtime counts as available.




source

Recorder
def Recorder(
    *a, **kw
):
A CachedChat keyed on what the model is asked: UNKEYED options and values that are not keyable reach only the live chat.




source

keyable
def keyable(
    v
):
Whether v hashes the same on every run: JSON data, not a callable or an object whose repr holds an address.



import tempfile
from ramabana.core import ModelSpec
from ramabana.runtime import make_backend

with recorded(Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'chats', record=False) as p:
    be = make_backend(ModelSpec('unrecorded', 'remote', 'openai/gpt-x', 8000))
    test_eq(be.oneshot('nothing was ever recorded for this'), '')
    assert 'no recording' in ' '.join(be.problems)
p.name

'chats'



import os
from unittest import mock
from ramabana.runtime import RishiBackend

def claude_key(home):
    "A fresh Claude backend's first-call key, on a machine whose home and config.toml are under `home`."
    with mock.patch.dict(os.environ, {'HOME': str(home), 'RAMABANA_CONFIG': str(Path(home)/'config.toml')}), recorded(Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'chats', record=False):
        be = RishiBackend(ModelSpec('sonnet', 'claude', 'claude-sonnet-4-5', 200_000))
        be.start()
        return be.chat._key('call', 'hi', {}), be.chat.live

(k1, live), (k2, _) = claude_key(tempfile.mkdtemp()), claude_key(tempfile.mkdtemp())
test_eq(k1, k2)   # a recording made on one run, in one home, replays on the next
test_eq(sorted(live), ['on_stall', 'timeout_hint'])
assert keyable({'n': [1, 'a', None]}) and not keyable(print) and not keyable(object())


from ramabana.core import resolve


with patch('ramabana.core._claude_available', lambda: False):
    with recorded(Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'chats', record=False): test_eq(resolve('claude/claude-sonnet-4-5').backend, 'claude')
    assert resolve('claude/claude-sonnet-4-5').missing

VaultHost is the host with durable memory from the vault notebook. It rebuilds its memory graph in a background thread with a chat called graph_chat. no_model returns a stand-in chat that answers {} to every prompt. Pass it as graph_chat or as mk_chat, and the thread starts no model. nbdev’s test runner runs several notebooks in each worker process. Two notebooks that load a model onto the GPU at once can crash the worker.


source

no_model
def no_model(
    model:NoneType=None, **kw
):
Return a stand-in chat that answers {} to everything, for use as graph_chat or mk_chat in tests.



test_eq(no_model('any/model', sp='x').oneshot('extract the entities'), '{}')
test_eq(no_model()('hello')['content'], '{}')

title: testing
text:
Compaction, end to end
Compaction replaces the older part of a conversation with a summary followed by the most recent messages. The agent compacts on its own when the tokens used reach the threshold, and agent.compact() compacts on demand. The threshold is max(1, ctx - min(reserve, max(1, ctx // 4))), which is 750 tokens for the 1,000-token window of SPEC. After twelve more questions the fake_agent history is below 750 tokens, and agent.compactor.due(backend) returns False. Compaction always keeps the 18 most recent messages, so the loop asks enough questions to leave older ones to summarise. The cell after the loop compacts anyway. The fake’s one-shot answer is the summary.

for i in range(12): agent.ask(f'question {i} about the exporter')
len(backend.hist), agent.compactor.due(backend)


summary = agent.compact()
agent.compactor.note

The history now begins with the summary. The text after it tells the model what happened: its conversation was rewritten, but the Python kernel was not, so the user’s variables are still there.

print(backend.hist[0]['content'][:200])


test_eq(backend.hist[0]['content'].startswith('Previous conversation summary:'), True)
test_eq(agent.compactor.count, 1)
agent.compactor.last[:60]

title: testing
text:
A backend that mutters
Local model engines sometimes fail without raising. The engine prints its error to its own output stream and returns an empty string. The caller sees an empty reply with no reason. Ramabana’s local backend keeps what the engine printed and adds it to the backend’s problems. MutteringBackend reproduces the failure, and a test can check that handling. GEMMA is a real error line from the LiteRT engine, kept as the engine printed it.


source

MutteringBackend
def MutteringBackend(
    spec:NoneType=None, mode:str='empty', **kw
):
A backend that fails the way litert does: it prints, returns nothing, and raises nothing.



mute = MutteringBackend()
mute.send('anything'), mute.problems

send returns a sentence that says the model returned nothing and gives the reason. It does not return an empty string. last_native keeps the engine’s own words for the status line. Sending again does not add the same problem twice.

test_eq(mute.last_native, GEMMA.strip())
mute.send('again')


test_eq(len(mute.problems), 1)
mute.spec.ctx

title: testing
text:
A backend that performs
ScriptedBackend plays a list of Steps. A step can call a tool, say some text, or both, and can pause first. The text streams out one word at a time, token_delay seconds apart. The delay is for screenshots. At zero the turn finishes before the screen repaints, and every capture shows a finished answer instead of one in progress.
A tool step looks the tool up by name in the backend’s tool list, which refresh sets, and calls it. The agent’s own tools are in that list. The activity feed, the approval gate and the file snapshots then run as they do in production. A step that names a tool missing from the list skips the call, and the step’s text still plays. Use FakeBackend to test logic. Use ScriptedBackend for demos where the tool calls have to happen.


source

ScriptedBackend
def ScriptedBackend(
    spec:ramabana.core.ModelSpec=ModelSpec(name='scripted', runtime='scripted', model_id='scripted/model', ctx=8000, note='', opts={}, missing=''),
    steps:tuple=(), token_delay:float=0.02, **kw
):
Play a list of Steps, streaming words one at a time every token_delay.




source

Step
def Step(
    text:str='', tool:NoneType=None, pause:float=0.0
):
One scripted model action: call a tool through the real tool list, or say something.



script = [Step('Looking at the file.', tool=('view_file', {'path': '/proj/a.py'})),
          Step('It returns 1, so the caller gets an int.')]
play = ScriptedBackend(steps=script, token_delay=0)
play.refresh('', [t for t in agent.tools if t.__name__ == 'view_file'])
play.send('what does a() return?')

The tool really ran. Its result is in the history as a tool message, where compaction or a UI would find it.

[m['role'] for m in play.hist], play.hist[2]['content'][:40]

spawn returns the backend for a sub-agent. The sub-agent answers with the first SUB_ANSWERS value whose keyword appears in the lower-cased question, and with nothing found when no keyword appears. Different questions give different answers. The usage of a ScriptedBackend is fixed at 1,840 tokens in and 96 out, 1,936 in total. The last cell checks the total.

sub = play.spawn()
''.join(sub._run('which files import fastllm?')), ''.join(sub._run('what shape is df?'))


test_eq(play.use.total, 1936)
play.use

title: testing
section: A real model with every tool
text:
A real model with every tool
The doubles above check control flow. This last section checks the assembled product: a FullHost, an Agent over it on a made-up remote model, and every tool the host supports handed to the model’s conversation.
Everything runs inside recorded(). It starts no model and makes no network call. Two cells would talk to the model. Both carry #| eval: false, and the test suite skips them. Run by hand, they check that the model compiled every tool schema and that it can answer.

from contextlib import ExitStack

replay = ExitStack()
replay.enter_context(recorded())

# `remote`: `resolve` refuses a runtime that is not installed
register_model('release-model', 'openai/release-model', 'remote', 32_768)
real_host = FullHost(
    files={'pkg/sizes.py': 'RESERVE = 16_384\n\ndef threshold(ctx):\n    return ctx - RESERVE\n'},
    pages={'https://example.test/nbdev': '# nbdev export\n\nOne module belongs to one notebook.'},
    terminal='$ pytest -q\n69 passed')
real_agent = Agent(real_host, model='release-model', extensions=False)
for job in ('classify', 'summary', 'completion', 'subagent'):
    real_agent.routing.set('release-model', job)
real_agent.start() is not None, real_agent.note

(False,
 'turn job: release-model needs OPENAI_API_KEY; set it in the environment. `/login` adds a provider in a session, `ramabana setup` from a shell')


Agent.tools is the complete tool list: code, files, notebooks, web, memory, the live session, the shell, skills, delegation, the plan and git, plus image generation when a key for it is set. None of them is a stub that always fails. The next cell checks the list group by group.

real_tool_names = [tool.__name__ for tool in real_agent.tools]
real_tool_names


FILES = {'search_code', 'outline', 'grep', 'ls',
         'view_file', 'replace_text', 'create_file', 'add_root'}
NOTEBOOK = {'notebook_cells', 'view_cell', 'edit_cell', 'add_cell'}
WEB = {'web_search', 'read_url'}
MEMORY = {'memory_search', 'memory_read', 'remember', 'memory_forget'}
SESSION = {'run_python', 'inspect_python', 'restart_kernel', 'read_terminal'}
SHELL = {'run_shell', 'run_shell_bg', 'shell_output', 'shell_stop'}
SKILLS = {'read_skill'}                      # `create_skill` is the `author` opt-in
DELEGATION = {'delegate_search', 'delegate_async', 'delegate_result', 'delegate_cancel', 'delegate_tell'}
PLAN = {'set_plan', 'update_todo'}
# only with a key for the endpoint
IMAGE = {'generate_image'} if image_available() else set()
GIT = {'git_status', 'git_divergence', 'git_remote', 'git_checkout',
       'git_commit', 'git_diff', 'git_log', 'git_stash', 'git_sync', 'git_conflicts'}
expected = (FILES | NOTEBOOK | WEB | MEMORY | SESSION | SHELL | SKILLS | DELEGATION | PLAN | IMAGE
            | GIT)
test_eq(set(real_tool_names), expected)
len(real_tool_names)

Attaching the tools to Agent does not prove the model accepts them. The backend’s live chat compiles a schema for each tool. Comparing the number of compiled schemas with the number of tools catches a missing type annotation, a lost functools.wraps or a tool signature the runtime rejects.

real_backend = real_agent.backend
test_eq(real_backend.ready, True)
test_eq(len(real_backend.chat.toolspecs), len(real_agent.tools))
test_eq(len(real_backend.chat.toolspecs), len(expected))
(real_backend.spec.model_id, len(real_backend.chat.toolspecs))

Then the model is asked for a one-word reply on the classify job, which is routed to the same model. A non-empty reply shows the model really generates text, which accepting the tool schemas alone would not show.

real_reply = real_agent.oneshot(
    'Reply with exactly READY and nothing else.',
    'Return only the requested answer.', job='classify', max_tokens=192)
assert real_reply.strip()
real_reply


real_agent.close()
replay.close()
real_agent.status()['model'], real_agent.use.total

text:
source

History
def History(
    cfg:NoneType=None, # config folder; None uses the folder containing `config_path()`
    history_name:str='agent', # history file prefix
):
Read turn logs and memory without changing them.


sessions lists each conversation in a log, newest first. The example writes a log of two conversations into a temporary config folder and reads it back with History.

import tempfile


cfg = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
rows = [{'at': 1, 'session': 'a', 'prompt': 'Fix the parser. Then test it.', 'model': 'gpt-mini'},
        {'at': 2, 'session': 'a', 'prompt': 'Run the tests.', 'model': 'gpt-mini'},
        {'at': 3, 'session': 'b', 'prompt': 'Explain the index', 'model': 'gpt-mini'}]
(cfg/'agent-history.jsonl').write_text(''.join(json.dumps(r) + '\n' for r in rows))
before = sorted(p.name for p in cfg.iterdir())
History(cfg).sessions()

Reading creates no file in the config folder, not even the session index.

assert sorted(p.name for p in cfg.iterdir()) == before
before

title: Peer work
text:
This page is the peer-work skill. Claude Code, Codex and Ramabana sessions on one Mac can send each other notes and asks. The skill tells each side how to do that work without bad code. The user cares most about this: the code must follow the rules of the repo that owns it.
The skill text is this module’s docstring, as in coding_patterns. pyproject.toml registers the module under the pyskills entry point as peer_work. ramabana setup peers copies the text into the Claude Code and Codex instruction files. To change what an agent reads, edit the exported cell below.
Read this before you work for another session, or ask another session to work for you. Sessions are Claude Code, Codex and Ramabana sessions on this Mac.
Two roles exist. The worker does the work. The owner holds the repo. One session can have both roles.

title: Peer work
section: When you do work for another session (worker)
text:
When you do work for another session (worker)

Read the repo rules before you write code. Read CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md and the repo skills. Some repos have their own pattern. For example, vedicreader builds features from small lego blocks. Read the repo’s rules to find its pattern.
Follow the user’s general rules. Use functional style. Write short and efficient code. Write one-line docstrings. Add no comments that are not needed. Write prose in STE. Do not add code that you do not need. Do not write a helper that already exists.
Agree the shape with the owner before you add code that the owner’s repo will keep. Send an ask: ramabana tell OWNER "..." --ask --repo R --wait N. Name the blocks to use, the place for the code and the API. Wait for a reply from the owner that starts with agreed:. Then write the code.
Do not edit a folder that another live session works in. The tool or hook refuses the write and names the folder. Ask the owner to make the change.
Show proof before you say “done”. Show the test command and its output. For UI, check the page in Chrome for Testing and show the screenshot path. Never use the user’s own Chrome. No proof means the work is not done.

title: Peer work
text:
When you own the repo (owner)

Review the diff against your repo’s rules. Do this before you accept the work.
If the code is too large or does not follow the repo’s patterns, ask for changes.
Accept the work only when the code follows the rules.
Before you do the work in an ask, read your repo rules. If the ask breaks them, reply refused: <why> and name the rule.
When you agree to the shape that a worker sends, start your reply with agreed:.

title: Peer work
text:
Find sessions

If the hook gave you a full command for ramabana, use that command.
Run ramabana peers to list live sessions. Add --ids to see the session ids.
After /add-dir, run ramabana peers --add-folder PATH. The folder guard then knows the new folder.
Inside Ramabana, use the peers() tool.

title: Peer work
text:
Send

ramabana tell TARGET TEXT sends a note. A note needs no answer.
Add --ask to request work. Add --repo R so that the receiver knows whose rules apply. Add --wait N to wait N seconds for the reply.
Add --all to send to every live session.
Inside Ramabana, use tell(session, text, kind='note'|'ask', wait=60).
An ask needs the user’s approval, unless work together mode is on with that sender.
Work together mode does not change tool permissions. Your own permission mode still applies.
The peers reference lists the default limits. Replies do not count against the message allowance. Set RAMABANA_PEER_MESSAGES, RAMABANA_PEER_ASKS, or RAMABANA_PEER_HOPS before process startup to override a limit. Values must be positive integers. Running processes keep their loaded limits.

title: Peer work
text:
Receive

Run ramabana inbox to read your messages. Add --wait N to wait for new ones.
A note is information only. If a note asks for work, treat it as an ask: ask the user unless work together mode is on with that sender.
Answer with ramabana tell TARGET TEXT --reply-to THREAD. Take THREAD from the message.
End a finished reply with these two lines:

changes: file or commit; file or commit
proof: command → result; screenshot path

If you decline, start the reply with refused: <why>. If you fail, start it with failed: <why>.
Do not reply to a reply that has no new request.

title: Peer work
text:
Work together mode

ramabana together on lets those sessions send asks to you without approval. Add --with A,B to name them. Add --until HH:MM to set the end. Without --until, it ends after 12 hours.
ramabana together off ends it. ramabana together status shows it. In Claude Code and Codex it also ends when the user types. In Ramabana it stays on, and work_together() turns it on or off when the user tells you to work with peers.
ramabana report shows what the sessions did: changes, proof and the user’s action list.

The test reads the skill text. It checks that each rule, each reply line and each command the protocol needs is present, with the agreed: signal and the rule that stops an endless chain of replies. It also checks that the skill stays short and that skill discovery finds it.

from ramabana.peer_work import __doc__ as skill
from ramabana import tools
rules = ['CLAUDE.md', 'AGENTS.md', 'one-line docstrings', 'Agree the shape', 'owner', 'another live session',
         'Chrome for Testing', 'screenshot', 'changes:', 'proof:', 'refused:', 'failed:',
         'ramabana tell', '--reply-to', '--ask', 'ramabana peers --add-folder', '/add-dir', 'ramabana inbox',
         'work together mode', 'ramabana together', 'tool permissions', "Never use the user's own Chrome", '--wait', '--all', 'ramabana peers', '--ids', '(worker)', '(owner)',
         'agreed:', 'Do not reply to a reply that has no new request.', 'If the hook gave you a full command for `ramabana`, use that command.']
missing = [r for r in rules if r not in skill]
assert not missing, missing
assert len(skill.splitlines()) <= 60
assert 'peer_work' in {s.name for s in tools.discover()}

title: mcp
text:
server builds an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that gives an outside client access to Ramabana’s tools. Pass a host to serve its tools. Pass an agent as well to mount the agent’s own tools. These are the same objects a turn uses. A client’s calls appear in the same activity feed and changes() report as a turn’s.
Agent._record wraps each tool with functools.wraps. The wrapper keeps the tool’s signature and docstring, and FastMCP builds each tool’s schema from them. A tool is described in one place. A client sees the same description as a model. Without an agent, the server builds the tools from the host with tools_for.
readonly defaults to True. The client is another agent, and this server cannot show an approval prompt to the client’s user. Read-only mode leaves out every write tool. It keeps the read tools and the acting tools such as inspect_python and generate_image. With readonly=False the server also mounts the write tools, and the client’s own approval settings stand in front of them. delegate=False leaves out ask even when an agent is given. Any other keyword goes to FastMCP.
INSTRUCTIONS is the text the server sends to a client when it connects. It tells the client’s model how to read and edit with these tools.


source


def server(
    host:NoneType=None, agent:NoneType=None, name:str='ramabana', readonly:bool=True, delegate:bool=True, **kw
):
An MCP server over one host’s tools, and optionally over Ramabana’s own agent.


The server below runs over FullHost, a test host from testing. It declares the code, file, git, memory, notebook, session, shell and web tool groups. The server is read-only by default. replace_text and create_file are absent. Without an agent, the server also mounts shalya’s legacy group (list_files, list_vars and others) for one release. Clients written against version 0.1 keep working. edit_file belongs to the opt-in exhash group and is not mounted.

host = FullHost(files={'pkg/sizes.py': 'RESERVE = 16_384\n\ndef threshold(ctx):\n    return ctx - RESERVE\n'})
mcp = server(host)
tools = await mcp.list_tools()
[t.name for t in tools]


test_eq(set(t.name for t in tools) & WRITE_TOOLS, set())
assert {'view_file', 'list_files'} <= {t.name for t in tools}
len(tools)

FastMCP derives each tool’s schema from the tool function. The description is the docstring a model reads in a turn. The parameters come from the type annotations.

t = next(t for t in tools if t.name == 'view_file')
t.description.splitlines()[0], t.inputSchema['properties'], t.annotations.readOnlyHint

MCP tool annotations tell a client which calls only read, which are destructive, and which reach the open world. Open-world tools are the tools in the web and api groups. _annotate sets the annotations from the same catalog entry that approvals and the activity feed use. A client can use them to decide which calls to ask its user about. The server below is built with readonly=False. replace_text is mounted, and its annotations can be compared with those of the read tool view_file.

mcp_w = server(host, readonly=False)
{t.name: (t.annotations.readOnlyHint, t.annotations.destructiveHint, t.annotations.openWorldHint)
 for t in await mcp_w.list_tools() if t.name in ('view_file', 'replace_text', 'web_search')}

A client call runs through the same code path as a turn. The client receives the same text the model would receive. view_file returns one lineno|hash|content line for each line of the file.

out = await mcp.call_tool('view_file', {'path': 'pkg/sizes.py'})
print(out[0][0].text if isinstance(out, tuple) else out)

A read-only server does not mount write tools. Calling a write tool by name returns an error. The last line lists the write tools that readonly=False mounts.

with expect_fail(): await mcp.call_tool('replace_text', {'path': 'pkg/sizes.py', 'edits': []})
with expect_fail(): await mcp.call_tool('edit_file', {'path': 'pkg/sizes.py', 'commands': []})
[t.name for t in await mcp_w.list_tools() if t.name in WRITE_TOOLS]

title: mcp
text:
Skills as resources
The server offers skills as resources. A resource is text a client can read. A tool is a call that can have an effect. The server publishes three resources:

ramabana://skills is an index of every skill, with a one-line description of when it applies.
skill://{name} is one skill in full. It is the same text read_skill returns in a turn.
ramabana://status is a JSON summary of the open folders, the mounted tools and the skills. With an agent, it also holds the agent’s status.

A client reads the index and fetches only the skill it needs. A model does the same with read_skill in a turn. Without an agent, the server finds skills in the served folders and in ~/.agents/skills.

[str(r.uriTemplate) for r in await mcp.list_resource_templates()] + [str(r.uri) for r in await mcp.list_resources()]


print((await mcp.read_resource('ramabana://status'))[0].content[:200])

title: mcp
text:
The agent as one tool
With an agent passed in, the server also offers ask. ask runs a whole Ramabana turn behind one call. The client sends one task and receives one answer. The tool loop, the tool results and any compaction of the history happen inside the server. The client never sees them. The example below uses fake_agent from testing, an agent with a scripted reply. It needs no model.

agent, be = fake_agent(replies=['`threshold` is defined in pkg/sizes.py, and subtracts the reserve.'])
full = server(agent.host, agent)
[t.name for t in await full.list_tools() if t.name == 'ask']


out = await full.call_tool('ask', {'task': 'where is the threshold defined?'})
out[0][0].text if isinstance(out, tuple) else out

ask runs the turn on a worker thread. A turn blocks, and an MCP server is asynchronous. The client’s one call sent one message to the agent’s backend.

test_eq(len(be.sent), 1)
(await full.read_resource('ramabana://status'))[0].content[:60]

title: mcp
text:
Running it
ramabana-mcp is the command-line entry point, main. It splits --root into folders and serves them over --transport, which is stdio by default. --model builds a full agent on that model and turns on the ask tool. Without --model there is no agent to receive a task, and the server offers tools only. --write mounts the write tools. The other options build the host the same way the terminal does.
The agent behind ask is built with approve='none'. This setting means no approval gate. A turn that ask runs can use the agent’s write tools without asking anyone. --write controls only which tools the client can call directly.


source

main
def main(
    root:str='.', # comma-separated folders to serve
    model:str=None, # model for `ask`; omit to serve tools only
    write:bool=False, # mount the write tools too
    web:bool=True, # let web tools reach the network via fossick
    read_outside:bool=False, # reads may name any path; writes stay inside
    vault:bool=False, # keep reads in a vishalakshi vault
    pii:str='off', # off | redact | refuse PII from the vault, and from shell, Python and web reads a hosted model gets
    pii_ner:bool=False, # --pii also gates titled names, not only patterns
    transport:str='stdio', # stdio | sse | streamable-http
    cfg:str=None, # config dir, for skills and extensions
):
Serve Ramabana tools over MCP.


A client that launches its own servers needs the command and its arguments. This configuration serves one repository and runs ask on a local model:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ramabana": {
      "command": "ramabana-mcp",
      "args": ["--root", "/path/to/repo", "--model", "qwen-4b"]
    }
  }
}
The defaults are read-only tools and no model:
ramabana-mcp --root .

title: setup
text: This module holds what must happen before a session starts. The terminal session runs best inside tmux, a terminal multiplexer that divides one window into panes. tmux gives Ramabana a split for the now pane, the live view of the turn described in pane. With the extended keys setting on, tmux also delivers the alt keys and shift+enter to the program as keys of their own. shift+enter arrives only from a terminal that sends it. The first run therefore starts Ramabana inside a tmux server of its own and offers to install tmux when it is missing. ramabana --doctor reports what it found. The module also decides whether the code index needs rebuilding.

title: setup
text:
Extras and scripts
Every console script that the package installs starts in this module. The module imports only fastcore and the standard library, and never ramabana.core. A script starts quickly this way and can check for its dependencies before it imports them.
installed(mod) says whether a module would import, without importing it. need(extra) checks the modules of an extra, as listed in EXTRAS. It returns '' when all are installed. Otherwise it returns a message that names the missing modules and gives the pip install command. SCRIPTS names each console script other than ramabana, with the module whose main it runs, the extra it needs and the modules it needs. A lookup of one of these names on this module returns that main. When a needed module is missing, the lookup returns a stand-in that prints the message and exits with status 2. follow_cmd(log, snap) is the shell line a transcript pane runs: the pane module following log in the palette of the snapshot snap, or tail -f when the terminal extra is missing. ramabana.core re-exports installed, need, EXTRAS and SCRIPTS.

The main a console script in SCRIPTS calls itself, so call_parse reads the command line; or one naming the missing extra.

title: setup
text:
The config
Each session gets a tmux server of its own, started as tmux -L ramabana-<id> with the config file <cfg>/tmux.conf. A new server reads the current tmux.conf and inherits the current environment. A second session therefore never picks up the first one’s API keys or virtual environment. That server never reads ~/.tmux.conf. Your own tmux setup stays as it was.
Extended keys are a tmux setting that passes key combinations such as shift+enter through to the program in the pane. Without it, tmux folds them into plain enter. tmux_conf(version) returns the config for a tmux version. It adds only the lines that version understands. An older tmux prints an error for each line it does not know. tmux_version reads the version from the output of tmux -V. The config claims true colour (RGB) only when $COLORTERM says the terminal draws it. The cell below prints the config for tmux 3.5.



tmux version
Constant
Needed for




3.0
WRAP_MIN
launch relaunches inside tmux


3.1
SPLIT_MIN
The split for the now pane


3.2
KEYS_MIN
extended-keys


3.5
none
extended-keys-format csi-u

tmux_conf

    version
):
TMUX_CONF with the lines tmux version understands.




source

tmux_version
def tmux_version(
    s
):
The (major, minor) in tmux -V output such as tmux 3.5a, or None.



test_eq([tmux_version(s) for s in ('tmux 3.5a', 'tmux next-3.6', 'tmux master')], [(3, 5), (3, 6), None])
assert 'extended-keys-format csi-u' in tmux_conf((3, 5)) and 'csi-u' not in tmux_conf((3, 4))
assert 'extended-keys on' in tmux_conf((3, 2)) and 'extended-keys' not in tmux_conf((3, 1))
print(tmux_conf((3, 5)))

title: setup
text:
The relaunch
Setup collects everything about the tmux that Ramabana runs in: the config, the relaunch into it, the install offer and --doctor.
Setup.launch runs before an interactive session starts. Outside tmux it replaces the current process with tmux new-session on a new server. The new session runs the same command line in the same folder. Quitting Ramabana then ends that tmux session and returns you to your shell. launch does nothing in these cases: a one-shot prompt, --json, a stdin or stdout that is not a terminal, and --tmux off or $RAMABANA_TMUX=off. It also does nothing when $RAMABANA_WRAPPED is set, when tmux is older than 3.0, and when tmux is missing and you decline the install offer. The relaunched process has $RAMABANA_WRAPPED set. It never relaunches a second time. Inside tmux, --pane auto then opens the now pane.
The server sets destroy-unattached, which ends the session when you detach or close the window. Ramabana never keeps running where nobody can see it. The history is saved, and --resume latest reopens it. The command runs under sh with a short wrapper, HOLD. After a non-zero exit, HOLD waits for enter. An error stays on screen instead of vanishing with the tmux session. The command line goes to HOLD in $RAMABANA_ARGV, not in the tmux arguments. The tmux client then does not look like Ramabana to a tool that reads process arguments, such as Sanketa. The pane process still runs ramabana.
Inside a tmux server of your own, launch turns extended-keys on for that server when it is off. The change lasts until the server exits. Only programs that ask for extended keys receive them.
Every effect on the outside world goes through an argument of Setup: which, system, run, execvpe, ask and isatty, plus environ, argv and cwd. The examples pass fakes for all of them. They run without tmux and change nothing.


source

Setup
def Setup(
    cfg:str='~/.config/ramabana', # holds `tmux.conf` and `setup.json`
    environ:NoneType=None, # default `os.environ`
    argv:NoneType=None, # the command line to rerun; default `sys.argv`
    cwd:NoneType=None, # where the session starts; default the current folder
    which:function=which, system:function=system, run:function=run, execvpe:function=execvpe, ask:function=_no_stdin,
    isatty:NoneType=None, # whether stdin and stdout are terminals
):
The tmux ramabana runs in: its config, the relaunch into it, the install offer, and --doctor.




source

prune_sockets
def prune_sockets(
    folder, # a tmux socket folder, `$TMUX_TMPDIR/tmux-<uid>`
    prefix:str='ramabana-', # only sockets whose names start with this
    age:int=5, # keep sockets younger than this many seconds: their server may still be starting
):
Remove the sockets in folder that start with prefix and refuse a connection; return their names.


The example builds a fake machine, Box, that has tmux 3.5 on PATH and records each command run, each question asked and the execvpe it would make. launch reruns the command line on a new tmux server, starting in /work, with $RAMABANA_WRAPPED set. The original command line is in $RAMABANA_ARGV and not in the tmux arguments:

from types import SimpleNamespace
import shlex, tempfile

class Box:
    "Programs on PATH, the commands run, the prompts shown and the exec made."
    def __init__(self, have=('tmux',), version='tmux 3.5a', system='Darwin', answer='', ext='on'):
        self.have, self.version, self.system, self.answer, self.ext = set(have), version, system, answer, ext
        self.calls, self.asked, self.execd = [], [], None
    def which(self, name): return f'/bin/{name}' if name in self.have else None
    def run(self, cmd, **kw):
        self.calls.append(list(cmd))
        if 'install' in cmd: self.have.add('tmux')
        return SimpleNamespace(returncode=0, stdout={'-V': self.version, 'show': self.ext}.get(cmd[1], ''))
    def ask(self, q): return self.asked.append(q) or self.answer
    def execvpe(self, *a): self.execd = a

def mk(box, **kw):
    return Setup(tempfile.mkdtemp(), environ=kw.pop('environ', {'PATH': '/bin', 'TMUX_TMPDIR': tempfile.mkdtemp()}), argv=['-c', '--pane', 'on'], cwd='/work',
                 which=box.which, system=lambda: box.system, run=box.run, execvpe=box.execvpe, ask=box.ask, isatty=lambda: True)

box = Box()
mk(box).launch()
exe, argv, env = box.execd
test_eq((exe, env['RAMABANA_WRAPPED'], argv[argv.index('-c'):][:2], shlex.split(env['RAMABANA_ARGV'])[-2:]), ('/bin/tmux', '1', ['-c', '/work'], ['--pane', 'on']))
assert '--pane' not in argv
argv

['tmux',
 '-L',
 'ramabana-2258542c',
 '-f',
 '/tmp/tmplzycq9mb/tmux.conf',
 'new-session',
 '-s',
 'ramabana',
 '-c',
 '/work',
 'sh',
 '-c',
 'eval "set -- $RAMABANA_ARGV"; "$@" || { s=$?; printf "\\nramabana exited with status %s · enter closes this\\n" $s; read _; exit $s; }',
 'ramabana']


A one-shot prompt, --json and --tmux off stay in the current terminal:

for kw in (dict(prompt='hi'), dict(as_json=True), dict(tmux='off')):
    box = Box()
    mk(box).launch(**kw)
    test_eq(box.execd, None)

Each relaunch starts a tmux server on a new socket. A tmux server leaves its socket file behind when it exits, even after tmux kill-server. launch calls prune_sockets before each relaunch. prune_sockets removes each ramabana- socket that refuses a connection, because no server listens on it. It keeps live sockets and the sockets of other programs. It also keeps a socket younger than age seconds, because a server that is still starting refuses connections for a moment. An error on one socket skips that socket and does not stop the launch. The example binds one live socket and two dead sockets in a temporary folder. The new dead socket stays until age=0:

import socket


d = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(dir='/tmp'))
socks = {n: socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX) for n in ('ramabana-live', 'ramabana-dead', 'mine')}
for n, s in socks.items(): s.bind(str(d/n))
socks['ramabana-live'].listen()
for n in ('ramabana-dead', 'mine'): socks[n].close()
test_eq(prune_sockets(d), [])
test_eq(prune_sockets(d, age=0), ['ramabana-dead'])
socks['ramabana-live'].close()
left = sorted(p.name for p in d.ls())
shutil.rmtree(d)
left

The ramabana script, run_cli, makes the tmux decision before it imports the CLI. Importing the CLI takes about 0.4 seconds. Deciding first lets the process outside tmux hand over to tmux quickly. launch_args(argv) reads just enough of the command line to know the session is interactive, without the full option parser. It returns the cfg and tmux values that launch needs. It returns None to leave the decision to main in the CLI. It returns None for a prompt, for any option in EARLY (such as --json, --doctor and --help), for --tmux off, for a valued option with no value, and for options that refusal rejects. An option it does not know is skipped.
refusal holds the checks that main makes before it starts anything, such as --pii without --vault. It returns the reason or ''. Running it in run_cli refuses a bad option in your terminal and not on the tmux hold screen. bare_resume gives a bare --resume the value PICK_SESSION, which lists this folder’s sessions to choose from. When run_cli has called launch, it sets LAUNCHED. main then does not call launch again.

title: setup
text:
config.toml
~/.config/ramabana/config.toml holds this machine’s settings: one file, edited by hand, that every Ramabana on the machine reads. A session started with another --cfg, and an app that embeds Ramabana with a config folder of its own, read the same file and never write into their own folder for it. $RAMABANA_CONFIG names another file; the tests use it.
A value can come from four places, and the first that has one wins:







Source
Example




a command-line flag
--model gpt-5.4


an env var
$RAMABANA_MODEL, or $LEELA_MODEL inside Leela, the notebook editor that embeds Ramabana


config.toml
[jobs] turn = "gpt-5.4"


the built-in default
claude-opus-5-5



KEYS lists every key: its type, the env var and the flag that beat it, what it sets, and the values it may take. drop_tools, at the top level, names the tools a session leaves out of the model’s schema. Each tool’s schema costs tokens on every call. With no drop_tools, a session keeps every tool. The tables are [jobs], the model each job runs on; [window], the numbers the window guard works with; [compaction]; [runtime], what a model is started with; and [cli], the defaults of the terminal session’s flags that take a value. [jobs] image is the OpenAI-compatible model generate_image draws with. [azure] holds Azure OpenAI’s endpoint, which $AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT beats, read as named with no prefix (Key.plain), and the api_key_env that names the env var holding its key. A key an earlier release read, such as azure.deployments, is reported with what to do instead (RETIRED_KEYS). A [model."NAME"] table corrects the numbers fastllm’s table gives one model: max_input_tokens, max_output_tokens and supports_images. Given model_id, the same table defines a model of that name, with runtime, base_url, api_key_env, api_name, vendor_name and ctx; core registers it.
load_config reads the file again only when it changes. An entry it cannot use takes its default and gives one warning, which Agent.problems and ramabana config show repeat: a key nobody knows, with the nearest one it might mean; a value of the wrong type or outside its choices; a file that is not TOML. Nothing raises.
keys.env, beside config.toml, stores API keys saved by /login. A name already in the environment wins over the file. The CLI loads keys.env before any subcommand. The beat loads beat.env first and keys.env second. A name in beat.env therefore wins in the beat.
A value beginning with ! runs a shell command and uses its stripped output, for example OPENAI_API_KEY=!security find-generic-password -ws openai on macOS, or OPENAI_API_KEY=!op read op://vault/item/key. A command that fails, prints nothing or runs longer than 30 seconds leaves that name unset and prints a warning on stderr. To store a value that begins with a literal !, prefix it with $: $!text loads as !text.
Only the owner may read the file (chmod 600). load_keys refuses a file that other users can read and prints a warning on stderr. Saved values are never printed or logged.


source

set_table
def set_table(

title: setup
text:
Installing tmux
When tmux is missing, offer_install shows the install command and asks once whether to run it. The command is brew install tmux on macOS, and sudo apt-get install -y tmux or sudo dnf install -y tmux on Linux. installer picks the command from what is on PATH. The command runs attached to the terminal. sudo can therefore ask for a password.
offer_install stores the answer in <cfg>/setup.json. It never asks again after a no, after a yes whose install worked, or when no install command exists. Ctrl+c at the prompt and an install that failed or was interrupted store nothing. The next run asks again. ramabana --doctor asks even after an earlier no. Without tmux, the session starts in the current terminal and prints one line on how to get the now pane.
The first example says yes on a Mac with Homebrew, and the session relaunches in the tmux it installed. The second says no on Linux, and a second launch does not ask again:

title: setup
section: Whether the code index needs to run
text:
Whether the code index needs to run
The search_code tool searches a code index that kosha builds over the installed packages and the open folders. Rebuilding the index is called a sync. A sync takes time. The session skips it when nothing the sync reads has changed.
index_gate(cfg, roots) decides this without importing kosha. index_state takes a fingerprint of what a sync would read. The fingerprint holds the installed distributions that importlib.metadata finds, with their modification times (pkg_state). For each folder it holds the git HEAD and a digest of git status with the modification times of the paths it names (root_state). Outside git, a folder’s fingerprint hashes each visible file’s relative path, size and nanosecond modification time, skipping hidden files and folders. index_gate returns the fingerprint and a reason to run kosha, or '' to skip the sync. The reason is '' when the fingerprint matches the one that the last good sync saved in <cfg>/kosha-state.json, and each folder’s .kosha/code.db and kosha’s package database, kosha_env_db(), exist. When the fingerprint matches and a database is missing, the reason is index missing. Otherwise index_changes says what changed, such as packages changed: +foo 1.2.
After a good sync the session calls save_index to store the new fingerprint. Either way log_index appends one line to <cfg>/kosha.log, and --doctor shows the last line through last_index. The example walks a fresh folder through a first sync, a missing index, an unchanged state and a new package:

title: setup
text:
Peer hooks
ramabana setup peers puts the peer hooks of peer_hooks and the peer-work text of peer_work into the config of Claude Code and Codex, so those sessions can talk to each other and to Ramabana. It never writes before you say yes. For each agent it prints a unified diff of every file it would change, then asks once. --yes skips the question. --remove takes out only what this command put in.
The hooks go into the hooks table of ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.codex/hooks.json. Each hook command is the full path of this Python with -m ramabana.peer_hooks, so it runs this ramabana whatever is first on PATH. A hook group is ours when one of its commands has ramabana.peer_hooks or peer-hook in it, so the ramabana peer-hook groups of older setups are replaced or removed too. A second run replaces our groups where they stand and changes nothing when they are equal. Your own hooks and settings stay as they are. If the file is not valid JSON, the command names it and writes nothing for that agent.
merge_hooks does the merge. An empty block removes our groups, and an event with no groups left is dropped:


source

merge_hooks
def merge_hooks(
    cfg, block
):
cfg with our hook groups set to block (by event) where ours stood; empty block removes them.



theirs = {'hooks': [{'type': 'command', 'command': 'notify-me'}]}
ours = lambda e: {'hooks': [{'type': 'command', 'command': f'ramabana peer-hook claude {e}'}]}
cfg = {'model': 'opus', 'hooks': {'Stop': [theirs, ours('stop'), theirs]}}
new = merge_hooks(cfg, {'Stop': [ours('stop2')], 'End': [ours('end')]})
test_eq(new, {'model': 'opus', 'hooks': {'Stop': [theirs, ours('stop2'), theirs], 'End': [ours('end')]}})
test_eq(merge_hooks(new, {'Stop': [ours('stop2')], 'End': [ours('end')]}), new)
test_eq(merge_hooks(new, {}), {'model': 'opus', 'hooks': {'Stop': [theirs, theirs]}})
test_eq(merge_hooks({'hooks': {'Stop': [ours('stop')]}}, {}), {})
new_form = {'hooks': [{'type': 'command', 'command': '/usr/bin/python3 -m ramabana.peer_hooks claude stop'}]}
test_eq([_ours(g) for g in (ours('stop'), new_form, theirs, 'odd')], [True, True, False, False])
test_eq(merge_hooks({'hooks': {'Stop': [theirs, ours('stop')]}}, {'Stop': [new_form]}), {'hooks': {'Stop': [theirs, new_form]}})

The text and the files
Claude Code reads a skill from ~/.claude/skills/peer-work/SKILL.md. peer_skill gives it the docstring of peer_work under front matter that names the skill. Codex has no skills, but it reads ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, which is your own file. For Codex the text is one section between two marker lines. A new run replaces that section and no other part. --remove takes out that section only, and deletes the file only when nothing else is left in it.

text:
The command
setup_peers plans the changes of each agent as (path, text now, text after), prints a diff of each one that differs, and asks. A missing file has no text now, and is made on write. A text after of None deletes the file. The folders are made on write, and home replaces ~, so a test never touches your real config.


source

setup_peers
def setup_peers(
    argv, ask:function=_no_stdin, out:builtin_function_or_method=print, home:NoneType=None
):
ramabana setup peers [--agent claude|codex|all] [--remove] [--yes]: show each file’s diff, write after a yes; 0, or 1 when something was refused.



import tempfile
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    shown = []
    test_eq(setup_peers(['--agent', 'claude'], ask=lambda q: 'n', out=shown.append, home=d), 1)
    assert shown[0].startswith(f'--- {d}/.claude/settings.json (now)') and not (Path(d)/'.claude').exists()
    test_eq(setup_peers(['--agent', 'claude', '--yes'], out=shown.append, home=d), 0)
    assert '"SessionStart"' in (Path(d)/'.claude/settings.json').read_text()
    test_eq(setup_peers(['--agent', 'claude', '--remove', '--yes'], out=shown.append, home=d), 0)
    test_eq(json.loads((Path(d)/'.claude/settings.json').read_text()), {})

Each agent has a line in --doctor. peers_status reads the hook command in the config of the agent and runs it the way the agent would, but with no PATH, for the cheap event version. A command that works shows the Python it runs and the ramabana version. A command that fails, such as ramabana peer-hook from an older setup, says why and how to fix it. path_check asks the ramabana on PATH for its version in the same cheap way. When it is missing or reports another version, it gives one line that says how to fix it, because an agent that types ramabana tell gets that one:


source

path_check

    home:NoneType=None, which:function=which
):
A line when the ramabana on PATH is missing or reports a version other than the one the hooks run, else None.




source

def peers_status(
    home:NoneType=None
):
One line for each agent: whether its config has the peer hooks and what they run, or how to install or fix them.




source

hook_check
def hook_check(
    cmd, home
):
Run hook command cmd with the event version, with no PATH, as a check: (True, the ramabana version) or (False, why it fails).



from ramabana import __version__
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    test_eq(peers_status(d), [f'peers: {k} hooks not installed: run ramabana setup peers --agent {k}' for k in ('claude', 'codex')])
    setup_peers(['--agent', 'codex', '--yes'], out=lambda s: None, home=d)
    test_eq(peers_status(d)[1], f'peers: codex hooks installed (runs: {sys.executable}, ramabana {__version__})')
    (Path(d)/'.claude').mkdir(); (Path(d)/'.claude/settings.json').write_text(json.dumps({'hooks': {'Stop': [{'hooks': [{'type': 'command', 'command': 'ramabana peer-hook claude stop'}]}]}}))
    assert peers_status(d)[0].startswith('peers: claude hook command fails: ')
    fake = Path(d)/'ramabana'
    fake.write_text('#!/bin/sh\necho 0.0.1\n'); fake.chmod(0o755)
    assert 'is 0.0.1; the hooks run' in path_check(d, lambda n: fake)
    fake.write_text(f'#!/bin/sh\necho {__version__}\n')
    test_eq(path_check(d, lambda n: fake), None)

Ramabana reports a failure in one of two ways. AgentError is a refusal: an action Ramabana declines to perform, with a message the user can act on. Examples are a write outside the open folders and a model whose key is missing. AgentError is shalya’s HostError under another name. title: core
text:
The model tables
MODELS is the table of short model names you can type, such as sonnet or gemma-e4b. Each name maps to a pair: the runtime that serves the model, and the id that runtime knows the model by. Smaller tables make up MODELS. LOCAL holds the LiteRT models, MLX the models for Apple silicon, LLAMA the llama.cpp models, CLOUD the OpenAI and Codex models, and the Claude tables come from the catalog in models.
JOBS lists every job the policy can route on its own: the turn, one-shot prompts, inline edits, code completion, classification, summaries, and sub-agents. ONESHOT_JOBS are the jobs that send one prompt and read one answer back.
claude_ctx returns a Claude model’s context window, the number of tokens it can read at once. It returns DFLT_AGENT_CTX (128,000) for an id that no entry of CLAUDE_CTX matches. claude_wire returns the id to ask Claude Code for. The id has a [1m] suffix for a model with a million-token window.


source

claude_wire
def claude_wire(
    model_id
):
The id Claude Code is asked for: its plain id serves 200k, and the 1M window is <id>[1m].




source

claude_ctx

    model_id
):
A Claude Code model’s context window, else DFLT_AGENT_CTX.

title: core
text:
Probing the machine
Some questions are about this machine: whether a runtime is installed, which models an API key can list, which models a Copilot plan reaches. Each answer is too slow for a model picker to wait on. Each answer changes rarely. probed(key, fn) remembers these answers. Use it for a slow question whose last answer is good enough to show.

The first call runs fn() and returns its answer.
Later calls return the remembered answer at once. When the answer is older than ttl seconds (PROBE_TTL, 90 by default), a background thread calls fn() again. A later call returns the new answer. When the background call raises, the old answer stays and the next refresh waits another ttl seconds.
probed also saves the answer to a file under ~/.config/ramabana/probes. The next run of the program then has a value on its first call, and refreshes it in the background. Pass disk=False to keep the answer in memory only.

forget_probes drops every remembered answer. Call it from a refresh button. forget_probes(disk=True) deletes the files too. The hidden test below walks through each case.


source

forget_probes

    disk:bool=False, dir:NoneType=None
):
Drop every cached answer, and with disk its file too.

):
fn()’s last answer, refreshing a stale one in the background.

Where one probe’s last answer is kept between runs.

Extras
The core install is the agent, its hosts, and the file, code, shell and git tools. Each extra, such as ramabana[search], adds the packages for one more use. installed says whether a module would import, without importing it. need(extra, *mods) returns an empty string when the packages are present. Otherwise it returns a sentence that tells the user what to install. A command that needs an extra can refuse with that sentence. Both functions are defined in setup and re-exported here. The console scripts import setup first because it loads nothing heavy.

The console scripts, for a ramabana script installed while they lived here.

text:
Credentials
auth_status reports which credentials this machine has, one entry per vendor: an OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini key in the environment, a Codex login, a Claude Code login, a Copilot sign-in, and Azure OpenAI. It never returns, logs or stores a secret. For Claude Code it runs claude auth status rather than reading the credential file.


source

auth_status
def auth_status():
Which credential sources this machine has, per vendor, without reading or returning any secret.




source

    spec
):
Whether spec goes to Azure OpenAI: named azure/..., or its base_url is an Azure host.




source

azure_host

    url
):
Whether url is on an Azure host.

Whether Azure OpenAI has an endpoint and its key is in the environment.

The env var holding the Azure OpenAI key: config.toml’s azure.api_key_env, else AZURE_KEY_ENV.




source

azure_endpoint

The v1 base of $AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT, else of config.toml’s azure.endpoint, else ’’.




source

azure_base
def azure_base(
    url
):
Azure OpenAI’s v1 API base for a resource URL, however much of a path or query it carries; ’’ for none.


Every vendor appears whether or not it is connected. Each entry has the same two fields, available and source. A settings page can draw the whole list without special cases:

{k: v['available'] for k, v in auth_status().items()}

{'openai': True,
 'codex': True,
 'anthropic': False,
 'claude': True,
 'gemini': True,
 'copilot': True}



Azure OpenAI
Azure OpenAI needs AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT, the resource such as https://NAME.openai.azure.com, and AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY. config.toml’s [azure] table can hold the endpoint instead, as endpoint. It can also name another env var for the key with api_key_env. The key itself never goes in the file. Setting the endpoint and key does not select a deployment. Ramabana uses a deployment only where you name it, as azure/DEPLOYMENT or in a [model."NAME"] table. azure_base converts any form of the endpoint to the v1 base. It drops a deployment path and an api-version, which the v1 API does not use. azure_ready returns whether the endpoint and the key are both set. is_azure returns whether a spec goes to Azure.

for u in ('https://r.openai.azure.com', 'r.openai.azure.com/', 'https://r.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/', 'https://r.openai.azure.com/openai/deployments/x/chat/completions?api-version=2024-10-21'):
    test_eq(azure_base(u), 'https://r.openai.azure.com/openai/v1')
test_eq(azure_base('https://apim.azure-api.net/team/openai'), 'https://apim.azure-api.net/team/openai/v1')
assert azure_host('https://r.openai.azure.us/openai/v1') and not azure_host('https://api.openai.com/v1')

title: core
text:
Configurable models
register_model adds a short name of your own to the tables for the rest of this process. Use it for a model the tables do not list. A Hugging Face URL is enough, because rishi works out which runtime serves it. unregister_model removes it.


source

unregister_model
def unregister_model(
    name
):
Remove one process-local configurable model alias.




source

register_model
def register_model(
    name, model_id, runtime:NoneType=None, ctx:int=128000, note:str='custom model', **config
):
Add a model name until this process exits. save_model keeps a name on disk.


A name added with register_model is gone after a restart. save_model keeps a name in a file. Every application that offers its own model names needs this file, and this module manages it:

save_model(row) checks a row, registers it, and writes it to the file.
load_models() reads the file at startup, registers every row that still resolves, and skips the rest.
delete_model(name) removes a name from the file and from this process.
saved_models() returns the rows on disk.

A row holds name, model_id, runtime and ctx. A row for the remote runtime can also have base_url, vendor_name and api_name to name an endpoint, and api_key_env to name the environment variable that holds its key. The file never holds a key. Each function takes a path for the application’s own file. path defaults to ~/.config/ramabana/models.json, or to the file that use_aliases set.


source

delete_model
def delete_model(
    name, path:NoneType=None
):
Forget one alias, on disk and in this process.




source

save_model
def save_model(
    row, path:NoneType=None
):
Validate, register and persist one alias. Returns the row as written.




source

load_models
def load_models(
    path:NoneType=None
):
Register every saved alias that still resolves, and return those rows.




source

saved_models
def saved_models(
    path:NoneType=None
):
The alias rows on disk, or [] if the file is missing or malformed.




source

alias_path
def alias_path(
    path:NoneType=None
):
The file one application keeps its model aliases in.




source

use_aliases
def use_aliases(
    path
):
Set the alias file that calls naming no path use, as use_env_prefix does for env vars.


config.toml can define a model as well as correct one. A [model."NAME"] table with model_id registers NAME for this process, for [jobs], --model and /model, with the same base_url, api_key_env, api_name, vendor_name and runtime keys that a saved alias has. ctx is another name for max_input_tokens. The runtime defaults to remote when the table sets base_url, api_key_env, vendor_name or api_name. On an Azure host, api_name defaults to openai, the Responses API, and api_key_env defaults to AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY. Ramabana ignores a table that names a built-in model, an unknown runtime or a runtime that is missing here. It issues one warning for each ignored table. model_problems() and Agent.problems repeat the warnings. Nothing raises.
sync_models() registers the application’s saved aliases and then config.toml’s definitions. It registers them again whenever either file changes. resolve, available_models and Routing call it. The terminal session, ramabana-mcp, ramabana-acp, a headless run and an embedding app all see the same names without a call at startup. A name defined in both places belongs to config.toml. load_models skips it and save_model refuses it. An application with its own alias file calls use_aliases(path) to make that file the default for calls that name no file.
remote_models() lists the hosted models whose credentials are set. It covers models defined in config.toml and saved aliases, config.toml’s first. A setup page counts them. The routing never picks one of them by itself.
