title: core
text:
Listing models
available_models builds the list a model picker shows. Each row names a model this process can actually run. The on-device models appear when their runtime is installed, ollama’s models when its daemon answers, and a vendor’s models only when the credential for it exists. The hosted lists come from provider_models in models. copilot_catalog is the model list for your Copilot plan, which the Copilot server reports and probed remembers for five minutes. A model config.toml defines appears with source config.toml once it can run.


source

available_models
def available_models(
    include_legacy:bool=False
):
Models selectable here, with older generations only when include_legacy.




source

copilot_catalog
def copilot_catalog(
    ttl:int=300
):
Copilot’s catalogue for this account, cached: {id: entry}, or {} when it cannot be reached.


Each row has a value to pass to resolve, a label to show, its provider, and the source that made it available. The picker shows the source beside the label. This check fakes a Copilot plan with one chat model:

_orig_avail, _orig_cat = _copilot_available, copilot_catalog
_copilot_available = lambda: True
copilot_catalog = lambda ttl=300: {'test-chat': {'capabilities': {'type': 'chat'}}}
try:
    rows = available_models()
    test_eq({r['value'] for r in rows if r['provider'] == 'litert'}, set(LOCAL))
    test_eq([r['value'] for r in rows if r['provider'] == 'copilot'], ['copilot/test-chat'])
finally: _copilot_available, copilot_catalog = _orig_avail, _orig_cat

Older model generations, such as gpt-4.1, are left out unless you ask for them with include_legacy=True:

names = {r['value'] for r in available_models()}
legacy = {r['value'] for r in available_models(include_legacy=True)}
test_eq(names - legacy, set())
sorted(legacy - names)

['openai/gpt-4.1', 'openai/gpt-4.1-mini', 'openai/gpt-4.1-nano']

title: core
text:
Defaults and context windows
Every default route is a hosted model:



job
default model
through




turn
claude-opus-5-5
Claude Code


subagent
claude-sonnet-5-5
Claude Code


oneshot, inline, summary
gpt-6-luna
a Codex login


completion, classify
claude-haiku-5-5
Claude Code



DEFAULT_POLICY leaves turn empty. $RAMABANA_MODEL or DFLT_TURN fills it. It also leaves inline empty, and inline follows oneshot. A model on this machine runs the turn only when you name it with --model, /model or $RAMABANA_MODEL. Once you do, the other jobs follow the turn onto the machine. DFLT_LOCAL, qwen-4b, is the local model to suggest. It is never a route unless named.
When none of the hosted models for a job can run here, the job moves to DFLT_FALLBACK, Gemma 4 E4B on LiteRT, rather than failing. The turn never moves. Changing models in the middle of a conversation is your decision, not a default.
A local model’s context window is the size Ramabana uses. It can be smaller than the size the model was trained with. A larger window costs memory and time. local_ctx returns that size from the first of these that sets one: $RAMABANA_LOCAL_CTX, config.toml’s max_input_tokens for that model, config.toml’s window.local_ctx, then the built-in table. The engine still caps the size at the size the model was trained with. local_window reads the trained size from the model’s own config, for the runtimes that publish it.


source

local_ctx
def local_ctx(
    name, dflt:int=32768
):
The context window to use for local model name: $RAMABANA_LOCAL_CTX if it sets one, then config.toml’s [model."NAME"] and window.local_ctx, else the table.




source

local_window
def local_window(
    runtime, model_id
):
A local model’s trained context window from its own config, else 0.


Every job in JOBS has an entry in DEFAULT_POLICY. The check below fails when a job has none:

test_eq(set(JOBS) - set(DEFAULT_POLICY), set())

local_ctx takes the size from a table, with 32,768 tokens for a model the table does not name. $RAMABANA_LOCAL_CTX overrides it, either as one number for every model or as name:size pairs separated by commas:

local_ctx('gemma-e4b'), local_ctx('gemma-12b'), local_ctx('a-model-nobody-tabled')

(16384, 16384, 32768)



os.environ['RAMABANA_LOCAL_CTX'] = 'gemma-e4b:4096'
test_eq(local_ctx('gemma-e4b'), 4096)
test_eq(local_ctx('gemma-12b'), 16_384)
del os.environ['RAMABANA_LOCAL_CTX']
local_ctx('gemma-e4b')

16384

title: core
text:
Resolving a model
resolve(name) turns a model name into a ModelSpec: the runtime, the model id, the context window, any runtime options, and a note for the user. Every place that needs to run a model calls it. Code further down accepts the ModelSpec and does not resolve the name again. A runtime that is not installed here does not raise. The spec comes back with missing set to the binary or package that is absent and how to get it. A missing API key works the same way: Agent.start reports it. missing_runtime(spec) asks the same question live. Agent.start turns the answer into a failed turn that names a model from available_models that does run here. resolve raises KeyError with the closest known names for a name it cannot place.
azure/DEPLOYMENT names an Azure OpenAI deployment on the v1 API of azure_endpoint(), with the key in azure_key_env(), through the Responses API. It resolves whether or not the deployment is listed. A deployment named for a model fastllm knows, such as gpt-5.4, gets that model’s window and briefing. Any other name gets 128k and a note that names the [model."azure/NAME"] entry that corrects it.
A hosted model’s window comes from fastllm’s table, which can be out of date. A [model."NAME"] table in config.toml corrects it on this machine. max_input_tokens replaces the window. max_output_tokens sets the reply cap that the chat starts with. supports_images answers accepts(spec, 'image'). The table for the route name you chose the model by wins over the table for its model id.
spec_caps and accepts say what a resolved model can be sent, such as images or audio. A model rishi knows nothing about counts as accepting everything. model_note describes a spec in one line for a status bar.


source

ModelSpec
def ModelSpec(
    name:str, runtime:str, model_id:str, ctx:int=128000, note:str='', opts:dict=<factory>, missing:str=''
)->None:
urai’s ModelSpec, with backend and config as views of runtime and opts.




source

model_note
def model_note(
    spec
):
One line about a resolved model, for a status bar.




source

accepts
def accepts(
    spec, kind
):
Can spec’s model be sent kind? config.toml’s supports_images answers for a picture; unknown counts as yes.




source

spec_caps
def spec_caps(
    spec
):
What spec’s model accepts and what it hands back, or None where rishi cannot say.




source

resolve
def resolve(
    name
):
A ModelSpec for name: a short name from the tables, or any full vendor/model spec; none is DFLT_TURN. A runtime this machine lacks is named in missing, not raised.




source

reachable_hint
def reachable_hint():
Which model to try instead, from available_models. It suggests a model and switches nothing.




source

missing_runtime
def missing_runtime(
    spec
):
Why spec‘s runtime cannot run on this machine and how to get it;’’ when it can. Asked live, never cached.




source

unknown_model
def unknown_model(
    name
):
The error message for a model name nobody knows, with the closest known names.


A short name resolves from the tables. A full vendor/model name resolves even when no table mentions it. A model released this morning works this morning:

resolve('gemma-e4b')

ModelSpec(name='gemma-e4b', backend='litert', model_id='litert-community/gemma-4-E4B-it-litert-lm', ctx=16384, note='', config={})



spec = resolve('claude/claude-sonnet-5')
test_eq(spec.backend, 'claude')
test_eq(spec.local, False)
test_eq(set(RUNTIME_NAMES), set(urai.RUNTIMES))
test_eq({r for r in RUNTIME_NAMES if ModelSpec('x', r, 'x').local}, {k for k, v in urai.RUNTIMES.items() if v.local})
assert ModelSpec('fake', 'fake', 'fake/model').local
model_note(spec)

if runtime_available('mlx'):
    spec = resolve('mlx-community/a-model-nobody-tabled')
    test_eq((spec.backend, spec.model_id), ('mlx', 'mlx-community/a-model-nobody-tabled'))
else:
    assert resolve('mlx-community/a-model-nobody-tabled').missing
test_eq(resolve('somevendor/some-model').backend, 'remote')
test_fail(lambda: resolve('gpt-image-2'), contains='unknown model')

The tables list what the picker offers, not everything that runs. A Claude id the tables have moved past, such as claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-4-6 or opus-5, still resolves to the Claude Code runtime with the id passed through. A saved session or a pinned setting keeps working, and Claude Code decides whether it still serves that id. Any other unknown name is taken as a typo, and fails where it was typed rather than in the middle of a turn.

_orig_ra = runtime_available
runtime_available = lambda rt: rt == 'claude' or _orig_ra(rt)
try:
    for old in ('claude-opus-5', 'claude-sonnet-4-6', 'claude-haiku-4-5', 'claude-opus-4-8', 'claude-sonnet-5', 'claude-fable-5-1'):
        spec = resolve(old)
        test_eq((spec.backend, spec.model_id), ('claude', old))
    test_eq(resolve('opus-5').model_id, 'claude-opus-5')
    for full in ('claude/claude-opus-5', 'claude/claude-opus-4-8', 'claude/claude-haiku-4-5', 'claude/opus-5', 'claude/sonnet', 'claude/haiku', 'claude/claude-fable-5-1'):
        bare = full.split('/', 1)[1]

    test_eq({r['label'] for r in available_models() if r['provider'] == 'claude'}, set(CATALOG['claude']))

test_fail(lambda: resolve('gpt-9'), contains='unknown model')

    rows = [r for r in available_models() if r['provider'] == 'copilot']
    test_eq({r['value'] for r in rows}, {'copilot/gpt-5.5', 'copilot/claude-opus-4.7'})

_copilot_available = lambda: False

title: core
text:
What a model can afford
Before a turn, the agent sends the model a briefing: the system prompt with the project’s rules, the tool schemas, and sometimes the full text of a skill. On a small context window this fills most of the space before any work starts. On a full host the tool schemas cost about 4.7k tokens, an inlined skill 3k more, and the briefing 1.4k, which leaves a 16k model room for about one tool result.
budget_for(spec, tool_max) sizes the briefing to the model’s window and returns a Budget. For a window above 24k tokens the budget changes nothing except the cap on each tool result. For a smaller window it drops the memory and web tool groups, stops inlining skill text, and clips each tool result harder. It only holds things back: a skill it does not inline is still one read_skill call away. With channel='tags' it first subtracts the tokens the tool schemas will take inside the prompt (see below).


source

budget_for
def budget_for(
    spec, tool_max, channel:str='native'
):
A window-sized budget; tool_max=None selects an automatic cap up to 32000 characters.




source

Budget
def Budget(
    drop:tuple=(), inline:bool=True, tool_max:int=0, note:str=''
)->None:
What a model can afford to be told, and to be sent back.


The window sets how much a model has room for. It does not set how much a model can follow. The profile limits the tools and briefing that a model receives:

small offers the fourteen tools in SMALL_TOOLS, which cover a coding turn, and a one-screen briefing.
full offers everything.
auto picks small for a model on this machine or a window of 32k tokens or less, and full otherwise. A model whose window is unknown counts as full.

profile_for(spec, profile) makes the choice, and the budget above still sizes the tool results. The first cell below checks the profile, the next two the budget:

title: core
text:
Where the tool schemas travel
A tool schema tells the model what a tool is called and what arguments it takes. There are two ways to send them. The native channel uses the model API’s own tool field: the API checks the schemas, and tool calls come back as structured data. The tags channel, rishi’s tool_mode='tags', writes the schemas into the system prompt and reads tool calls back out of the reply text, written as Hermes-style tags. The local engines have always worked this way. urai provides parse_tool_tags for it.
Native is better wherever it is open. It is not always open. Claude Code receives tools as an in-process MCP server. A company-managed Claude Code configuration can forbid every MCP server it did not approve. Without the tags channel, that policy leaves the agent unable to read a file. rishi uses the native channel for Claude Code where its SDK can, and tags in the CLI or wherever the server is refused.
tool_channel(spec, chat=None, scope='turn', session='') returns 'native' or 'tags'. Nothing else picks the channel. A local engine takes no tool_mode, and tool_channel always returns native for it. For any other runtime, tool_channel uses the first of these that sets a channel:

$RAMABANA_TOOL_CHANNEL.
tags, for a model that force_tags marked because a request refused its schemas.
The session’s choice: /model tools for the turn, /subagents tools for sub-agents.
config.toml’s [model."NAME"] tool_channel.
The scope’s own key: runtime.tool_channel, or for sub-agents $RAMABANA_SUBAGENT_TOOL_CHANNEL and then subagents.tool_channel. A sub-agent falls back to runtime.tool_channel.
The runtime’s default: tags for Claude Code, native for the rest.

A person can write text for tags. tool_channel never asks the open chat, because a replayed chat has no such attribute. Native for Claude Code needs a rishi that carries tools through its in-process MCP server. With an older rishi the answer stays tags. forget_forced_tags clears the marks, and the native channel is tried again. budget_for takes the channel as an argument because the schemas cost prompt tokens on the tags channel.

title: core
text:
Routing
Routing decides which model runs each job. Nothing else decides. Build one with the turn model you want. Without an argument, the turn model is $RAMABANA_MODEL, then turn in config.toml’s [jobs], then DFLT_TURN. name_for(job) returns the model name for a job. spec(job) resolves that name to a ModelSpec ready to run. Four actions give one job a model of its own: set $RAMABANA_MODEL_<JOB>, name the job in config.toml’s [jobs] (the env var wins), call set(name, job), or type /model JOB NAME in a session. A job with no entry in the policy uses the turn’s model. A job added to JOBS always has a model.
When the turn runs on this machine, every job without a model of its own stays on it, sub-agents included. A job with a model of its own can run on a hosted model.
When a job’s model cannot run here, spec moves the job to another hosted route that the policy already names. spec never moves a job to a local model that nobody named, except the last resort DFLT_FALLBACK. A job with no model of its own goes to the turn’s model first. That move is the plan and writes no note. One model that runs is enough for every job. A job that someone gave claude-haiku-5-5 tries claude-sonnet-5-5 first. alternatives(job) lists the routes in the order spec tries them, ending with DFLT_FALLBACK. A job that follows a local turn has no alternatives. A hosted model whose key is missing counts as a model that cannot run, for every job but the turn. Agent.start reports the turn’s missing key. A model whose answer failed or came back empty is set aside for DOWN_TTL, five minutes. spec writes each move to notes, keyed by job. news holds one line per model that fell, for the chat to show once. When no route is left, the error names the job, the model, and the key or command it needs. missing_key and needs build that part of the message.
A machine with no Claude Code login cannot run DFLT_TURN. Building a Routing never changes its turn. Suppose nobody named the turn for this run, with turn= (the --model flag), set or $RAMABANA_MODEL, and its model cannot run here. Then settled() names where the turn should go: ready_turn(), the first provider in READY_ORDER that is ready, subscriptions before keys. Agent.settle moves the turn there once, when a session starts. Ramabana never replaces a turn named for this run. Ramabana never picks Azure, Bedrock or a custom endpoint, because each needs a name only its owner knows.
PROVIDERS lists the providers Ramabana can use and what each needs. provider_ready says which providers are set up here. needs_setup(routing) returns why the turn’s model cannot run here: a missing runtime, a missing key, or a Claude Code that nobody signed in to. It returns an empty string when the model can run. setup_guide formats this for a person: the providers, then each job with the model it runs on, where that model was chosen, and whether it can run. job_source names the origin: env, config.toml, chosen (a set call), follows the turn or default. A one-shot or piped run whose turn cannot run prints the guide and exits. An interactive session opens anyway, on welcome(routing), which says why nothing runs and lists the commands that fix it. ramabana setup adds a provider from a shell.
AWS Bedrock is reached through its OpenAI-compatible Mantle endpoint, https://bedrock-mantle.<region>.api.aws/v1, with a Bedrock API key in AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK that goes out as a bearer token. Bedrock API keys can be short-lived. Renew them as AWS instructs. Model ids are Bedrock’s own, such as openai.gpt-5.4, and their windows come from fastllm’s bedrock_mantle table. Ramabana does not support Bedrock’s native Converse and InvokeModel APIs, and so does not support Claude on Bedrock. fastllm has no SigV4 signing, no AWS credential chain or profile, and no Converse wire format.
image_route resolves the image job, which generate_image uses. The model comes from $RAMABANA_MODEL_IMAGE, config.toml’s [jobs] image, or DFLT_IMAGE, OpenAI’s gpt-image-1. image_route returns the endpoint, key and model of an OpenAI-shaped images API, such as an Azure deployment of gpt-image-1. When no such API is usable, it returns a sentence that says what to set up. Bedrock’s Mantle endpoint and OpenRouter have no images endpoint.
video_route resolves the video job the same way, from $RAMABANA_MODEL_VIDEO, config.toml’s [jobs] video, or DFLT_VIDEO, Google’s Veo 3. It returns api, the endpoint, the key and the model id. api is gemini for Gemini’s long-running predictLongRunning API, or openai for an OpenAI-shaped /videos API such as sora-2 on OpenAI or Azure. video_route refuses a model that fastllm knows to return no video, a local model, and a host with no video endpoint. Each refusal says what to set up. video_route(name) resolves one named model. A job started earlier is then polled with the key it started with.

title: control
text:
A program that hosts agent jobs, such as a web app, often runs each job in a process of its own. Restarting the web server then does not kill a turn halfway through. The page that started the job needs a way to reach it: to send a prompt, steer the running turn, stop it, and answer the approval requests it raises. Control provides that way. It opens a Unix socket in the session’s run folder. A Unix socket is an address in the file system that only processes on this machine can connect to. Only the current user may connect.
The protocol is one JSON object per line in each direction. A request is {"id", "method", "params"}. A successful reply is {"id", "result"}. A failed reply is {"id", "error"}. METHODS lists the methods:

prompt(text) starts a turn on a worker thread. If a turn is already running, text is queued to run after it.
steer(text) gives text to the running turn with its next tool result. This redirects the model without stopping the turn.
tell(run_id, text) queues text for the running sub-agent run_id, as Agent.tell does, and returns what it said: told RUN, or why nothing is listening. A transcript pane uses it for the lines typed into it.
cancel() stops the running turn and drops the prompts queued behind it. The reply includes the number dropped as dropped.
asks() lists the approval requests waiting for an answer, oldest first. answer(id, ok, note) answers one of them.
status() returns running, queued (the number of queued prompts), session and last. last is how the last turn ended, or None before any turn has ended. It also returns what a peer lists: name, the session’s name for a person; state, one of idle, working and waiting for approval; folder, its first open folder; and at, when it was last active.
events(offset) returns events, the records in the session’s event file from byte offset on, and offset, the value to pass next time. It returns whole lines only, at most EVENTS_MAX bytes per call. When the file has rolled over since the last read, it starts from byte 0 and sets rotated to true. It raises an error until the runner has called agent.events_to(path).

control_call(path, method, **params) is the other end. It connects, sends one request and returns the result. On an error reply it raises RuntimeError with the error’s message. Its timeout argument is 30 seconds by default. The page uses it, and any script that needs to reach a running job can use it.
start refuses a path where another runner is listening and a path that holds anything other than a socket. It removes a socket that a crashed runner left behind.
A Unix socket path takes at most about 100 bytes (SOCKET_MAX). When you give no path and the session’s run folder is deeper, the socket goes in the temporary folder as ramabana-<session>.sock. An explicit path that is too long raises ValueError.








Constant
Value
Limit




SOCKET_MAX
100
Bytes of a socket path. macOS allows 104.


REQUEST_MAX
1,000,000
Bytes of one request line


EVENTS_MAX
1,000,000
Bytes of the event file that one events call returns

The example plays both sides in one process. fake_agent from ramabana.testing supplies an agent whose model replies with a scripted line. The first cell sends a prompt through the socket, waits for the turn to finish, checks how it ended and reads the turn’s events.

from ramabana import agent
from ramabana.testing import fake_agent

ctl = Control(a).start()
call = lambda method, **kw: control_call(ctl.path, method, **kw)

test_eq(call('prompt', text='hello'), {'started': True})
for _ in range(200):
    if not call('status')['running']: break
    time.sleep(.01)
st = call('status')
test_eq((st['running'], st['last']['state'], st['last']['reply']), (False, 'complete', 'the first reply'))
ev = call('events')
assert {'turn_start', 'turn_end'} <= {e['kind'] for e in ev['events']} and ev['offset'] > 0
test_eq(call('events', offset=ev['offset'])['events'], [])


out = {}
threading.Thread(target=lambda: out.setdefault('r', a.approvals.request('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'})), daemon=True).start()
for _ in range(200):
    if (waiting := call('asks')): break
    time.sleep(.01)
test_eq(waiting[0]['tool'], 'edit_file')
assert call('answer', id=waiting[0]['id'], ok=True)
for _ in range(200):
    if 'r' in out: break
    time.sleep(.01)
assert out['r'], 'answered through the socket'
test_fail(lambda: call('fly'), exc=RuntimeError)
ctl.close(); a.close()

title: control
text:
Peers
Every terminal session listens on its own socket, so one session can reach another. peers_of(agent) finds the other live sessions under the same config folder. It asks each socket in <cfg>/runs/*/ and each ramabana-<session>.sock of a session in that folder for its status, and leaves out a socket that does not answer within PEER_WAIT seconds. The list puts the most recently active session first.
status names a session for a person, the way the --resume picker lists sessions: its title, else its first folder’s name, then its model and how long ago it was active, as in orgs · claude-opus-5-5 · 2m ago. peer_lines numbers the list, and find_peer takes a number from it, as the picker takes one, or a session id.
peer_tools(agent) gives the agent the same reach as two tools. peers() lists the sessions of every kind with their ids. tell(session, text, kind='note') posts a note to the inbox of that session, through ramabana.peers.tell, and rings its socket. With kind='ask' it asks for work and waits up to wait seconds for the reply. The sender of each message is self_frm(agent): this session’s key and all its folders.


source

peer_tools

    agent
):
peers(), tell() and work_together(): the agent’s tools for reaching the other live sessions.

note_peer

    agent, row, text, kind:str='note', wait:int=0
):
Post text as a note or ask from this session to the session row, and with wait return the reply to an ask; what tell says. LookupError when it is gone.




source

self_frm

    agent
):
This session as the sender of a peer message: its kind, session, key, name and all its folders.

    rows, key
):
The row key names: its number in rows, or its session id; None when neither matches.

    row
):
A peer’s name without how long ago it was active, which a label kept on screen would leave stale.




source

peers_of
def peers_of(
    agent, timeout:int=2
):
The other live sessions under agent’s config folder, most recently active first: each one’s status plus the path it listens on, and the registered Claude Code and Codex sessions.


Two more agents in the same config folder show the peer side. listener writes its events to EVENT_FILE, as a terminal session does, so a reply can be read from them. asker lists the sessions it can reach: the one that listens, by its folder’s name since it has no title yet, and never itself.

listener, _ = fake_agent(cfg=d, replies=['nothing much'])
asker, _ = fake_agent(cfg=d)
listener.events_to(listener.runs_dir/EVENT_FILE)
listening = Control(listener).start()
peers, tell, work_together = peer_tools(asker)
listed = peers()
assert listed.startswith('1  proj · fake · 0m ago  idle') and listener.session_id in listed and asker.session_id not in listed
listed

status also gives the kind, the inbox key, all the folders and the permission mode of the gate, so peers, tell and together can use it.

st = control_call(listening.path, 'status')
assert (st['kind'], st['key']) == ('ramabana', f'ramabana-{listener.session_id}') and st['folders'] and 'approve' in st
st['key']

A note to an idle session waits there for its next turn. An ask starts a turn there, and tell returns its reply. listener is in work together mode, so its user is not asked first.

from ramabana.peers import together_on


assert tell(1, 'are you there?', wait=0).startswith('told')
together_on(peers_dir(d), f'ramabana-{listener.session_id}')
replied = tell(1, 'what are you working on?', kind='ask', wait=10)
listening.close(); listener.close(); asker.close()
assert replied == 'nothing much'
replied

title: control
text:
Messages from peers
A peer posts each message to this session’s inbox, ramabana-<session>.inbox.jsonl in the peers folder, and then rings the socket with message. do_message takes the new messages and hands each one to receive on its own thread. A reply that a tell here waits for stays in the inbox for that tell.
receive handles each kind:

A note or a reply goes into the running turn as a steer. With no turn running, it waits in agent.peer_notes for the next prompt.
An ask runs at once when work together mode is on and the sender is a partner. It runs as do_prompt runs a prompt. When a limit (hops or budget) refuses it, no turn starts, and the sender gets one reply, refused: <why>.
Any other ask goes to the approval gate as peer ask. Only a person answers it: no approval mode, saved rule or /approve switch decides it, and it waits with no time limit. While it waits, it is also in ramabana-<session>.pending.jsonl, so a session that quits raises it again when it starts. A no goes back to the sender as the reply refused: <note>.

start adds _turn_end to agent.turn_ends, which the agent calls with each turn’s log row however the turn ended, and close takes it off. _turn_end finds every ask the turn read, in its prompt (a terminal can join queued asks into one turn) or steered in. Each ask gets the turn’s text back as the reply, with its changes: and proof: lines. A failed turn replies failed: <error>. A stopped turn replies failed: cancelled by the user to every ask still open, the queued ones it dropped too. The send budget never holds back a reply, so the asker always hears back. When the hop limit stops a reply, the asker gets failed: <why> in its inbox; an asker with no live session, such as the cli, gets the reply there too.
A thread looks at work together mode every TOGETHER_CHECK seconds. When a mode it saw on has ended, it saves the morning report with save_report. When the user types, user_back gives the report to show, or says that a mode ended while the user was away. Typing does not end the mode. Only /together off, ramabana together off, the work_together tool or the end time ends it. A waited reply to tell is a peer’s text, so it marks the turn as peer_turn.
In the example, a Claude Code session, claude-s1, sends to a session with an approval gate. A note to an idle session waits for the next turn. An ask with no work together mode raises peer ask at the gate, and a no goes back to the sender as refused: <note>.

from ramabana.peers import post, register
os.environ['RAMABANA_PEERS'] = str(d/'peers')
register(peers_dir(d), 'claude', 's1', ['/r/abhyasa'], os.getpid())
frm = {'kind': 'claude', 'session': 's1', 'key': 'claude-s1', 'name': 'abhyasa'}
b, bbe = fake_agent(cfg=d, replies=['ok'], approvals=agent.Approvals(tools={'edit_file'}, no_listener='wait'))
bc = Control(b).start()
def ring(kind, text):
    post(bc.d, bc.key, Envelope(kind, text, frm, bc.key))
    return control_call(bc.path, 'message', id='')
test_eq(ring('note', 'v2 is out'), {'took': 1})
for _ in range(100):
    if b.peer_notes or b.approvals.waiting: break
    time.sleep(.02)
test_eq([e.text for e in b.peer_notes], ['v2 is out'])
ring('ask', 'add a Card part')
for _ in range(100):
    if b.approvals.waiting: break
    time.sleep(.02)
ask = b.approvals.waiting[0]
test_eq((ask.tool, ask.args['text']), ('peer ask', 'add a Card part'))
b.approvals.answer(ask.id, False, 'not now')
for _ in range(100):
    if (got := take(bc.d, 'claude-s1')): break
    time.sleep(.02)
bc.close(); b.close(); del os.environ['RAMABANA_PEERS']
test_eq([(e.kind, e.text) for e in got], [('reply', 'refused: not now')])

title: peer_report
text:
In work together mode, sessions work while the user is away. This module reads the log of messages and tells the user what happened.
The table, the glossary and the action items that cannot wait come from code. The simple examples come from one summary model call. If that call fails, the report is still saved, with one line that says the examples are missing.
The module loads no model code until it needs it, so ramabana report stays light.

title: peer_report
text:
Threads
threads joins the log rows of one conversation. A thread starts with an ask. Its state tells the user how it ended:

replied: a reply with proof.
not proven: a reply with no proof.
refused: a reply that starts with refused:.
waiting: no reply yet.
stopped: a limit ended the thread.



source

threads
def threads(
    rows, known:NoneType=None
):
One dict per thread in log rows: id, asker, worker, ask, state, why, folders, changes, proof; known maps keys to sessions that rows do not show.


A small log with an ask that got a reply with proof, one that got none, and an ask with no reply. The last thread was stopped by the hop limit.

test_eq([t['state'] for t in threads(LOG)], ['replied', 'not proven', 'waiting', 'stopped'])

The state not proven is the one to watch: the worker says it is done and shows no proof.

test_eq(threads(LOG)[1]['proof'], [])
test_eq(threads(LOG)[0]['worker'], 'Ramabana')

Only a reply that starts with refused: is a refusal. An ask from before the report, or a stop with no ask, gets no made-up asker.

test_eq(threads([LOG[0], dict(LOG[1], text='refused: not my repo')])[0]['state'], 'refused')
test_eq(threads([LOG[0], dict(LOG[1], text="I can't reproduce it, but I fixed X")])[0]['state'], 'replied')
t, = threads([LOG[1]])
test_eq((t['asker'], t['worker'], t['ask']), ('c1', 'Ramabana', NO_ASK))
t, = threads([LOG[-1]])
test_eq((t['asker'], t['worker'], t['ask']), ('?', '', 'hop limit: 6 of 6 hops used'))

title: peer_report
text:
Checked changes
A worker lists the changes it made. checked_changes looks in git log of the worker’s folders since the mode started. An item that git does not show gets (not in git). Without folders, nothing can be checked, so the items stay as they are.


source

checked_changes
def checked_changes(
    t, since
):
The changes of thread t, each marked (not in git) when no commit or file of the worker’s repos since since matches it; no repo, no marks.


A temporary repo with one commit. The real commit and file pass; the others are marked.

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    run = lambda *a: subprocess.run(['git', '-C', d, '-c', 'user.name=t', '-c', 'user.email=t@t', *a], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
    run('init', '-q'); (Path(d)/'a.py').write_text('x'); run('add', '.'); run('commit', '-q', '-m', 'one')
    sha = run('rev-parse', 'HEAD')[:8]
    t = dict(folders=[d], changes=[sha, 'deadbeef1', 'a.py', 'gone.py'])
    test_eq(checked_changes(t, time.time() - 3600), [sha, 'deadbeef1 (not in git)', 'a.py', 'gone.py (not in git)'])
    test_eq(checked_changes(dict(folders=[], changes=['x.py']), 0), ['x.py'])
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d: test_eq(checked_changes(dict(folders=[d], changes=['x.py']), 0), ['x.py'])

The table
table makes one Markdown row per thread. A | in the text is escaped, and a long ask is cut short.

table

A Markdown table of the threads ts, one row each.



test_eq(table(threads(LOG)).splitlines()[0], '| Asked by | Done by | What | Changed | Proof | State |')
test_eq(len(table(threads(LOG)).splitlines()), 6)
assert '| Leela | Ramabana | Fix card |' in table(threads(LOG))

The glossary
The report uses a few terms that a new reader may not know. glossary gives the meaning of only the terms in a text.

glossary

    text

The lines of GLOSSARY for the terms that text uses.



g = glossary('One ask, one reply, one thread.')
test_eq(g.count('\n'), 2)
assert 'budget' not in g and '**thread**' in g

title: peer_report
text:
Actions and examples
A waiting ask, a not proven thread, a refusal and a stopped thread always need the user. derived_actions writes each one as “what to do: where”. The model adds more items and one plain sentence for each change.


source

summarise
def summarise(
    ts, agent:NoneType=None
):
The simple examples and the action list for threads ts, from one summary model call.




source

derived_actions
def derived_actions(
    ts
):
The action lines that the table alone shows: each one is what to do: where.


The action lines of the small log. No model is called here.

test_eq(derived_actions(threads(LOG)), ["- Ask for proof of 'Fix card': Ramabana", "- Get an answer to 'Wait': Ramabana", "- Restart 'Loop' (hop limit: 6 of 6 hops used): Ramabana"])

A stub agent shows how the model reply is split. Its oneshot is the only part of the agent that summarise uses.

class _Agent:
    def oneshot(self, prompt, sp, job): return 'EXAMPLES\nRamabana added tell.\nACTIONS\nRead the diff: cli.py'
test_eq(summarise(threads(LOG), _Agent()), ('- Ramabana added tell.', '- Read the diff: cli.py'))

title: peer_report
text:
The report
report joins the parts. The action list has the derived lines first, then the model’s own lines without repeats. If the summary fails, the report says why in place of the examples. With no thread, the model is not called.


source

report
def report(
    since, cfg:NoneType=None, agent:NoneType=None, summary:NoneType=None
):
The Markdown report of the log since time since; summary is summarise unless given.


A log in a temporary folder and a model that fails. The table, the actions and the glossary are still there, with the reason.

from unittest.mock import patch
from ramabana.peers import log


def _down(ts, agent=None): raise RuntimeError('down')
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d, patch.dict(os.environ, RAMABANA_PEERS=d):
    for r in LOG: log(d, r)
    out = report(0, summary=_down)
    assert out.startswith('# Night of ') and f'{MISSING}: the summary model failed: RuntimeError: down' in out
    assert "Restart 'Loop'" in out and '**proof**' in out

title: peer_report
text:
Saving it
save_report writes the report to reports/<date>-<HHMM>.md in the peers folder, named by since, so two modes on one date do not share a file. report_path gives that name, so a hook can find the file. It builds the file again when the log has newer rows, or when the saved file lacks the examples.


source

save_report
def save_report(
    since, cfg:NoneType=None, summary:NoneType=None
):
Write the report since since to the reports folder; a file with examples and newer than the whole log is kept.

title: tools
text:
A model can only write text. To read a file or run a command, it calls a tool. A tool is a Python function. The backend turns its name, docstring and typed parameters into a schema that the model sees. Ramabana’s tools come from shalya.
The tools act through a host. A host is the object that decides which folders are open (its roots), whether files may be written and which other services exist. Such services include a shell, a Python kernel, git and the web. Each service is a capability group. A host declares a group by inheriting the class that names it, such as CodeHost or WebHost. Host.provides lists the groups a host declares. Every host has the file group. The tools that need one capability group form a tool group. The shell group, for example, is run_shell, run_shell_bg, shell_output and shell_stop.
Shalya holds the host classes, the functions that build each tool group, the conventions tool results follow (err writes a failure that failed recognises), and the skills registry. This module re-exports all of them. Code that imports them from ramabana.tools keeps working. The alias sys.modules[__name__] = ramabana.tools, which Leela (the notebook editor) uses, keeps resolving. New code imports them from shalya.
What this module adds depends on parts of the agent that shalya does not know. A sub-agent needs a Backend to talk to and a Run to record it. draws_itself needs a ModelSpec. The sections below cover a host that refuses everything, the image tools, tools_for, which builds the tool list a turn gets, delegation to sub-agents, and attachments.
source

getattr
def __getattr__(
    name
):
Resolve the deprecated Shalya compatibility surface without mirroring it here.
The re-exported names are shalya’s own objects, not copies. A copy could drift into a second implementation. The cell below checks that every name in _all_ resolves and is the same object that shalya holds. Shalya’s own notebooks test what the objects do.
len(_all_), sorted(_all_)[:8]
import shalya.core, shalya.host, shalya.skills, shalya.tools
here = sys.modules[__name__] if False else __import__('ramabana.tools', fromlist=['x'])
missing, different = [], []
for n in _all_:
    if not hasattr(here, n): missing.append(n); continue
    src = next((m for m in (shalya.core, shalya.host, shalya.skills, shalya.tools) if hasattr(m, n.lstrip('_')) or hasattr(m, n)), None)
    if src is None: continue
    theirs = getattr(src, n, None) or getattr(src, n.lstrip('_'), None)
    if getattr(here, n) is not theirs: different.append(n)
test_eq(missing, [])
test_eq(different, [])
test_eq((_cmds, _edits, _apply_edits, _diff),
        (shalya.core.cmds, shalya.core.edits, shalya.core.apply_edits, shalya.core.diff_text))
WRITE_TOOLS names every tool with an effect: tools that change files, the repository, the kernel, the shell, the vault or a browser page. It comes from shalya unchanged.
sorted(WRITE_TOOLS - shalya.core.WRITE_TOOLS)
assert {'replace_text', 'run_shell', 'git_commit'} <= WRITE_TOOLS

Drawing
Shalya’s generate_image tool makes pictures. Some models can draw themselves when they are given the image tool. For any other model the prompt goes to a separate image model. Which case applies is a fact about the turn’s model, so shalya asks for it as a callable, and this module supplies the callable.

title: tools
text:
Assembling the tool list
tools_for decides which tools a host gets. It asks Host.provides for the capability groups and adds the tool group for each. A get_skills callable adds read_skill, and extra adds extension tools. drop removes groups by name, such as 'shell' or 'image'. optin adds groups that are off by default: exhash (the hash-addressed edit_file), research, author, legacy (tool names from older releases) and browser.
Shalya has a tools_for of its own. Use this one in Ramabana code, because it also builds the image group from the turn’s model through get_spec and on_media, which a host cannot know. The image group comes only when an image key is set and the host can write, since generate_image saves files. On a LocalHost without litesearch installed, search_code is left out.
small_tool marks an extension tool to keep in the small profile, the short catalog a local model or a small context window gets. ToolCatalog wraps a tool list once and answers questions about it: each tool’s group, which tools write, which have effects, and a read-only copy. ToolEntry is one row of it.

title: tools
text:
Sub-agents
A sub-agent is a separate conversation with a model, started to answer one question for the agent that asked. Handing a question over this way is delegation. Delegation saves context. It does not save time. A broad question can take twenty tool calls to answer. If the main agent made them itself, every result would stay in its conversation. Delegated, the same work costs the main conversation one question and one answer. The sub-agent’s conversation is thrown away when it finishes.
A sub-agent gets read-only tools unless the session allows it to write. NO_SUB lists the tools it never gets by default: the five delegation tools and the two watch tools (watch and cancel_watch). A watch would outlive the sub-agent’s task. A session that allows nesting passes its own block. The sub-agent may then delegate in turn. These constants set the limits:








Constant
Value
Meaning




SUB_MAX_STEPS
80
Steps a delegation gets when it names none.


SUB_STEP_CEILING
400
Most steps a delegation may ask for under auto, and the most a numeric session cap may be.


SUB_MIN_STEPS
20
Fewest steps a delegation runs with when it asks for fewer.


SUB_TIMEOUT
1800
Seconds before a delegation is stopped. 0 never stops it.


SUB_STEP_SECONDS
20
Under auto steps, a delegation with the default time limit gets its steps times this many seconds, when that is more than SUB_TIMEOUT.


SUB_TIMEOUT_CEILING
10800
Most seconds that step-based limit can reach.


SUB_UNFINISHED
300
A reply with no tool call and no state: line, shorter than this many characters, counts as a progress line and not a report.


SUB_SLOTS
4
Sub-agents working at once across one agent’s whole delegation tree.



A briefing is the standing instructions a model gets before the conversation starts, its system prompt. sub_briefing builds a sub-agent’s briefing from parts in this order: SUB_SP_HEAD, which every sub-agent gets, then SUB_READ_SP or SUB_WRITE_SP, then an optional note on how much of the answer the caller will read, then notes for the model’s family.


source

sub_briefing
def sub_briefing(
    writes:bool=False, answer_max:int=0, # characters the caller reads of the answer; 0 says nothing about it
    notes:str='', # the sub-agent model's family notes, after the rest
):
The sub-agent standing instructions: the shared half, the read-only or the write half, the answer budget and the family notes.




source

inbox_note
def inbox_note(
    key
):
The one tag the model may take as the user: it carries key, which no file or page knows.


SUB_SP is the read-only briefing with nothing added, and it is the default. A sub-agent allowed to write gets SUB_SP_HEAD followed by SUB_WRITE_SP.

SUB_MAX_STEPS, len(SUB_SP.split()), len(SUB_WRITE_SP.split())


assert SUB_MIN_STEPS < SUB_MAX_STEPS

read_only, from shalya, filters a tool list down to what an agent may have when it must not change anything. Write tools are dropped, or swapped for a safe version where the tool has one. block drops tools by name, and Ramabana passes NO_SUB. effects=False also drops the acting tools, those that do something without writing a file, such as inspect_python, shell_stop and generate_image. Shalya marks them with acts and lists them in ACTING_TOOLS. Use effects=False for a surface that may look and propose but never act.
A safe version can fix an argument. In the second cell below, read_url still fetches the page, but its remember parameter is gone and it no longer stores the page in the vault.

[t.__name__ for t in read_only(ts, block=NO_SUB)]


import inspect


test_eq(set(t.__name__ for t in read_only(ts, block=NO_SUB)) & WRITE_TOOLS, set())
shut = set(t.__name__ for t in read_only(ts, effects=False, block=NO_SUB))
test_eq(shut & (WRITE_TOOLS | NO_SUB | ACTING_TOOLS), set())
test_eq('search_code' in shut, True)

kept = []
class Page: text = 'page'
class Keeps(MemHost, WebHost):
    def web_search(self, query, n=20): return []
    def research(self, query): return ''
    def read_url(self, url, remember=True): kept.append(remember); return Page()
fetch = next(t for t in read_only(tools_for(Keeps({'/proj/a.py': 'x = 1\n'}))) if t.__name__ == 'read_url')
fetch(url='https://example.com')
test_eq(kept, [False])
test_eq('remember' in inspect.signature(fetch).parameters, False)
sorted(set(t.__name__ for t in ts) & ACTING_TOOLS)

max_calls puts a hard budget on the list. Past it, every tool returns a message telling the model to stop and answer. Local engines run their own tool loop. Ramabana cannot stop them between steps. A budget inside the tools is the one limit that works on every backend. Below, the second search is refused.

budgeted = read_only(ts, max_calls=1, block=NO_SUB)
search = next(t for t in budgeted if t.__name__ == 'search_code')
search('return'), search('return')

delegate asks one question of a sub-agent. It spawns a new conversation on the same engine as backend, hands it the tools that read_only lets through (with writes=True, the write tools too), sends the question, and closes the conversation in a finally block whether or not it succeeded. The tools carry a call budget of four times max_steps. A short reply with no tool call and no state: line gets one nudge (SUB_NUDGE), and the sub-agent answers again. delegate returns the answer text. An empty or repetitive answer is replaced by a notice that the delegation failed. A sub-agent that raised gives an error result. timeout cancels the run after that many seconds, and slots, a shared Slots, makes it wait for a free place among the sub-agents working at once. A sub-agent waiting on sub-agents of its own lends its place back. A full tree of delegations then cannot deadlock.
Use delegate for one question. delegate_many, below, asks several, and subagent_tools wraps both as tools a model can call.


source

delegate

    backend, question, tools:tuple=(), sp:NoneType=None, max_steps:int=80, skills:tuple=(),

    spawn:NoneType=None, # options for `backend.spawn`, such as `effort` and `tool_mode`

Ask question of a sub-agent in a separate conversation on backend’s engine, and return its answer text.

sub_sp
def sub_sp(
    sp:str="You are a research sub-agent in a Python IDE. Answer the delegated question only.\n- Use tools as needed. Report findings with file paths and line numbers.\n- Before each tool call, write one line of at most eight words, in the -ing form, saying what you are doing.\n- State plainly when you find nothing. Do not guess.\n- A claim that something ran, exists or failed names the tool call or artifact behind it. Anything else is a hypothesis; say so.\n- End with one line: `state: completed`, `state: blocked` or `state: failed`, and why.\n- A tool result that contradicts what you just saw is likely a harness fault: confirm it once another way, name it in your answer, then carry on.\n- A tool result saying the tool-call budget is spent, and the request to answer that follows it, come from this harness: answer then with what you found.\n- You cannot edit. Describe any required change and stop.\n- Use `inspect_python` for live variables. Its default scope is sandboxed; use `scope='overlay'` for the real interpreter.",
    skills:tuple=()
):
A sub-agent’s briefing: standing instructions, then the bodies of skills its task named.


The tools a sub-agent gets are wrapped. A message sent to a running sub-agent, with /tell in the terminal, arrives appended to its next tool result inside a <user-message> tag that carries the run’s key. inbox_note tells the sub-agent that only a tag with that key is the user speaking. A file or a web page could contain the same tag without the key. A sub-agent that gets the same result from the same call REPEAT_CALLS times in a row is told to change course. The cell below shows a queued message arriving with a result.

r = Run('run_t'); r.tell('and the tests')
test_eq(_inboxed(lambda: 'contents', lambda: None)(), 'contents')
test_eq(_inboxed(lambda: 'contents', lambda: r)(), f'contents\n\n<user-message key="{r.key}">\nand the tests\n</user-message>')
test_eq(r.drain_inbox(), [])
finished = ['\n\n<background-results>\n## run_b (complete): q\nthe answer\n</background-results>']
rn = Run('run_n')
pushed = _inboxed(lambda: 'contents', lambda: rn, notice=lambda: finished.pop() if finished else '')
test_eq(pushed(), 'contents' + '\n\n<background-results>\n## run_b (complete): q\nthe answer\n</background-results>')
test_eq(pushed(), 'contents')   # a finished answer arrives once

Each wrapped call also updates the run’s status (Run.on_call). The now pane, the side panel that lists live runs (see pane), shows what a sub-agent is doing from that status. Some backends, LiteRT for one, never pass on the text a model writes between calls. Their sub-agents get a status tool from status_tool to report one line. STATUS_NOTE in the briefing tells them to use it.

class _Quiet(FakeBackend):
    narrates = False
    def spawn(self, sp='', tools=(), **kw):
        self.sub = FakeBackend(self.spec, sp=sp, tools=tools, shared=True)
        self.sub._send = lambda msg, **kw: next(t for t in self.sub.tools if t.__name__ == 'status')(text='Reading the tests')
        return self.sub

qb, qr = _Quiet(), Run('run_quiet', 'child', 'q')
delegate(qb, 'q', tools=ts, run=qr)
test_eq(qr.status, 'Reading the tests')
assert STATUS_NOTE in qb.sub.sp

delegate_many
def delegate_many(
    backend, questions, tools:tuple=(), sp:NoneType=None, max_steps:int=80, n_workers:int=4, skills:tuple=(),
    writes:bool=False, approve:NoneType=None, parent:NoneType=None, images:tuple=(),
    block:frozenset=frozenset({'delegate_cancel', 'delegate_result', 'delegate_async', 'watch', 'cancel_watch', 'delegate_search', 'delegate_tell'}),
    timeout:int=0, slots:NoneType=None,
    spawn:NoneType=None, # `spawn` options for every question, or a list with one per question
):
Ask several questions of one sub-agent each, and return the answers in question order. backend, sp and spawn may be lists, one per question, and tools a callable from a backend’s spec to its tools; see lanes for what runs at once.




source

lanes
def lanes(
    backends, writes:bool=False
):
Question indices grouped into what runs one after another: every write in one lane, the questions on a local engine in one, each cloud question alone.


Here a fake backend answers a delegated question. The caller gets back only the answer text.

be = FakeBackend(replies=['the caller never sees this'])
delegate(be, 'which files import fastllm?', tools=ts)


from urai import ToolCallError


# a sub-agent whose tool call was cut off reports why in its answer
class _Cut(FakeBackend):
    def spawn(self, sp='', tools=(), **kw):
        s = super().spawn(sp, tools, **kw)
        def _send(msg, **kw): raise ToolCallError("openai/gpt-5.6's tool call was cut off at its 16384-token output limit")
        s._send = _send
        return s
out = delegate(_Cut(), 'edit the notebook', tools=ts)
assert 'tool call was cut off' in out and 'JSONDecodeError' not in out, out

The spawned conversation was separate. It held only the question and the answer, and delegate closed it before returning.

test_eq(len(be.spawned), 1)
be.spawned[0].hist

delegate_many asks several questions at once, one sub-agent each, and returns the answers in the order the questions were asked. It registers every child run with the parent before any starts. Cancelling the parent then reaches all of them. The last example on this page shows that. Questions to cloud models run in parallel, up to n_workers (default 4) at once. Questions run one at a time when sub-agents may write, and questions to local models run one at a time. An engine such as LiteRT holds one conversation at a time, and parallel runs would race for it.

delegate_many(be, ['what imports fastllm?', 'where is compaction triggered?'], tools=ts)

The delegation tools take a callable that returns a backend. Each call asks for the current session’s backend. After a /model switch the next sub-agent runs on the new model.
delegate_async starts a sub-agent in the background and returns at once. The turn can carry on while the sub-agent works. Background keeps track of those runs. start registers a run before its thread begins. A status call therefore always finds the id that start returned. At most mx runs reach a model at once (ASYNC_MAX, 4 by default) and the rest wait as pending. status, result and cancel answer for one run, and status with no id answers for all. The last keep answers are held. close, called when the session ends, cancels every run and refuses new work.
The examples hold two runs behind a Background with one place, cancel a run still waiting, close a Background, catch a run that raised, and show an answer dropped once newer ones push it out.


source

Background
def Background(
    mx:int=4, # how many reach a model at once
    keep:int=50, # answers held before the oldest is dropped
    on_done:NoneType=None, # called with `(run, answer)` when a run finishes
):
Delegations running behind the turn that asked for them, and the answers they leave.



bg = Background(mx=1)
gate, seen = threading.Event(), []

def slow(run):
    run.start()
    seen.append(run.id)
    gate.wait(5)
    return f'answered {run.question}'

a = bg.start(slow, Run('run_a', 'child', 'first'))
b = bg.start(slow, Run('run_b', 'child', 'second'))

named_skills
def named_skills(
    get_skills, names
):
The skills a delegated task named, and a note about any name that matched nothing.


A skill is a markdown document of instructions that an agent reads when the work calls for it, and a delegated task can name the skills its sub-agent needs. named_skills finds them by name. When a name matches nothing, it returns a note that lists the skills that do exist. It does not raise. The model can then correct the name. sub_sp appends the full text of the found skills to the sub-agent’s briefing.

def parse_plan_items(
    items

The item texts from newline text, a JSON list, or a Python list.


parse_plan_items turns a list a model sent into a list of strings. Models send a list as JSON text, as one item per line (with or without - or * bullets), or as a real list. The function accepts all three. The agent’s set_plan tool reads its todo items through it.
The next cell returns to skills. It asks named_skills for one skill that exists and one that does not. It then checks what sub_sp adds to the briefing.

skills = [Skill('house-style', 'md', 'How code is written here.', _text='Dense lines.'),

A pyskill is a skill shipped as a Python module whose docstring is the skill text. Listing skills needs each one’s description, and shalya imports the module to read it. Some of those imports are slow: vishalakshi.skill and kosha.skill pull in litesearch and model2vec, about 0.7 seconds before the first prompt. mod_doc reads a module’s docstring from its source file without importing anything, and this cell swaps shalya’s pyskill loader for one that uses it. The module is imported only when the skill’s full text is read.

subagent_tools builds the five tools a model uses to delegate. delegate_search asks one or more questions and waits for the answers. delegate_async starts one question in the background and returns a run id. delegate_result collects a background answer, or with no id lists every background run, delegate_cancel stops one, and delegate_tell sends a running one a message. Most arguments are callables that subagent_tools reads on each call. The backend, the step budget, the time limit and the write setting follow the session as they change. An answer longer than the tool-result limit is cut. The whole text is saved to a file, and the cut answer names the path.

subs = {t.__name__: t for t in subagent_tools(lambda: be, lambda: ts)}
delegate_search = subs['delegate_search']
list(subs)

With no model to delegate to, the tools return a message saying so instead of raising into the turn. With a model, several questions come back with one heading each.

delegate_tell sends a message to a sub-agent that is still running, in the background or in the calling turn’s tree. The sub-agent reads it attached to its next tool result, and an unknown or finished run is refused with an error.

A sub-agent sees pictures only when they come with its first message. images names them by path inside the open folders, and read_pictures reads them, refusing any path outside the folders or any file that is not a picture. The question then ends with a note naming the pictures in order, so the sub-agent knows which is which. A model that cannot take images gets an error rather than a question without its pictures, and so does a session with no way to read them. A cloud_model that names no reachable model gets an error saying to leave it empty and use the sub-agent model.

for _ in range(300):

    time.sleep(.02)
test_eq(pic_be.spawned[-1].sent[0][0], png)

assert failed(blind['delegate_search'](['q'], images=['refs/rama.png']))
missing = pt['delegate_search'](['q'], cloud_model='gpt-6-typo')
assert 'gpt-6-typo' in missing and 'leave `model` empty' in missing, missing
assert 'images' in get_schema(pt['delegate_search'])['input_schema']['properties']

model and effort name a model and an effort level for every question, or give a list with one per question. A list of another length is refused before any sub-agent runs. get_sub(model, effort) turns each pair into a backend, the options spawn takes and a note for the answer. It runs in the caller’s thread, before any sub-agent starts. A pair named twice is resolved once. A question whose model cannot run gets the error as its answer. The other questions still run. cloud_model is still taken as model and is not in the schema. delegate_many runs the questions in lanes: every write in one lane, the questions on a local engine in one, and each cloud question in its own. Sub-agents on different cloud models therefore answer at once.
picture_mime recognises a PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF by its first bytes, whatever the file is called. A fake.png that holds text is therefore refused below. The limits are the terminal’s: at most MAX_ATTACH (8) pictures, each at most MAX_MEDIA (20 MB). Every question’s sub-agent receives every picture. Pictures times questions may not exceed MAX_ATTACH.
A read-only sub-agent’s generate_image refuses a path, because saving there would be a write. With path empty, it saves under media/. PATH_WRITES, path_write and write_targets tell the approval gate about this case. A call to a tool in PATH_WRITES counts as a write when it names a path. write_targets lists the files any call will write.

for name, body in (('Makefile', 'all:\n'), ('.env', 'K=1\n'), ('fake.png', 'text'), ('logo.svg', '<svg xmlns="x"/>')):
    (pic_root/name).write_text(body); assert 'not a picture' in read_pictures(pic_host, [name])[1], name
test_eq(read_pictures(pic_host, ['refs/rama.png'])[0], [png])
assert 'at most' in read_pictures(pic_host, ['refs/rama.png'] * (MAX_ATTACH + 1))[1]
with open(pic_root/'big.png', 'wb') as f: f.write(png); f.truncate(MAX_MEDIA + 1)
assert 'over' in read_pictures(pic_host, ['big.png'])[1]
too_many = pt['delegate_search'](['q%d' % i for i in range(MAX_ATTACH + 1)], images=['refs/rama.png'])
assert 'at most' in too_many, too_many
def generate_image(prompt: str, path: str = '') -> str: return f'drew {path or "media"}'
drawn = FakeBackend()
delegate(drawn, 'draw', tools=[generate_image])
sub_draw = {t.__name__: t for t in drawn.spawned[-1].tools}['generate_image']
assert failed(sub_draw('x', path='main.py')) and 'read-only' in sub_draw('x', path='main.py')
test_eq(sub_draw('x'), 'drew media')
delegate(drawn, 'draw', tools=[generate_image], writes=True)
test_eq({t.__name__: t for t in drawn.spawned[-1].tools}['generate_image']('x', path='a.png'), 'drew a.png')

delegate_many registers every child run before any work starts. Cancelling the parent stops the child that is running, and the children still queued never spawn. The fake backend below blocks on its first question until it is cancelled.

class _Sub:
    max_steps = 0
    def __init__(self, owner): self.owner, self.release = owner, threading.Event()
    def send(self, question, run=None):
        self.owner.started.append(question); self.release.wait(); return 'late'
    def cancel(self): self.owner.cancelled += 1; self.release.set(); return True
    def close(self): pass

class _ParentBackend:
    def __init__(self):
        self.spec = AttrDict(name='fake-child', local=False)
        self.started, self.spawned, self.cancelled = [], 0, 0
    def spawn(self, **kw): self.spawned += 1; return _Sub(self)

backend, parent, box = _ParentBackend(), Run('run_parent', grace=.03), []
parent.start()
t = threading.Thread(target=lambda: box.extend(delegate_many(backend, ['a', 'b', 'c'], n_workers=1, parent=parent)), daemon=True)
t.start()
while not backend.started: time.sleep(.001)
test_eq(len(parent.children), 3)
parent.cancel(); t.join(.2)
test_eq((backend.spawned, backend.cancelled), (1, 1))
test_eq(len(box), 3)
assert all((isinstance(x, dict) and x['state'] in ('cancelled', 'detached'))
           or (isinstance(x, str) and 'cancelled' in x) for x in box)

title: tools
History core
pane
text:
While a turn runs, the chat shows the streaming answer and one line per tool call. It does not show how many tool calls the turn has made, how far the plan has got, what each sub-agent is doing, or which files have changed. The now pane shows these in a narrow column beside the chat. It shows the present: what runs now, what this turn has done, and the files the session has written.
The pane is a separate program, ramabana-pane, that runs in a tmux split. tmux is a terminal multiplexer. It divides one terminal window into panes, and each pane runs its own program. The session and the pane share information through a file. Up to five times a second the session writes a snapshot to now.json in the session’s run folder. The pane reads that file and draws it. This page covers the snapshot, the layout of a snapshot as rows of text, and the viewer that draws the rows and answers keys and clicks.

title: pane
text:
The snapshot
now_snapshot(agent) returns a dict that json.dumps can write. Its keys are:

at, the time of the snapshot, and busy, whether a turn is running.
root, the foreground turn: its tool-call count (steps), how long it has run, its state, the call it is waiting on (current), and its status, the last line the model wrote before calling a tool.
plan, the agent’s checklist, with each item’s text and status.
subs, one row per sub-agent. A sub-agent is a second agent that the turn starts to do part of the work. The list holds every delegation this turn started. It also holds every background delegation that is running or has finished since the turn began. A row has the sub-agent’s status, its tool-call count (steps), its last CALLS_KEPT calls with results cut to OUT_CHARS characters, and, once it has finished, its answer cut to ANSWER_CHARS characters. A finished sub-agent stays listed until the next turn starts.
files, every file written this session, the turns before this one included: path, lines added and removed against the file’s text at its first write, and the diff cut to DIFF_LINES lines. A file whose text is back to what it was, for example after /rewind, is not listed. A notebook is diffed as its cell sources.
notes, what the model wrote before each of this turn’s calls, in full and with a timestamp.
background, the work running behind the turn: background delegations, commands started with run_shell_bg, and folder watches. Each row has a kind, an id, a label, a state, the seconds it has been running (elapsed) and a detail text. A finished shell command and a folder watch have elapsed set to None.

The session writes a snapshot up to five times a second (PANE_EVERY in ramabana.cli, 0.2 seconds). A snapshot must be cheap to take when nothing has changed. The list of files is computed again only after a call finishes. The host is asked for the state of a running background shell command at most once every SHELL_EVERY seconds. It is never asked again once the command has ended.








Constant
Value
Limit




CALLS_KEPT
8
Latest calls kept for each sub-agent


OUT_CHARS
200
Characters kept of each call’s result


ANSWER_CHARS
500
Characters kept of a finished sub-agent’s answer


DIFF_LINES
80
Lines kept of each file’s diff


SHELL_EVERY
1.0
Seconds between state requests for a running background shell


SHELL_LINES
20
Output lines kept for a background shell



Each recorded call (an Act) names the run whose model made it. The steps value of a sub-agent is its tool-call count, the number of calls with its run id. The steps value of the main turn is its tool-call count, the number of calls whose parent_action_id does not name another call in the activity log. A sub-agent’s calls name the delegate call that started it. They never count toward the main turn’s tool-call count.

The rows now_snapshot carries under background: sub-agents started in the background, shells and folder watches.


The example builds an agent with fake_agent and a scripted model, Root. The model reads a file, then asks a sub-agent one question with delegate_search. The sub-agent reads the same file before it answers. The activity log’s on_change hook takes a snapshot when the sub-agent’s read starts. At that moment the pane shows both agents working. The main turn has taken two steps, and the one sub-agent is running with one step:

from ramabana.runtime import current_run
from ramabana.testing import ScriptedBackend, Step, fake_agent

READ = ('view_file', {'path': '/proj/a.py'})
a, _ = fake_agent()
seen = []
a.activity.on_change = lambda act: seen.append(now_snapshot(a)) if not act.done and current_run().kind != 'root' else None
class Root(ScriptedBackend):
    def spawn(self, sp='', tools=(), **kw):
        return ScriptedBackend(self.spec, steps=[Step(tool=READ), Step('a() is defined')], token_delay=0, tools=tools)
be = Root(steps=[Step(tool=READ), Step(tool=('delegate_search', {'questions': ['what does a.py define?']})), Step('done')],
          token_delay=0, tools=a.tools, sp=a.system_prompt())
a._be = a._be_or_none = lambda job='turn': be
list(a.stream('go'))
mid = seen[0]
test_eq((mid['busy'], mid['root']['steps'], [(s['state'], s['steps']) for s in mid['subs']]), (True, 2, [('running', 1)]))
mid

Once the turn ends, the sub-agent stays listed as completed. The next turn clears it:

test_eq([s['state'] for s in now_snapshot(a)['subs']], ['completed'])
be.steps = [Step('ok')]
list(a.stream('again'))
test_eq(now_snapshot(a)['subs'], [])

The plan and the files the session wrote are part of the snapshot too, each file with its diff. Here the example sets a two-item plan and changes a.py by hand:

a.plan.set('ship', ['read a.py', 'fix it']); a.plan.update(a.plan.todos[0].id, status='active')
a.before['/proj/a.py'] = 'def a(): pass\n'; a.host.files['/proj/a.py'] = 'def a(): return 1\n'
snap = now_snapshot(a)
test_eq(snap['plan'], [{'text': 'read a.py', 'status': 'active'}, {'text': 'fix it', 'status': 'pending'}])
test_eq([(f['path'], f['added'], f['removed']) for f in snap['files']], [('a.py', 1, 1)])
print(snap['files'][0]['diff'])

write_snapshot writes the snapshot to a file and read_snapshot reads it back. The writer writes a temporary file and renames it into place. The pane never reads half a file. The reader returns None when the file is missing or does not hold valid JSON. The pane then keeps showing what it had. The example checks both cases and checks that the temporary file is gone afterwards:

title: pane
text:
Drawing it
board(snap, width) lays a snapshot out as rows for a pane width cells wide, one row per screen line. Each row is a (key, Text) pair, where Text is a rich styled string. Lines longer than the width are cut, not wrapped. Use board to get the rows, as the viewer does to find the row under a click. Use render to get something to print. It returns the same rows as one rich renderable.
From the top, the board shows:

A header with main, its step number, its clock and its status line. The header leaves out the call the main agent is waiting on, because the chat shows it. An idle agent’s header reads idle with the step count of the last turn.
The plan as a checklist, with the active item highlighted.
The sub-agents. The first row is main, with the text talk to the main agent. Then comes one row for each sub-agent: id, status line (or its question when it has none), clock, and a mark: ▶ running, ✓ completed, ✗ stopped or failed. An open row is marked ▾ in place of ▸. It adds the question, each recent call with its result, and the answer once there is one. An arrow marks the row that the terminal is aimed at.
The files the session wrote, each with its lines added and removed. An open row shows the diff, drawn by hl.diff_rich with the code coloured for the file’s language and the added and removed lines tinted.
The background work: kind, label, state and clock. A row opens to a shell command’s last SHELL_LINES lines of output, a watch’s pattern and last review, or a background sub-agent’s detail.
The notes, newest first, for reading back what the model said along the way. Each is a ▸ row with its time and first line, and opens to the whole note wrapped to the pane. The newest note starts open.

Empty sections are left out. A row that can open or be picked carries a key: ('main', 'main'), ('sub', id), ('file', path), ('bg', id) or ('note', at). The caller passes the keys of the open rows in open. A row stays open when the next snapshot arrives. A running clock adds the time since the snapshot was written. A long call does not look frozen between writes. The colours come from the snapshot: the terminal session writes its active palette as palette and its name as theme, so the board draws in the same colours as the main view, and a diff’s code in the matching HL_THEMES style. ramabana.cli imports this module, so this module cannot look the palette up in cli.THEMES, and the snapshot carries the colours themselves. PALETTE is the default github-dark palette, for a snapshot written without one.

render

    snap, width:int=40, now:NoneType=None, open:tuple=()
):
The pane for snap as a rich renderable, width cells wide, with the rows keyed in open opened.

    snap, width:int=40, now:NoneType=None, open:tuple=(), err:str=''

The pane for snap as (key, row) pairs, one per screen line, in the snapshot’s palette; a row with a key opens and closes.

palette_of

    snap
):
The palette snap was written with, over PALETTE for any colour it lacks.


A snapshot of a busy turn, written five seconds before now, with every row closed. The turn’s clock reads 47s: 42 seconds plus the five since the write:

call = lambda line, ok=True, done=True, out='': {'line': line, 'ok': ok, 'done': done, 'out': out}
now = time.time()
busy = {'at': now - 5, 'busy': True,
        'root': {'turn_elapsed': 42, 'steps': 7, 'state': 'running', 'status': 'Checking the pane tests', 'current': 'Run shell: pytest'},
        'plan': [{'text': 'Read the viewer', 'status': 'done'}, {'text': 'Rewrite render', 'status': 'active'},
                 {'text': 'Wire the CLI', 'status': 'pending'}, {'text': 'Poll the file', 'status': 'cancelled'}],
        'subs': [{'id': 'run_aaa', 'question': 'which files import fastllm?', 'elapsed': 12, 'state': 'running', 'steps': 2,
                  'status': 'Searching for imports', 'current': 'Search code: fastllm',
                  'calls': [call('Search code: import fastllm', out='agent.py:12: import fastllm'), call('Search code: fastllm', None, False)],
                  'answer': ''},
                 {'id': 'run_bbb', 'question': 'is the pane tested?', 'elapsed': 8, 'state': 'completed', 'steps': 1, 'status': '',
                  'current': '', 'calls': [call('Read tests/test_pane.py')], 'answer': 'Yes, in tests/test_pane.py.'}],
        'files': [{'path': 'ramabana/pane.py', 'added': 1, 'removed': 1, 'diff': '@@ -1 +1 @@\n-from rich.live import Live\n+from teleprint.keys import Parser'}],
        'background': [{'kind': 'shell', 'id': 'cmd_1234abcd', 'label': 'pytest -x tests', 'state': 'running', 'elapsed': 30}]}
def show(snap, open=()):
    con = Console(record=True, width=40, color_system=None)
    con.print(render(snap, 40, now=now, open=open))
    return con.export_text()
out = show(busy)
assert '47s' in out and 'Run shell' not in out and '▸ run_aaa' in out and 'import fastllm' not in out
assert all(len(l) <= 40 for l in out.splitlines())
print(out)

Passing the keys of the running sub-agent and the file in open shows the sub-agent’s calls and the diff:

out = show(busy, {('sub', 'run_aaa'), ('file', 'ramabana/pane.py')})
assert 'Search code: import fastllm' in out and '+from teleprint.keys import Parser' in out
print(out)

In an open file the diff is drawn by hl.diff_rich in the pane’s palette. The code in each hunk is coloured by the file’s language, and added and removed lines get a tinted background. The cell checks that an added line carries more than two styles. That check shows the code is highlighted and not drawn in one colour:

py = {**busy, 'files': [{'path': 'a.py', 'added': 1, 'removed': 1, 'diff': diff_text('x = 1\n', 'def f(): return 2\n', 'a.py')}]}
rows = [t for _, t in board(py, 40, now=now, open={('file', 'a.py')})]
added = next(t for t in rows if 'def f' in t.plain)
test_eq(added.plain, '  +def f(): return 2')
assert len({str(s.style) for s in added.spans}) > 2, 'the code is highlighted, not one colour'
added

title: pane
text:
The viewer
Viewer(path, tty) is the program that runs in the pane. It reads the snapshot at path and draws the board on tty. A tty is any object with read(timeout), write, size and restore, as teleprint’s RealTty has. PaneTty is RealTty with a read that returns None at the end of input, so the viewer can tell that its terminal has gone.
The viewer switches the terminal to the alternate screen and asks the terminal to report mouse clicks. The alternate screen is a separate screen for full-screen programs. The shell’s scrollback returns unchanged when the program exits. Each tick waits up to every seconds for input and acts on it. The controls are:

A click on a row picks it, and the mouse wheel scrolls. Picking the main row aims the terminal at the main agent: the viewer writes main to the talk_mark file beside the snapshot, and the CLI reads and removes the file, as /talk main would. Picking a sub-agent row leaves the terminal aimed where it was and opens that sub-agent’s transcript pane, which takes the lines typed to it. Picking a sub-agent, file, background or note row also opens or closes it.
j and k, or the arrow keys, move the cursor over the rows that open. Past the first or last such row they scroll, so a board taller than the pane can be read to its end.
Page up and page down scroll by a page, and g and G jump to the top and the bottom.
Enter picks the row under the cursor, as a click does. Space opens or closes that row and does not aim the terminal.
p on a background shell command opens a tmux pane below the viewer that follows the command’s log with less -R +F. q in that pane closes it.
q or ctrl+c quits.

The last line of the pane is always HINT. The main keys stay on screen however far the board scrolls. Every line is filled to the pane’s edge on the palette’s bg0, and the cursor row on its bg2.
Picking a running sub-agent that has a log opens a transcript pane. That pane is a tmux split left of the chat pane (the snapshot’s chat_pane) that follows the log in the board’s palette, as described under transcript panes below. The viewer keeps at most one transcript pane. Picking another sub-agent reuses it. Picking main closes it. The viewer closes it PANE_LINGER seconds (3.0) after the sub-agent ends or leaves the board, unless the snapshot’s close_done is false. The viewer never closes a pane that it did not open.
The viewer reads the snapshot again only when its file has changed. It lays out the board on every tick and writes only the lines that differ from what is on screen. A clock that moves once a second rewrites one line a second. A board that is not changing writes nothing. When the terminal changes size, the viewer clears it and draws everything again.
A failed frame does not stop the viewer. If drawing fails, the viewer keeps the last good snapshot and shows the error as a row until a good snapshot arrives. However the viewer exits, it restores the terminal’s normal screen and modes. When the user quits, the viewer leaves a file named by quit_mark beside the snapshot (now.closed). The terminal session checks for that file. It leaves a pane that the user closed closed, and it can tell such a pane from one that crashed. A hangup (tmux closing the pane), SIGTERM and the end of input count as quitting too.


source

Viewer
def Viewer(
    path, tty, tmux:function=_tmux
):
The board for the snapshot at path, drawn on tty: the last good snapshot, the open rows, the cursor and the scroll.

PaneTty

RealTty whose read returns None at the end of input, where RealTty.read would spin.




source

talk_mark

    path
):
The file a viewer writes the run id (or main) in when the user picks who to talk to; the CLI reads and removes it.




source

quit_mark
